text:
A federal judge on Nov. 2 determined that Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers repeatedly violated an existing court order restricting warrantless immigration arrests in Oregon and expanded it, requiring the federal administration to provide new documentation to show it is complying with the order.

In a sharply worded opinion that opens with a quote from Tim Snyder's "On Tyranny," which says that to abandon facts is to abandon freedom, U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai said ICE officials in Oregon continued making warrantless arrests without first making an individualized assessment of whether a person was likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.

Kasubhai also determined an ICE deportation officer intentionally fabricated details in an official arrest report to make an arrest appear lawful.

“The judge found that ICE has been making warrantless arrests that don’t comply with the law or his order. Now ICE has to turn over evidence and footage for every arrest its agents make in the state,” said Jordan Cunnings, legal director at Innovation Law Lab. “The people who have been unlawfully taken from their families, pulled out of their cars on their way to work, or had their windows smashed deserve to know ICE is being held accountable.”

The ruling expands the documentation ICE must provide to attorneys representing immigrants in Oregon, requiring the agency to disclose records for all civil immigration arrests, regardless of whether ICE characterizes an arrest as warrant-based.

"What they claim to be warrant-based arrests in this record are simply not. And no amount of insistence or table-pounding will make them so. Defendants, through their own conduct, have lost trust," Kasubhai wrote. "Both warrant-based and warrantless arrests documents are now subject to this preliminary injunction, because Plaintiffs have shown that many of Defendants' warrant-based arrests are in fact warrantless."

Opinion related to lawsuit against warrantless immigration arrests

The order follows a two-day evidentiary hearing in Portland in September on a motion brought by lawyers for Innovation Law Lab, who claimed the federal government is "routinely, openly and brazenly" violating a preliminary injunction prohibiting warrantless immigration arrests in the state.

The organization sued the Trump administration after Operation Black Rose began, a monthslong federal immigration enforcement campaign conducted by the Department of Homeland Security that started in late September 2025 and resulted in more than 1,500 arrests statewide.

On Feb. 4, Kasubhai granted a preliminary injunction largely barring ICE from conducting warrantless arrests.

The government has "not halted their illegal warrantless arrest policy and practice," wrote lawyers with Innovation Law Lab in a motion filed Sept. 4. "In fact, the Defendants have doubled down on their illegal policy or practice by issuing instructions to their agents that blatantly violate the Court's injunction with respect to the subclass."

Four immigrants testified during the hearing and described being boxed in by vehicles, handcuffed, searched, and transported before federal agents even confirmed who they were.

Officer admitted to inaccurate report under oath, troubling Oregon judge

Kasubhai was particularly troubled, he said, about the arrests involving an ICE officer identified only as J.G.

The government called the officer as a witness during the trial, who said he currently works out of the Medford office and has been with ICE for 11 months. According to his testimony, he is a former Grants Pass police officer and former officer with the Department of Veterans' Affairs.

J.G. testified about being physically present in two encounters involving men identified as HDGH and CJVM.

CJVM, a Medford McDonald's employee, filed a declaration saying two vans boxed him in around 4:05 a.m. on June 13 as he arrived for work.

CJVM, who said he no longer works for the restaurant, remembered five men and one woman surrounding his vehicle. He said he reached over to the passenger seat to grab his cellphone to record as officers began shouting. He estimated 30 seconds passed before agents broke the driver-side window.

CJVM said agents forcibly grabbed his arm and handcuffed him. He was released with an apology after agents discovered he had an active asylum application and was complying with release terms.

HDGH, a 22-year-old who has lived in Medford since 2021, spoke about being arrested alongside a friend, MTM, after they were followed by ICE officers for 30 minutes from a Walmart parking lot to Emigrant Lake on July 26.

The deportation officer testified that officers that morning were running license plates of cars in the Medford Walmart lot at random to find cars whose owners were unlawfully present in the country. They discovered the registered owner of the car HDGH was reportedly in the country unlawfully.

HDGH said agents handcuffed both men and identified them only after they were taken to the Medford ICE office.

In the arrest of HDGH, J.G testified that officers followed the vehicle to Emigrant Lake because ICE has instituted a policy barring vehicle stops. That policy came in the wake of two fatal ICE shootings in Maine and Houston.

In court, J.G. acknowledged that the ICE report known as an I-213 he authored about HDGH's arrest described a different sequence of events than what actually occurred, claiming officers had identified HDGH before approaching the vehicle and obtained an arrest warrant before placing him in handcuffs.

"The I-213 for H-D-G-H-’s arrest describes a series of events that Officer J.G. now admits never occurred," Kasubhai said.

J.G. acknowledged he wrote the report as if he "already knew who the person was, but I did not" on the stand and said he "did not even know" HDGH existed.

Kasubhai said "it defies logic" that "consequential errors" in the I-213 forms, like those made in HDGH's arrest, are "merely a 'mistake'" and cited the deportation officer's more than decade of law enforcement experience.

"Officer J.G. is well-versed in law enforcement practices. This Court finds that he did not make a mistake in the I-213. He lied in an official record to facilitate the impression he was conducting a lawful warrant-based arrest. The I-213 form that Officer J.G. crafted for H-D-G-H- demonstrates intentional, coordinated falsification that would in all likelihood never have been uncovered but for this evidentiary hearing," Kasubhai said.

Two other arrests improper, Oregon judge finds

Kasubhai said JCCV's arrest was also improperly classified and lacked a valid warrant. He again referenced a copy of his I-213 form submitted to the court at the evidentiary hearing where agents incorrectly described JCCV's vehicle. The form listed a Toyota Camry, but he was driving a 2010 Toyota Corolla and had the wrong license plate. It also misstated the arrest location as Napa, California, rather than Hood River.

Kasubhai also rejected the government's explanation for why it shifted from characterizing JCCV's arrest as warrantless to warrant-based. The government was maintaining that a three-year-old warrant issued in April 2023 provided a legal basis for JCCV's rearrest.

The 2023 warrant states that an ICE officer served it on JCCV in Texas. JCCV testified about being detained by ICE for eight days that year. ICE's lawyers argued that the same warrant allowed officers to rearrest JCCV in 2025. Kasubhai said defendants had ignored a "key detail": an attorney general must first revoke a bond or parole to do so.

Kasubhai wrote that no evidence of revocation was presented and noted that lawyers instead argued that the I-213 form for JCCV indicated "there was an intention to revoke the bond or parole.”

"Intention does not constitute revocation, and the Court admonishes counsel that they are expected to make good faith arguments as officers of the court. Real people’s lives and liberties are at stake and they should remember that. Evidentiary hearings are not first-year law school examinations where one can score points with a scattershot strategy," Kasubhai added.

He found a third arrest report also "unreliable." The arrest involved a man identified as HFMJ, a Eugene resident.

HFMJ said he works as a landscaper to support three children. He and his roommate were traveling to work on July 3 when ICE vehicles began following their car. HFMJ said agents arrested his coworker and then approached the car. HFMJ said agents then arrested him without showing him any paperwork.

Kasubhai said the arrest report narrative "differs significantly" from HFMJ's testimony. Kasubhai noted narratives for HFMJ and his arrested coworker "are nearly identical." Kasubhai said he was "skeptical" that both men received identical information so promptly, given HFMJ's testimony that he never even gave officers his name before being arrested.

New order expands documentation required around Oregon arrests

Kasubhai referred to evidentiary hearings as "essential tools to ensure that a rigorous record of something closer to the truth is preserved, and to hold liars to account," and added that the federal government has tried to circumvent compliance with the law and preliminary injunctions.

In his order, Kasubhai said both warrant-based and warrantless arrest documents are now subject to his preliminary injunction. He also ordered the government to disclose documents and body-worn camera footage related to all civil immigration arrests in the state.

I-213s alone, he explained, do not accurately reflect the facts of warrantless arrests and said Innovation Law Lab presented "copious evidence" of the federal government's violations in Oregon.

"There is no telling how many other agents in Oregon engaged in similar misconduct, which calls into question the veracity of all I-213 forms completed by ICE officers in Oregon," reads part of Kasubhai's order and opinion. "Based solely on the evidence presented in this case, Defendants have clearly violated the Court's preliminary injunction order."

Under Kasubhai's new order, ICE must retransmit the injunction to relevant officers, employees, and contractors every 30 days. He also ordered the agency to provide previously disclosed records without redactions.

The agency must also provide body camera footage for arrests made on or after Sept. 1.

Kasubhai rejected the government's argument that modifying the order would improperly interfere with immigration enforcement.

He said other district courts have also found it necessary to enforce or modify prior orders against ICE officials in light of repeated violations.

"The presumption of regularity directs the courts to assume, unless clear evidence indicates differently, that government officials have properly discharged their duties, acted in good faith and followed required procedures. This presumption no longer holds for Defendants," Kasubhai said. "The evidence in this case proves as much. Defendants are held to the same expectation as any other litigant before this Court. One must earn credibility by acting with integrity."

This story may be updated.

text:
Standing at a podium to tout the Trump administration’s “fraud task force” achievements on Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told a reporter that it would be a “waste of our time” to investigate ICE’s recent purchase of a prison from a private company for hundreds of millions of dollars over a prior asking price.

Bessent responded sternly when a reporter suggested at a press conference in Minnesota on Friday that the Trump administration look into a recent, questionable $496 million purchase of a prison by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

“If the administration has declared war on waste and fraud, could you explain the 420 million overpayment for a prison in Appleton, Minnesota, when the company offered it to the state of Minnesota for 75 million?” a reporter asked the treasury secretary.

“I don’t know anything about that. What we are here to do is prosecute criminal fraud and any question like that that deflects away from it, I think, is a waste of our time,” Bessent responded.

The reporter was referring to an investigation by local outlet KARE 11 last week that found that, in August, ICE spent nearly half a billion dollars for a vacant prison in Appleton, Minnesota, being sold by major private prison company and ICE contractor CoreCivic. Communications obtained by KARE 11, however, showed that CoreCivic had offered to sell the facility to the state of Minnesota for $75 million in May 2025, which the state declined.

This means that the administration may have overpaid $420 million for the facility. CoreCivic, a major Trump donor, is one of the top contractors tapped by the Trump administration in its mass deportation campaign. The company swiftly announced the new ICE contract for CoreCivic to run the prison for an expected profit of $75 million a year.

The Department of Homeland Security responded to the investigation by saying that the purchase price was set through a different process than the company’s offer to Minnesota.

“The 1,600-bed site gives ICE immediate capacity to detain and remove those who have no legal right to remain, protecting American communities and restoring the integrity of our borders without waiting years for new construction,” the agency said. CoreCivic’s offer to Minnesota “was not based on replacement-cost analysis and did not reflect the intervening rise in construction costs or federal operational standards,” it added.

Bessent’s dismissal of the question is ironic considering the press conference that took place immediately beforehand. The secretary and other officials like FBI Director Kash Patel announced in a lengthy presser that the administration is taking even further action to insert the federal government in the state’s investigation of the welfare fraud scheme, as part of its supposed “war on fraud.” For over a year, the administration has used this scheme to justify a wide range of actions against Minnesota and its Democratic leaders, including Operation Metro Surge and President Donald Trump’s open attacks on Somali immigrants.

Standing in front of a sign that read, “the vice president’s fraud task force,” the officials made lofty statements about the administration’s supposed work on the issue.

“President Trump has made clear that the war on fraud is not the work of one department, but a mandate that we must carry across the entire administration,” said Bessent. “That is why I visited Minnesota in January to make clear that the U.S. Treasury is employing every tool to bring an end to this egregious, unchecked fraud and hold perpetrators to account.”

“This FBI follows the money. This FBI will put in prison anyone who commits fraud anywhere in the world against any American citizen,” said Patel.

text:
In July 2025, the Trump administration suddenly adopted a new radical misinterpretation of immigration law, declaring that anyone who entered the country without inspection must be detained without any individualized bond hearing. The administration’s mandatory detention policy does not take into account a person’s family or community ties or how long they have lived in the country.

Millions of immigrants are affected, including people who were previously released by the government, people who are eligible for legal status, as well as those with long-pending immigration applications who have been waiting years due to administrative backlogs.

This policy is cruel, inhumane, and illegal. That’s why it’s been repeatedly rejected by the federal courts, with hundreds of federal district judges ruling on thousands of related habeas petitions. Nine out of 10 of those judges have ruled that the administration’s misinterpretation of the law is illegal. When the government appealed those rulings, the ACLU and partners defended those decisions at the courts of appeals, where nine out of 11 circuits agree that the administration’s new policy violates the law.

Our client in this case, Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, has been living in the United States for over 20 years, has two U.S. citizen children, owns a home and a business, and has had an application for legal status pending since 2016 and permission to work legally in the U.S. Nonetheless, in September 2025, the Department of Homeland Security detained him under the government’s new no-bond policy.

A district court judge found this unlawful and ordered a bond hearing. An immigration judge then found that Mr. Barbosa da Cunha was not a flight risk or a danger to the community and ordered his release.

The Second Circuit unanimously affirmed the district court’s decision and agreed that the administration’s new policy violated existing immigration law. The vast majority of federal appeals courts have ruled against the policy, including the ruling at the center of this case.

The law is clear: Try as it might, the government cannot lock up immigrants for months or even years without giving them the basic protection of a bond hearing.

text:
A federal judge ruled Monday that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have continued to make arrests in Oregon without warrants.

Attorneys with Innovation Law Lab originally filed a class action lawsuit against ICE last year, arguing that the agency could not arrest someone without a warrant.

U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai issued a preliminary order earlier this year that ICE could only make a warrantless arrest if the person is likely to flee, and the agency must send documentation of those arrests to Innovation Law Lab.

Lawyers for Innovation Law Lab had said ICE was not complying with that order. They argued that ICE has continued to conduct hundreds of warrantless arrests since the judge’s order went into effect. Attorneys for the federal government have denied those claims.

In his new order, Kasubhai is now requiring the federal government to provide all arrest documents to Innovation Law Lab.

ICE must also produce all body-worn camera footage for arrests conducted on or after Sept. 1, 2026.

During a hearing in September, four immigrants — all arrested by ICE in 2026 — testified that they were each arrested without a valid warrant. An ICE deportation officer testified that, in two of the arrests, agents used license plate readers to identify the people detained.

In his order Monday, Kasubhai found that ICE has continued to conduct warrantless arrests and failed to properly document those instances, both in violation of his February order.

False and incorrect information found in reports, judge finds

The judge was particularly critical of an ICE deportation officer, identified as J.G. During the September hearing, J.G. testified that, while arresting a man in Medford last July, he had written false information in an arrest report, known as an I-213.

In the report, the agent attested that he knew the detainee’s immigration status before making the stop. On the witness stand, he admitted that was not true.

Innovation Law Lab argued that the warrant was invalid because it was issued after the arrest occurred.

Kasubhai said in the Monday ruling it was clear the agent had fabricated details, and had not simply made a mistake.

“It defies logic that such consequential errors in the I-213 form are merely a ‘mistake,’” he wrote. “The Court finds that he did not make a mistake in the I-213. He lied in an official record to facilitate the impression he was conducting a lawful warrant-based arrest.”

ICE did not immediately respond to OPB’s requests for comment Monday.

Kasubhai also wrote, “There is no telling how many other agents in Oregon engaged in similar misconduct, which calls into question the veracity of all I-213 forms completed by ICE officers in Oregon.”

The judge also admonished the “sloppy work” found in some reports. Other I-213s contained incorrect information, with one saying that an arrest took place in California when it was actually in Oregon. Also, many reports of different arrests contain nearly identical language, evidence ICE was using boilerplate language in arresting documents, he said.

“ICE agents’ boilerplate repetition of their ‘unawareness’ of community ties is a clear example of their failure to conduct simple law enforcement investigative duties. This is sloppy work,” Kasubhai wrote.

The judge also called into question the federal government’s own figures about the number of warrantless arrests. In documents provided to Innovation Law Lab, the government had said only 13 arrests were conducted without a proper warrant.

Kasubhai wrote that number is highly unlikely, since so many of the warrants used by ICE were invalid.

“The Court finds that ICE officers conducted significantly more than 13 warrantless arrests in Oregon between February 2026 and August 2026,” he wrote.

The order was issued as Kasubhai considers a similar case in federal court in Eugene. During an evidentiary hearing Monday, a man identified as L.A.M.A testified that he was arrested in a Walmart parking lot in Albany on June 18.

After saying they would drive him to the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, the agents eventually left him on the streets of Portland. L.A.M.A told the judge that his son had to drive from Albany to pick him up.

He said he was never shown a warrant during his arrest. Clearly emotional, he told the court in Spanish the experience left him feeling, “Anguish, quite a bit of it. Anguish, frustration — how your life can change in 24 hours.”

text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday threatened the Trump administration with legal action over federal immigration agents’ use of city parking lots to stage raids, which the Democratic elected official said amounted to “unlawful commandeering” of public property.

“This use of city property in furtherance of federal immigration enforcement is unauthorized and is therefore illegal, endangers city residents, and sows fear among those who seek to access city property,” Mamdani wrote in a letter addressed to U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) acting director, David Venturella.

Mamdani’s letter notes that ICE agents have “reportedly parked their vehicles and conducted meetings in several city-owned, unstaffed parking lots” — including ones near a park and a city-run preschool.

“ICE has not secured any authorization from the city to use these lots for immigration enforcement. To be clear: the city does not authorize ICE using its property in this manner,” Mamdani wrote. “Parking lots connected to city parks are reserved for the safe use and enjoyment of New Yorkers and visitors who wish to use our parks. Use of these lots for other purposes, including ICE’s reported use of these lots, amounts to unauthorized activity on City property. Accordingly, you must immediately issue guidance to your agents prohibiting them from using any City lots to stage or conduct enforcement operations.”

Mamdani’s letter comes weeks after a plainclothes ICE agent shot a Dominican immigrant in the Bronx while his 5-year-old son was in the car, infuriating community members and intensifying pressure on the mayor to do everything in his power to remove the rogue agency from New York City.

“We know that ICE is rotten to its core,” Mamdani said after the shooting. The mayor has called on President Donald Trump to end all ICE operations in New York City and has demanded abolition of the agency, saying it is “making a mockery of what law and order is supposed to be.”

In mid-October, Mamdani and more than 100 other elected New York officials called on private parking lot owners to bar ICE agents from using their property.

text:
In the months leading up to the 2026 midterm elections, congressional Republicans and federal prosecutors have targeted dozens of local officials in cities and counties across the country that have adopted some sanctuary policies. The investigations have increasingly focused on prosecutors and law enforcement officers, many of whom have publicly announced plans to go after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents who commit crimes in their jurisdictions or refuse demands to cooperate with federal immigration policing.

In total, 65 officials in 16 states have been targeted since January, according to a review of documents released by the House Judiciary Committee and the Department of Justice (DOJ), as well as interviews with senior officials who have direct knowledge of individual investigations. The House Judiciary Committee has issued subpoenas and other demands for testimony, documents, and records to more than 40 officials, 15 of them local prosecutors. Alongside that, the DOJ has initiated investigations into 50 local or state officials since 2025, including five involving local prosecutors. In all, 17 local prosecutors have been swept up in House Judiciary or DOJ investigations and lawsuits related to immigration policies.

House Judiciary Committee Chair Rep. Jim Jordan said in a recent report that “Democrats’ open-borders policies at the federal level and sanctuary policies at the state and local level allow millions of illegal aliens to pour into the country and ensure that criminal aliens, after encountered by local law enforcement, are released back into American communities,” echoing language the committee has commonly used in its investigations.

Many experts describe these investigations as unprecedented, and view the move as retaliation against local officials who refuse to cooperate with federal immigration agents or threaten legal action against ICE officers.

“These [prosecutors] are being intentionally intimidated by congressional and federal authorities,” said Mona Sahaf, the director of the Reshaping Prosecution initiative at the Vera Institute of Justice. “The use of [the] DOJ to target perceived political opponents is new. It’s busting norms, and it’s highly dangerous.”

The targeting of local prosecutors appears to be a matter of policy in the second Trump administration. “Sanctuary Jurisdictions Directives” issued by the attorney general’s office on February 5, 2025, held that the DOJ Civil Rights Division should “identify state and local laws, policies, and practices that facilitate violations of federal immigration laws or impede lawful federal immigration operations,” and “where appropriate, take legal action to challenge such laws, policies, or practices.”

The DOJ, in a June 18 press release announcing an investigation into local officials in Philadelphia — including District Attorney Larry Krasner — concerning a policy prohibiting federal agents from wearing masks, said that its “series of lawsuits brought by the Civil Division” targeted “illegal policies designed to thwart federal law enforcement across the country.”

Rebecca Roiphe, the Joseph Solomon Distinguished Professor of Law at New York Law School, said the investigations into local prosecutors represented “a wholesale abandonment” of the principle of separation between the DOJ and the political branches of government. “This administration has pretty openly suggested that it is normal and appropriate and even laudable for the political branches to have some degree of control over the Department of Justice,” she said.

Referring to the DOJ investigations, Roiphe said, “The bottom line is that these federal prosecutions can end up threatening local prosecutors to fall in line with federal priorities, and that’s illegitimate in our system.”

These overlapping investigations, reports, and the DOJ directives follow the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 threat to “initiate legal action against” prosecutors who refuse to adhere to the priorities of the Trump administration. For many of the targeted prosecutors, the political influence has become impossible to ignore.

Among the targeted is Parisa Dehghani-Tafti, the top prosecutor in Arlington, Virginia, who drew the ire of Representative Jordan’s committee on multiple occasions, including when she declined to charge an activist who handed out flyers containing the home address of Deputy White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, citing concerns over First Amendment-protected free speech.

In a July 1 letter to Dehghani-Tafti, Jordan described Dehghani-Tafti’s decision not to charge as “politically-motivated actions in a case involving a far-left agitator’s disturbing campaign to threaten, harass, and dox a senior White House official and his family” and accused her office of having “sanctuary policies that prioritize illegal and criminal aliens over American citizens.”

Dehghani-Tafti, who characterized the House Judiciary actions as “pathetic,” denies any wrongdoing and suggests that these investigations are the result of her political opponents’ inability to defeat her electorally.

“They can’t beat us at the polls, and so they’re being undemocratic about it and trying to undermine the voters,” she told Truthout.

In total, Jordan and the House Judiciary Committee have issued three letters and a subpoena to Dehghani-Tafti, in addition to writing an interim report on her in September, which was largely based on a July closed-door deposition. Following the report, the DOJ Civil Rights Division informed Dehghani-Tafti that she was under investigation following a referral from the House Judiciary, according to a senior official with direct knowledge of the investigation.

“None of this is normal,” Dehghani-Tafti said. “What they’re doing is taking mechanisms that are designed to uphold the rule of law and perverting them. And that is not normal, except for authoritarians.”

Dehghani-Tafti was not the only Northern Virginia prosecutor to be on the receiving end of both House Judiciary and DOJ investigations. The top prosecutor for Fairfax County, Virginia, Steve Descano, similarly received three letters and a subpoena, and was the subject of an interim report from Jordan’s committee. The report, “Fairfax County, Virginia: The Dangerous Consequences of Sanctuary Policies,” claims that a 2019 campaign promise to make “charging and plea decisions that limit or avoid immigration consequences” is discriminatory and violates federal law. The report goes on to accuse Descano’s office of “efforts to erase national borders and undermine immigration enforcement.”

Descano declined to comment for this story, citing the ongoing investigations. His chief of staff, Laura Birnbaum, directed Truthout to prior official statements issued by his office, including an October 20 response to the House Judiciary report. “This ‘report’ is nothing more than recycled Republican talking points put out weeks before the midterm elections as a desperate attempt to distract from widely anticipated Republican losses,” wrote Birnbaum.

Responding to the DOJ investigation, Descano’s office released a statement in May that accused the Trump administration “of misusing the Justice Department to launch partisan attacks.”

Both Dehghani-Tafti and Descano belong to a small coalition of prosecutors from cities across the U.S. that declared an intention to prosecute federal agents who commit crimes in their cities. The alliance — the Fight Against Federal Overreach — which intentionally takes its name from the slang acronym FAFO, formed in January in part as a response to the deadly ICE shootings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis that same month. Less than a year later, nearly half of the group’s founding members have found themselves under investigation by the DOJ.

“No other administration has ever done things like this,”said Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, who has been a target of DOJ investigators.

Moriarty, whose jurisdiction includes Minneapolis, made national headlines in January when she announced a state-level investigation into the shooting of Good by ICE agent Jonathan Ross. Just days later, the DOJ subpoenaed four Minnesota officials, including Gov. Tim Walz and Attorney General Keith Ellison, as part of an investigation into whether they impeded federal immigration agents during “Operation Metro Surge.” News reports initially incorrectly named Moriarty among the officials who received a subpoena, though it was later revealed that she did not receive one. Moriarty told Truthout she believes that her name was released intentionally by government officials to intimidate her.

Viewed in isolation, these actions may appear to be singular responses during an exceptional political moment, but taken together, the data suggest a wider attempt to punish officials who try to thwart federal immigration policies.

“The story is there — if you speak up and work to hold police accountable, we will come after you,” said Sahaf, referring to the House Judiciary and DOJ investigations. Sahaf, a former DOJ trial attorney, warned that should local prosecutors fear becoming a political target for investigating federal agents and police, “we’ll have no one … to deter this kind of conduct from happening again.”

Clarissa Delgado contributed additional reporting for this article.

text:
A proposed settlement was reached today in a sweeping class action lawsuit against the GEO detention center for forcing thousands of immigrants detained inside to do hard labor for $1 a day, plaintiffs attorneys confirmed to CPR News.

Details of the settlement agreement, which will still need to be approved by a federal judge, were not disclosed, but the agreement reached between attorneys representing thousands of immigrants detained between 2004 and 2014 in Aurora and the for-profit company GEO Group was confirmed by plaintiff attorneys David Seligman and Hans Meyer.

The GEO Group operates for-profit prisons and immigration detention centers across the country, and lawyers have argued its business model enriches the company and its shareholders on the backs of people detained inside.

In previous interviews before the agreement was reached Monday morning, Meyer and Seligman said the fact that the case, which is more than a decade old, was finally going to trial was a victory in and of itself.

“At its core, this case is about our clients who are real people in our community standing up to a multinational corporation that engaged in profiteering from this forced labor,” Meyer said. “This is the first step in holding this corporation accountable for exploiting human beings.”

The so-called Menocal v. GEO case has had quite a journey since it was initially filed more than a decade ago. Alejandro Menocal, who was detained in Aurora for a few months in 2014, said he was forced to do hard labor inside the facility or else he would be physically restrained in solitary confinement. Immigrants also alleged they were paid $1 per day that unjustly enriched the company because immigrants were keeping up the maintenance.

So Menocal sued on behalf of immigrants detained at the immigrant detention facility in Adams County over the course of a decade, claiming the GEO Group was “unjustly” enriching themselves by running the detention center, the food, janitorial and laundry services, for pennies by the hour, which allowed them to maximize profits.

GEO pushed back, essentially claiming that as a federal contractor they couldn’t be held accountable for the same laws that applied to other businesses because they were doing what the federal government asked them to do. The case took years and wound its way to the U.S. Supreme Court, which decided 9-0 last year that Menocal could proceed with his claims.

Jury selection in the trial had been scheduled to start Monday morning.

“That’s what this trial is about,” said Seligman, who runs the advocacy law firm Towards Justice, on Friday. “GEO is all about cutting costs. And it makes billions of taxpayer dollars a year. So whatever corners it’s able to cut, that money goes to its executives and shareholders and the evidence we’re going to put forward in this trial, is that the way they’ve been able to do that is through exploiting a captive labor force.”

As of Monday morning, potential jurors were gathering and answering questions about serving and opening statements were expected Tuesday morning.

The Geo Group did not have an immediate comment on the proposed settlement agreement. Lawyers representing the plaintiffs said “in the face of long odds” they kept fighting for justice and “this settlement shows that our legal system can still sometimes provide justice, even for the most marginalized.”

“Our clients suffered the inhumane treatment alleged here while locked up in a detention center just a few miles from the federal courthouse,” the attorneys said, in a statement. “And like so many across the country, they’ve been victimized by a broken immigration system.”

This story was updated at 2:47 p.m. on Nov. 2, 2026 with additional comments from the plaintiff’s attorneys.

text:
Community members and elected officials are speaking up in response to the recent surge of ICE activity on the Central Coast, following a wave of public incidents that included the detention of special needs student and U.S. citizen Erik Zepeda, a 20-year-old who was detained in an aggressive encounter with federal immigration enforcement while on his way to Santa Maria High School on October 21.

Students walked out of their classrooms at Santa Maria and Lompoc high schools on Friday in a demonstration of solidarity with Zepeda, who according to witnesses at the scene that day, was tackled, restrained, and questioned before being left on the street with bruises and a wrist injury that later required surgery.

The student walkout was just one of the many public repudiations of the increased ICE activity during the month of October, following reports of more than 114 community members who were arrested by federal immigration enforcement on the Central Coast from October 5 through October 11, according to 805 UndocuFund’s Rapid Response Network.

The nonprofit 805 UndocuFund keeps track of daily ICE activity in Santa Barbara, Ventura, and San Luis Obispo counties, verifying reports through its 24/7 hotline and sending alerts through its messaging network. The group noted an uptick in ICE presence and arrests throughout the region in the past several weeks, consistent with reports of a 45-day surge in communities across the state. (The Department of Homeland Security has not publicly confirmed or denied the existence of the operation, reportedly known as “Operation Safe California.”)

From January 2025 through October 2026, the Rapid Response Network reported at least 2,983 arrests in the three counties, with more than 1,350 in Santa Barbara County. Of these arrests, most have occurred in the northern parts of the county, with 848 taken in Santa Maria and 316 in Lompoc. In South County, 143 people were taken in Santa Barbara, 28 in Carpinteria, and 10 in Goleta.

Santa Maria Councilmember Gloria Soto and District School Boardmember Ricardo Valencia have both spoken out publicly to call for an end to aggressive ICE enforcement. On October 29, Congressmember Salud Carbajal filed an official response with DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin calling for an investigation into the immigration enforcement on the Central Coast, specifically asking that the government provide details about the detention of Zepeda just a half mile away from the Santa Maria High School campus.

Carbajal’s letter describes recent reports from Rapid Response groups and community residents who have witnessed ICE on a nearly daily basis throughout the month of October. These include arrests at workplaces, farms, community churches, neighborhoods with high populations of Latino residents, in marketplace parking lots, and near school campuses, such as the arrest of a parent reported at Allan Hancock College on October 5.

“I have seen alarming reports of U.S. citizens being detained and injured and heard of families and farmworkers with no criminal record who have been caught up in aggressive interior enforcement actions,” Carbajal wrote. “I have serious concerns that a growing number of individuals are being targeted based on their race, ethnicity, or perceived immigration status. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) must be accountable to the public and to the communities they serve, including my constituents.”

Carbajal noted a “rising tide of rhetoric” inflaming division in the community, painting immigrants as criminals despite data from the Migration Policy Institute’s most recent analysis, which showed that only about 20 percent of the estimated 980,000 individuals deported in the first 18 months of the second Trump administration had criminal convictions.

“These findings raise important questions as to whether the people being targeted match the administration’s stated focus on individuals who pose a public safety threat and have criminal convictions,” Carbajal said.

Rapid Response volunteers have been on the ground every day to track immigration enforcement activity, and multiple volunteers told the Independent they have noticed a shift from targeted enforcement to seemingly random pickups, with convoys of masked agents now going after community members based on skin color and appearance. In the case of Zepeda, an ICE spokesperson said he was apprehended because agents “believed he matched the description” of their target.

ICE denied that Zepeda sustained any broken bones, and the agency said they never called for an ambulance because the 20-year-old “never requested medical assistance.” School officials said Zepeda made his way over to the campus himself, where administration arranged for medical help.

Over the past weekend, ICE has also ramped up activity outside local jails. Every day of Halloween weekend, ICE officers were seen at the Santa Barbara County Main Jail, where each day, a convoy with anywhere from six to eight agents — most of them masked — stood in and around the jail lobby waiting to apprehend an individual being released from custody.

While the agents rarely speak with the public, on Sunday morning, November 2, one of the ICE officers began reciting verses from the Bible toward Rapid Response volunteers who were standing outside the lobby: “For I tell you that unless your righteousness surpasses that of the Pharisees and the teachers of the law,” the agent could be heard saying in one recording, ”you will certainly not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

That same morning, the agents took one individual from the jail and reportedly drove him back to ICE’s regional office in Camarillo. The same group of immigration officers was seen back at the Santa Barbara jail again the next morning on Monday, November 2.

DHS has not responded to Carbajal’s request for an investigation, which calls for details into Central Coast operations, the number of U.S citizens who have been apprehended or detained, and the protocols for verifying identity or approaching individuals with disabilities. The agency typically does not comment on day-to-day operations.

text:
A U.S. federal appeals court has paused a lower court order requiring the U.S. Department of State to reopen registration for the FY 2027 Diversity Visa (DV) Lottery program, leaving the program’s status uncertain.

Appeals Court Halts Order to Reopen DV-2027 Lottery

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit has granted the U.S. Department of State’s request to stay a preliminary injunction that would have required the government to reopen the FY 2027 Diversity Visa (DV) Lottery registration process.

The ruling follows a lawsuit filed by an immigration law firm that challenged the government’s decision not to launch the DV-2027 registration period. The Department had not opened the lottery registration window as expected, effectively suspending the FY 2027 Diversity Visa program.

Diversity Visa Lottery 2027: What Happened?

Under U.S. law, the Diversity Visa Program must make up to 55,000 immigrant visas available annually to individuals from countries with historically low rates of immigration to the United States. Normally, the U.S. Department of State conducts a lottery and selects approximately 100,000 individuals who may then apply for a diversity visa.

According to the court order:

The Department did not open the FY 2027 DV Lottery registration period.

A federal district court ordered the government to reopen the program and publish a registration timeline.

The government appealed that decision and sought an emergency stay.

The Ninth Circuit granted the stay while the appeal proceeds.

Why the Appeals Court Granted the Stay

The Ninth Circuit found that Red Eagle Law, L.C. was unlikely to succeed on the merits because the firm may not have legal standing to challenge the suspension of the Diversity Visa Program. The court concluded that the program was designed to promote immigration diversity, not to protect the business interests of immigration law firms.

The court emphasized that it was not endorsing the Department’s failure to open the DV-2027 lottery but determined that the plaintiff had not established an appropriate legal basis to bring the claim.

Employer and Applicant Impact

At this time:

The FY 2027 Diversity Visa Lottery registration period remains closed.

No new registration timeline has been announced.

The underlying appeal remains pending before the Ninth Circuit.

Prospective applicants should monitor future announcements from the U.S. Department of State regarding the DV-2027 program.

text:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who is accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston turned himself in Monday, his attorney said.

Mario Alberto Morales made his first court appearance on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon for striking Miguel Parra Hernandez with an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as Morales chased the 48-year-old construction worker through a parking lot. A grand jury indicted Morales, 33, on Friday.

During Monday's hearing, Judge Matthew Peneguy set bond at $30,000. Prosecutors had asked that bond be set at $75,000, according to the Harris County District Attorney's Office.

Morales is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown. Other encounters have come under investigation.

READ MORE: An ICE officer is charged with assault for striking a man with a car in Houston

ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of Morales' vehicle, an account that prosecutors say is contradicted by video. Surveillance camera video shows Morales' vehicle drive over a median and strike Parra Hernandez as he runs away.

David Lindenmuth, Morales' attorney, has said his client was "truly a good man" and did not commit a crime.

Parra Hernandez broke his leg and is recovering at a rehabilitation facility while in federal custody, according to Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare.

Morales had worked as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Lindenmuth said. He unsuccessfully ran for Congress this year and previously served in the Army.

Morales was charged with a misdemeanor in 2013 for stealing four DVDs, according to Harris County Court records. Those charges were dismissed under a plea deal in which he paid a $270 fine.

Wilder is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

text:
An unfavorable immigration decision can affect your ability to remain in the United States, obtain legal status, or reunite with family. However, some decisions can be challenged through administrative appeals or federal court proceedings, depending on the circumstances.

Immigration Litigation involves legal action to challenge certain government decisions, policies, or procedures related to immigration. Understanding your options, deadlines, and legal rights can help you determine the appropriate next step.

What Is Immigration Litigation?

Immigration Litigation is an area of law where people, entities and government authorities are in conflict on immigration decisions. Such cases can pertain to visa refusal, removal orders, detention, asylum claims and potential breaches of legal processes.

An immigration attorney will be able to review it, check for any legal mistakes, and decide if an appeal, motion, or court challenge is necessary. Not all of the bad choices can be appealed in the same manner; options are dependent on the specific situation.

Immigration litigations and court rulings.

Understanding Immigration Lawsuits and Court Decisions

Immigration Lawsuits can be against a single action or a policy of the government. In some cases, the proceedings are before the immigration courts, in other cases the proceedings are before the Board of Immigration Appeals, and in other cases, the proceedings are in federal district court.

Immigration Court Decisions typically are about removal actions, asylum applications, and some types of relief. Appeals may be available, through the Board of Immigration Appeals, but further judicial review will depend on the case and applicable law.

Changes in Immigration Policy, Immigration Laws, and recent Immigration Law Updates can also affect how cases are handled. It is essential to examine the legal principles used in reaching a decision before filing a lawsuit.

The Role of Immigration Attorneys

Immigration Attorneys provide information to their clients regarding their options and challenges to government decisions. They might be involved in reviewing case files, locating procedural mistakes, and creating legal arguments, or they may represent clients in court.

An attorney can also provide a determination if an administrative appeal, motion to reopen, motion to reconsider, or federal lawsuit may be suitable. Filing deadlines may be tight and it is crucial to obtain legal counsel in a timely way.

Injunctions in Immigration Litigation

In some cases, a person or organization may ask a court to temporarily or permanently restrict a government action. The type of injunction requested depends on the urgency of the situation and the legal grounds.

Temporary Restraining Order: A short-term court order that may prevent an action while the court considers whether further relief is appropriate.

Preliminary Injunction: A court order that may preserve the situation while a lawsuit is pending.

Permanent Injunction: A lasting court order issued as part of a final judgment when the legal requirements are met.

Courts consider specific legal standards before granting these remedies. An injunction is not automatic simply because someone disagrees with an immigration decision.

Supreme Court Immigration Cases and Their Impact

The decisions made in Supreme Court Immigration Cases can impact the interpretation and application of immigration law all over the country. These decisions can relate to executive authority, constitutional safeguards, detention, removal processes and access to judicial review.

But a Supreme Court decision does not always impact all immigration cases. The impact of its ruling will be shaped by the legal question, the decision’s scope, and how lower courts are applying the ruling.

What Evidence Can Strengthen an Immigration Litigation Case?

An effective immigration litigation case will always require that one has clear evidence that a decision should be reviewed. The applicants might have to submit copies of immigration applications, official notifications, court documents, letters to immigration officials, and documents showing their eligibility. If the wrong information or a mistake in procedure was used, the records may help to clarify the mistake and why it may be necessary to rethink the decision.

It’s also a good idea to group the evidence around the particular issue that’s being disputed. An immigration attorney can help determine a situation by looking at a timeline of events, copies of prior submissions and communications. While good documentation does not ensure success, it can clarify the legal arguments, and can help in the contest.

Conclusion

Immigration Litigation is a legal process which may be used to challenge some of the Government’s decisions and actions in Immigration matters. Depending on the specific situation, an appeal, court petition and injunction may be available.

Knowing the immigration law, knowing the deadlines and ensuring your immigration lawyer is knowledgeable about the situation can help you determine what options you have and help you fight for your legal rights.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is immigration litigation?

Immigration litigation is a legal action against government decisions, actions or policies in the proper courts.

Can I challenge an immigration denial?

An appeal, a motion or a lawsuit may be filed to challenge certain denials. The option available will vary depending on the application type and agency that made the decision.

How long does immigration litigation take?

The timeline varies depending on the court, complexity of the case, evidence, and procedural requirements. There are things that take months and others that might take years.

Can an immigration attorney reverse a removal order?

A lawyer can determine grounds for an appeal, motion or judicial review. But it will depend on the facts and the applicable law.

What is the difference between an appeal and immigration litigation?

Appeals are an application to a higher administrative authority or Court to reconsider a decision. Immigration litigation may encompass more comprehensive case law litigation that is related to immigration issues and/or government interpretation.

What is a temporary restraining order in immigration cases?

It is a short-term court order that may temporarily prevent a government action while the court considers the request for further relief.

When is a preliminary injunction used?

A preliminary injunction may be requested to prevent harm while a lawsuit is ongoing. The court must determine whether the legal requirements for granting it are satisfied.

Can immigration policies be challenged in federal court?

Some immigration policies and some government actions can be challenged in federal court – but only under conditions and limitations of judicial review.

Do Supreme Court immigration cases affect individual applications?

They can help shape the interpretation of immigration laws, though only as it relates to the ruling being made and the circumstances of the individual case.

When should I contact an immigration attorney?

It’s important to seek legal counsel at the first sign of an unfavorable decision, removal notice or any other significant immigration communication. Early guidance can help you understand deadlines and available remedies.

text:
James Talarico, a U.S. Senate candidate in Texas, briefly praised Frederick Haynes III, a Democratic congressional candidate who compared President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement efforts to the KKK, at a get-out-the-vote event on Thursday as part of his Clear Eyes Full Hearts tour.

"Give it up for your next congressman, Dr. Freddy Haynes. Thank you, Dr. Haynes, for those kind words and for your service to this community," Talarico said, following an introduction and speech from Haynes.

Although Talarico has not issued a formal endorsement of Haynes, the moment is notable for Talarico as he pitches himself as a Democrat who can represent the values of the Republican-leaning Lone Star State — and as he tries to distance himself from controversy over past remarks Republicans have characterized as woke.

TALARICO RALLY WARMUP ACT CALLS FOR ABOLISHING ICE, CONTRASTING SENATE HOPEFUL'S MESSAGE

Haynes, the pastor of Friendship-West Baptist Church, has framed many of his political views in the context of race and did so again on the event with Talarico.

"You transformed ICE into the new KKK and brought about terror in this nation," Haynes said of Trump's use of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

"It’s time to melt ICE. It’s time to abolish ICE," Haynes added.

Haynes is running to fill the seat of Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, the incumbent in Texas' 30th Congressional District who gave up her seat in a Senate bid she ultimately lost. During his campaign, Haynes has framed his support for climate policy as a fight against "environmental racism." He has also accused conservatives and the Trump administration of benefiting from fears of Black advancement.

"They have used Black people and perceived Black progress as the boogeyman. We have not witnessed this kind of corruption, this kind of blatant corruption," Haynes said in an October interview.

"We are witnessing the demolishing of what democratic infrastructure was built by the gains of the civil rights movement," Haynes added.

Even before his congressional run, Haynes made political commentary that relied heavily on a racial lens.

After the death of Charlie Kirk, a conservative political commentator who started Turning Point USA, Haynes described Kirk as a man with views "rooted in White supremacy" and contrasted it with the deaths of Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X.

"A White Christian gets killed, murdered — not assassinated. We going to tell the whole truth today. Martin King got assassinated. Malcolm X got assassinated. Medgar Evers got assassinated. Don’t compare Kirk to King," Haynes said in a September 2025 address to his church.

UN PUSHES NATIONS TO CONSIDER SLAVERY REPARATIONS BUT LEGAL GROUP SAYS IDEA 'NOT GOING TO FLY IN THE US'

Haynes would go on to condemn Kirk's death and political violence.

Haynes has also said he was a personal supporter of reparations.

text:
WASHINGTON (OSV News) — An Oct. 29-30 interfaith immigration policy summit hosted by the Catholic Legal Immigration Network, also known as CLINIC, brought together faith leaders, legal practitioners, advocates and scholars from Catholic, Protestant and Jewish faith traditions to find areas of commonality in their work serving immigrant communities.

Anna Gallagher, executive director of CLINIC, said in remarks at the summit, “We have much to learn from one another.”

“Across the traditions represented here, we encounter teachings about hospitality, justice, compassion, refuge, and responsibility,” she said.

The summit came during what participants described as a challenging time for their cause. A joint report from the National Association of Evangelicals, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops’ Migration and Refugee Services, the Center for the Study of Global Christianity at Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary, and World Relief estimated that more than 10 million Christians living in the U.S. would be vulnerable to deportation under Trump administration policies implemented in 2025, and 61% were Catholic.

It also found more than 1 in 6 Catholics are either vulnerable to deportation themselves or could see a family member deported, barring law or policy changes.

In reference to their interfaith dialogue, the Rev. Enid Almanzar, board chair at the National Latino Evangelical Coalition, said in remarks at the summit, “Migration is not a footnote in the biblical narrative.”

“Even Jesus began his earthly life as a child whose family had to flee political violence and seek refuge in Egypt,” she said.

Acknowledging broader doctrinal differences between the organizations, Rev. Almanzar said, “we may not agree on some of the larger theological questions, but we don’t have to agree on every doctrine to recognize the moral urgency of protecting the vulnerable.”

“Because ultimately, compassion without action becomes sentimentality and conviction without courage becomes rhetoric, and so our calling is to move beyond both to become communities where dignity is defended, where families are accompanied, and where love is made visible,” she said.

The summit also came shortly after a divided panel of the U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia allowed a lawsuit against the federal government from a coalition of more than two dozen religious organizations to proceed. The group is challenging a Trump administration policy that rescinded long-standing restrictions on arrests at sensitive locations, also including schools and hospitals, with exceptions for public safety or national security threats. Multiple panelists at the summit shared concerns about that policy change.

It also came soon after the Archdiocese of St. Louis filed a separate lawsuit against the federal government over a policy it said prohibits priests from distributing holy Communion to and hearing confessions of Catholics detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Pope Leo XIV sent a special message of support to the summit, thanking CLINIC for its work, “together with that of the many people, families, civic bodies and church communities who strive to uphold the dignity of migrants and refugees.”

“Too often, these most vulnerable members of society are caught in situations which strip them of their human rights — an injustice that cries out to heaven,” he said. “It is my hope, therefore, that this summit will encourage the participants to stir the hearts and minds of their fellow citizens to overcome that indifference and detachment which reduces the human person to a statistic.”

Pope Leo said he would pray the meeting “will help find new ways to awaken consciences to our shared moral duty for these brothers and sisters of ours, who, as Sacred Scripture and the saints untiringly remind us, are Christ visiting us in disguise.”

Gallagher said Pope Leo’s message was “a meaningful charge for the beginning of an interfaith gathering.”

“We are here to learn from one another, to strengthen our work, and to consider how we can help our communities see more clearly and respond more faithfully,” she said.

Rev. Almanzar argued that religious communities are well suited to advocate for humane immigration policies.

“Maybe the most prophetic thing we can do in this environment is refuse that false binary choice between security and humanity,” she said. “A nation should be able to uphold its laws without surrendering its conscience, and faith communities have a responsibility to remind our leaders and ourselves of that truth.”

“As faith communities,” she added, “I think we can be leaders in reframing the conversation and casting a vision about a future where people flourish, where people are welcome, where people are loved, and there’s not that false binary choice.”

Gallagher added, “Migration brings us into contact with questions that are central to religious life. Where do we belong? What do we owe one another? How do we respond to suffering? What does it mean to welcome someone whose language, history, or circumstances differ from our own?”

text:
Recently obtained government documents reveal that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has lost count of miscarriages in its custody while detaining a record number of pregnant women with limited access to medical care, according to new reporting from the Guardian.

The Guardian obtained the documents with free legal support from Reporters Committee attorneys, who filed a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit on the news outlet’s behalf in March. In response to the lawsuit, ICE released records that document the number of pregnant, postpartum, and nursing people in the agency’s custody during a roughly 15-month period starting in October 2024.

The records show — and a U.S. Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed — that ICE stopped counting miscarriages a year ago, according to the Guardian. The agency has never before acknowledged that fact — not even in response to inquiries from U.S. senators.

In addition to obtaining the data, journalists for the Guardian spoke with detained pregnant women who said they are “struggling to access routine and emergency medical care.” Experts have raised concerns that inadequate medical treatment at detention facilities could lead to dangerous — and preventable — health complications, the news outlet reported.

Will Craft, data editor for the Guardian U.S., said he and journalist Maanvi Singh began digging into how the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement campaign was impacting families after the duo reported on leaked deportation flight manifests from an approximately 100-day span in 2025. Their analysis found that, within that time frame, ICE’s largest airline contractor transported nearly 500 children under the age of 10 — 22 of whom were infants.

“We had all these questions,” Craft told Reporters Committee in an interview. “Are women giving birth in immigration detention? In what conditions are they giving birth? What are the conditions that they’re forced to endure as they’re carrying their children?”

In early January, Craft submitted a FOIA request to ICE seeking documents that could provide answers. But ICE let the request languish for months without releasing any records. So, on behalf of the Guardian U.S., Reporters Committee attorneys Adam A. Marshall and Gunita Singh sued.

ICE released some records, including data tracking the number of miscarriages in ICE detention facilities, but the miscarriage tally cut off on Oct. 3, 2025. Craft said the documents attributed the missing data to a change in the agency’s medical accounting system, and a DHS spokesperson at first claimed that ICE was tracking miscarriages in monthly reports.

It took several months of follow-up reporting to determine that ICE had indeed lost count of miscarriages in its custody, Craft said.

“The data’s important because it’s an accountability thing,” Maanvi Singh, one of the journalists who reported the story with Craft, told WBUR. “If there’s going to be so many pregnant people in detention, we want to know what’s happening to them.”

The records show ICE recorded 18 miscarriages in the first nine months of the Trump administration, which experts told the Guardian is likely an undercount because some women who have a miscarriage don’t notice symptoms.

And last fall and winter, “ICE held more pregnant individuals in detention than at any time over the previous year,” the news outlet reported, raising questions about ICE’s adherence to a 2021 federal policy that states the agency should avoid detaining pregnant, postpartum, and nursing immigrants but for exceptional circumstances.

A DHS spokesperson told the Guardian that the agency is abiding by the 2021 policy. “The 2021 directive is still in place,” said spokesperson Chandler Rebel. “Pregnant women receive regular prenatal visits, mental health services, nutritional support, and accommodations aligned with community standards of care.”

The Guardian’s reporting is the latest in the news outlet’s effort to shed light on how the Trump administration is carrying out its immigration enforcement crackdown.

Earlier this year, the newsroom’s analysis of records obtained through a FOIA lawsuit filed by Reporters Committee attorneys revealed that the vast majority of people who were targeted for deportation for the first time in 2025 had no criminal conviction — undercutting the government’s claims that its enforcement operations are focused on arresting “dangerous criminals.”

Craft said these lawsuits have been essential to pierce the veil of secrecy surrounding the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement campaign. Without taking the government to court, he said, it could take years to shake loose records of great public interest.

“The American people deserve to know what the government is doing in its name with taxpayer money and the impact that it is having on people that live here, the impact that it’s having on families, the impact it’s having on their communities,” Craft said. “If we don’t get access to these records, if we don’t use the tools available to us to try to report on what is happening, then the people will not know what the government is doing in their name.”

Craft said Reporters Committee’s free legal help has been an “invaluable resource.”

“Even before they were helping me sue the government, which I love doing, their FOIA guides on every state have helped me basically since the moment I was an intern,” he said. “We would not be able to do a lot of this reporting without the help of so many people at the Reporters Committee.”

text:
The most anticipated provisions of Massachusetts PROTECT Act, which aims to counter the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign, are scheduled to go into effect Nov. 3.

Section 12 of the legislation, signed by Gov. Maura Healey Aug. 5, prohibits federal agents from making civil immigration arrests in state courthouses without judicial warrants. Yet many legal experts are concerned about how effective that part of the law could be.

“I think those provisions in the act are more symbolic than real,” said Peter Margulies, a law professor at Roger Williams University who specializes in immigration law. “Those provisions are likely unconstitutional under the U.S. Constitution.”

A representative from the Massachusetts Immigrant and Refugee Advocacy Coalition, which led the charge to pass the PROTECT Act, also acknowledges the concerns.

“I do think that there is skepticism, and rightfully so,” said Gil Calderin, director of advocacy at MIRA. “This is true whenever you’re entering uncharted territory.”

Indeed, the very premise of the law — a state effort to counteract federal government action — could bring it into conflict with the U.S. Constitution.

Courthouse provisions

State courthouses have become frequent locations of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests during President Donald Trump’s deportation campaign.

In New Bedford, ICE has arrested at least 10 immigrants inside the District Court building this year‚ up from eight when The Light reported on the question in August.

“People are afraid to go to court, to testify, as victims and witnesses,” Healey said at a news conference in January. “This is all making us less safe.”

Section 12 prohibits all civil immigration arrests in courthouses without a judicial warrant and any arrests at all in courtrooms. It says any such action will be viewed as false imprisonment under state law. It allows the state attorney general to pursue civil litigation against ICE for violations at the office’s discretion.

Yet that may be a challenge, according to one expert.

“Requiring [ICE agents] to jump through hoops that federal law doesn’t require would be an overreach,” Margulies said. “It would be an assertion of state authority that is barred by the U.S. Constitution.”

Margulies pointed to the U.S. Constitution’s Supremacy Clause, which prohibits states from making laws that impede federal action. He said the federal government may challenge the law, either in court or by ignoring it. Though federal agents do need a judicial warrant to enter a private space, courthouses are public, he added.

The PROTECT Act also does not “require” a court or law enforcement officer “to interfere with or assist the actions of a federal official engaged in civil immigration enforcement.”

Magulies said that line points to an awareness from lawmakers that Section 12 dances perilously close to a constitutional violation.

In September, the Massachusetts Trial Court issued new guidance about interactions with ICE, set to take effect on Nov. 3, the same day as Section 12. The guidance goes further than the law, stating “Trial Court employees shall not under any circumstances interfere with or assist” ICE’s civil arrests.

“That means if an ICE officer comes to a courthouse and has only an administrative warrant … no state official or local official can say: ‘Well, that’s not enough,’” Margulies said. “The state doesn’t want to make its officials liable for obstruction of justice.”

Calderin, of MIRA, said that such concerns about the enforceability of the law “are valid.” He said the experiences of states that established similar laws, like Connecticut, could provide some answers.

“Rather than invoking their state laws, they’re continuing to battle this in federal district courts,” he said.

He also found comfort in the law’s civil litigation provisions and its requirement that trial court security must record civil immigration arrests at courthouses and provide a report to the Legislature and public about them annually by July 1.

“We’re hopeful that state trial courts will enforce their part of this as part of the law,” Calderin said.

Attorney General Andrea Campbell declined a request by The Light for an interview but sent a statement.

“The PROTECT Act strengthens protections for our residents in the face of the aggressive tactics employed by ICE,” Campbell’s statement said. “Tactics that do not enhance public safety and instead spread fear among families and our communities.

“Immigrants are an essential part of our communities, workplaces, and economy, and we will continue to use every tool available to defend their rights,” she concluded.

Other PROTECT Act provisions

The PROTECT Act also required Campbell to issue legal guidance to schools, healthcare facilities, and state property on how to navigate an interaction with federal agents carrying out civil immigration enforcement there.

The guidance includes: the designation of on-site contact people if officers performing civil immigration enforcement appear; procedures in case situations escalate; training to distinguish a judicial warrant from an administrative warrant; drills for when such an action takes place nearby, and more.

During an ICE surge in New Bedford on Sept. 21 and 22 — part of a three-day operation in the South Coast that resulted in the detention of 82 people, according to the agency — agents were spotted near schools. That prompted procedures for civil disturbances to be implemented.

The Light identified 35 of those detained on the South Coast shortly after their arrests. It was able to review statewide court records for 23 of the men and found that only four of the 23 men had criminal charges on their records in Massachusetts. An ICE news release identified only seven men of the 82, and claimed that seven of those had criminal charges on their records.

“This week, New Bedford saw the MA PROTECT Act up close,” New Bedford Public Schools Supt. Andrew O’Leary said in a social media post during the September ICE operations. He said that New Bedford Public Schools already had such procedures in place “for at least two years” and that the system’s experiences during the surge demonstrated why the PROTECT Act’s requirements for school plans were necessary.

On Oct. 5, the School Committee made the guidelines official policy in a near unanimous vote, with only Chris Cotter voting against.

But as the Nov. 3 date for the courthouse provisions arrives, the question remains: What will the federal government do?

“We’re thrilled that these protections will come into place,” said Calderin of MIRA. “And the hope is that these federal agents will follow state law.”

text:
By: Jude Joffe-Block, NPR

A day before Election Day, the Department of Justice is asking the U.S. Supreme Court to wade into its unprecedented feud with California over the state's voter rolls.

The appeal is the department's latest foray into state election administration, which a federal judge referred to last week as "a broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference by federal officials."

After that judge, David Carter, a Clinton appointee, and a divided 9th Circuit Court of Appeals panel rejected the DOJ's request to order California to set aside and stop processing the ballots of thousands of people, the DOJ filed a notice Monday that it is seeking injunctive relief from the high court.

It remains to be seen whether the Supreme Court will agree to intervene and, if so, whether it would weigh in before Tuesday's Election Day.

The DOJ says it has identified 20,000 "likely" noncitizens on California's voter roll whose ballots should not be counted until their citizenship can be verified.

Courts so far have sided with California and Los Angeles County's arguments that the federal government's list is unreliable, and that creating a novel system to segregate ballots while voting is already underway is infeasible.

"[T]here is a material risk that granting the United States its requested relief would result in disenfranchisement and could jeopardize the County's entire election," 9th Circuit Judges Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, and Gabriel Sanchez, a Biden appointee, wrote in their Friday decision rejecting the Justice Department's emergency request.

The two judges cited longstanding legal precedent, known as the Purcell principle, that election rules should not be altered on the eve of an election, as well as the fact that the Constitution gives states authority to run elections. The opinion also cited the National Voter Registration Act, which bars states from systematically removing ineligible voters within 90 days of a federal election.

The panel's third judge, Patrick Bumatay, also a Trump appointee, dissented.

The actual number of ballots in dispute is likely much smaller than 20,000, since county election officials have found that many of the people on DOJ's list did not have active voter registrations and were not mailed ballots.

Over the weekend, data scientists at University of California Los Angeles' Voting Rights Project were granted access to the DOJ's list through a court order in another lawsuit and found that 42% of the names on the list do not appear on California's current voter roll. That analysis also found naturalized citizens on the DOJ's list.

The Justice Department's appeal to the Supreme Court comes as it has been escalating its feud with California election officials.

In recent weeks, the Department of Justice has sent subpoenas to election officials in California, and reminded officials that they could be criminally prosecuted for allowing ineligible voters to cast ballots.

A federal judge in San Francisco issued a temporary restraining order late Friday barring the Trump administration from threatening, intimidating or coercing election officials to demand they stop processing the ballots of registered voters that the federal government alleges are ineligible to vote. The federal government has appealed the order.
