text:
Where the appellants — two immigration attorneys, a law firm and a legal services organization — filed suit to enjoin the Department of Homeland Security from routing discovery in immigration proceedings through Freedom of Information Act requests, the dismissal of the complaint should be affirmed because the appellants do not have standing to assert their claims.

“A group of two immigration attorneys, a law firm, and a legal services organization (collectively, the ‘Appellants’) filed suit to enjoin the Department of Homeland Security (‘DHS’) from routing discovery in immigration proceedings through Freedom of Information Act (‘FOIA’) requests. Appellants brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act (‘APA’), 5 U.S.C. §706, et seq., challenging this alleged ‘Nondisclosure Policy’ as violative of the Due Process Clause, the Immigration and Nationality Act, and DHS regulations. The district court dismissed all the claims at the motion to dismiss and summary judgment stages. Appellants appealed those decisions. After our own review, we conclude that Appellants lack Article III standing to challenge the Nondisclosure Policy. Accordingly, we affirm the district court’s judgment for the government, albeit on different grounds. …

“Appellants’ sweeping challenge is based on examples of FOIA referrals which occurred within different component agencies of DHS, i.e., removal proceedings undertaken by ICE, and asylum adjudications conducted by USCIS. But specific, disjointed instances of such referrals, without more, do not amount to an ‘agency action’ in the form of an agency-wide policy. … Further, because the ‘action’ Appellants allege is a collection of decentralized immigration interactions that vary in their details among the varying Agencies, it is not even entirely clear whether the harm that is asserted (i.e., the withholding or delay in making information available) will even occur in any specific instance. For example, the complaint itself alleges, and the summary judgment record confirmed, that the information a noncitizen obtains in affirmative asylum proceedings depends on a wide range of factors, including the discretion of the asylum officer. The purported Nondisclosure Policy is simply Appellants’ conclusory label that describes practices whereby various Agencies make varying degrees of information available by varying means in various proceedings. As we see it, because Appellants have failed to establish the existence of the so-called Nondisclosure Policy occurring throughout the entirety of DHS in a uniform manner, we cannot conclude that their alleged injury is ‘concrete.’ …

“Moreover, even if we assume, for the sake of argument, that a Nondisclosure Policy does exist, we find Appellants’ arguments in support of organizational standing unpersuasive. Appellants liken their bid for standing to the plaintiff organization in Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982). There, says Appellants, the Supreme Court found that the plaintiff organization suffered an injury in fact because defendants’ actions affected their ‘core business activities.’ …

“We do not think Appellants’ alleged injury is analogous to the harm present in Havens. …

“Havens‘ core-business-activities exception cannot mean that any lawyer, law firm, or ‘organization that provides free legal assistance’ may assert organizational standing, in lieu of representing an individual plaintiff, by alleging that a challenged policy increases the cost of representation or limits the size of a client roster. …

“In sum, if we accepted Appellants’ theory of standing in this case, it could functionally eliminate the Article III standing requirements for any lawyer who seeks to invalidate a government policy. If a lawyer wished to package his disagreement with the policy in a case or controversy, all he would have to do is represent a client whom the policy regulates. Then the lawyer could walk into court, leave the client at the door, and claim for his own sake that the policy makes it harder to represent the client. We do not think that this is what the Supreme Court had in mind as falling within Havens‘ context. …”

Greater Boston Legal Services, et al. v. United States Department of Homeland Security, et al. (Lawyers Weekly No. 01-240-26) (21 pages) (Gelpí, J.) Appealed from a decision by Casper, J., in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts. Sandra H. Masselink, with whom Adriana Lafaille, John T. Montgomery, American Civil Liberties Union Foundation of Massachusetts, Inc., and Ropes & Gray were on brief, for the plaintiffs-appellants; Susan M. Finegan, Emily Kanstroom Musgrave, Gabrielle Brown, Alexa Greco, Cassandra Harris, Savannah Wormley, Mintz, Levin, Cohn, Ferris, Glovsky, and Popeo, P.C., and Nicholas A. Butto on brief for American Immigration Lawyers Association, amicus curiae for the appellants; Simon G. Jerome, with whom Brett A. Shumate, Leah B. Foley and Charles W. Scarborough were on brief, for the defendants-appellees (Docket No. 25-1799) (Oct. 29, 2026).

title: Immigrant advocacy groups file lawsuit against TN over drivers license policies
description:
A new legal battle is brewing in Tennessee.
Immigrant advocacy groups have filed a lawsuit against the Department of Safety and Homeland Security over an abrupt shift in driver’s license policies.
The lawsuit, filed by the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition and the National Immigration Law Center, challenges a state rule restricting the federal documents accepted for temporary licenses.
Advocates say the change suddenly excludes thousands of legally authorized residents—including DACA recipients and work permit holders—who have driven safely in the state for decades.
The state has declined to comment on the pending litigation, but plaintiffs are asking a Davidson County court to immediately halt the policy, arguing it was implemented unlawfully without public input.

title: Andrea R. Flores: 'Democrats are a decade behind on coming up with an answer to immigration'
description:
Andrea Flores (Las Cruces, New Mexico, 1988) has spent years keeping that debate alive against all odds.
The question is: are Democrats building an immigration system where ICE is more professional, where agents don’t wear masks?
But after the Biden administration, Democrats were saying: we want to end asylum, we want to shut down the border.
Democrats are a decade behind on coming up with an answer.
For Democrats not to add that back as an advantage they actually have over Republicans would be a massive mistake.
text:
The United States is living through a strange moment. Thanks to Trump’s policies, border crossings have fallen to levels not seen in decades. At the same time, Americans have watched ICE and Border Patrol agents hunt down immigrants in their streets, with abuses and acts of violence that have provoked open outrage. And yet, in Washington, talking about a more humane immigration policy remains almost taboo, regardless of party.

Andrea Flores (Las Cruces, New Mexico, 1988) has spent years keeping that debate alive against all odds. She knows the problem from the inside: she grew up in southern New Mexico, near the border, and worked in the White House under Barack Obama and Joe Biden, in the Senate and at the Department of Homeland Security, trying to modernize the immigration system. On her Substack, Securing America’s Promise, and in outlets such as The New York Times and CNN, she presses one idea: the system is unjust and riddled with provisions that allowed Trump to push restrictions to an unprecedented extreme. Reforming it, to lift millions of people out of legal limbo, is urgent and yet nearly impossible, given the lack of will in both parties.

None of this discourages her. Although Trump has locked in ICE’s funding through the end of his term, Flores believes a Democratic victory in the midterm elections, even if only in the House, could reopen the national conversation on reform. But she warns that Democrats still lack an alternative of their own, and failing to build one would be a fatal mistake.

Q. How do you assess Trump’s immigration policies?

A. They are the most extreme immigration policies we’ve seen in modern American history. He brought a long-time, multigenerational anti-immigrant movement into the White House, and he took ideas that used to be very fringe — ending birthright citizenship, suspending the refugee program, ending asylum as we know it — and he is implementing all of those. One of the reasons he is able to operate such an extreme agenda is that immigration law itself, in many ways, permits it. Directing the secretary of state to revoke visas from students for their political views: that’s an existing immigration law. Picking up long-time immigrants who haven’t committed any crimes and sitting them in detention: that’s our current immigration system. It’s full of provisions that should have been removed long ago, and both parties left certain tools in place, assuming nobody would misuse them. It has always been possible for ICE and the Border Patrol to be deployed in the ways we’ve seen under this administration. If the laws are written that way, all you need is one president with the intent of turning it into a federal police force and changing the nature of who gets to be here.

Q. Where does that come from?

A. Since chattel slavery, we have been in a national debate over who gets to be a citizen. Then you had waves of immigration that built up the American economy as we know it: Chinese immigrants in the late 19th century, then European immigrants and, for really the last century, Mexican and Central American immigrants. When we bring in people who are actively building up certain industries, we tend to leave them undocumented, because our political bodies can’t answer whether they should stay, but we keep using their labor. That’s why the United States has the largest undocumented population in the world.

A lot of the reason I got into this work was that I felt this was deeply unfinished work from the Chicano movement and the civil rights movement: as long as we have a noncitizen workforce that is predominantly racial minorities, that is not good for the rest of the minority communities in this country. Trump has proven that by showing how easy it is to racially profile people of Latin American descent.

Q. Where does the idea of a multiracial democracy stand today?

A. If you’d asked me a year ago, I would have said Americans were nervous about demographic change after the Biden administration, when they saw a lot of people cross the border. But what you saw when thousands of federal agents invaded Minneapolis surprised many experts, including myself. In Washington, we operate as though Americans will only support one type of immigrant with one type of status. Instead, we witnessed Americans in a city standing up for their neighbors, sitting outside construction sites when roofers were trapped on a roof in the cold, organizing. That was a real rebuke to Trump. The Latinos who voted for Trump appear to be swinging back, as people realize what mass deportation really means. And we’re only getting started.

Q. Is this a turning point, or a backlash against excesses that doesn’t amount to support for an alternative?

A. I would say the latter. We are seeing a reaction to perceived overreach. People still think immigration enforcement has a role to play, but they do not like what they are seeing in terms of racial profiling. The reason I don’t believe it’s a bigger shift is that Americans are not yet being offered an alternative. There is not a pro-immigrant party offering an alternative right now. There is just a restrictionist party offering deportation.

The question is: are Democrats building an immigration system where ICE is more professional, where agents don’t wear masks? Or are they moving us toward a system where fewer people are subject to deportation — because we know they make up one in four construction workers in Texas, almost half of the dairy industry — using something like legalization? That’s the world I hope Democrats start fighting for, instead of just saying ICE reforms are the end of the road. Because what that says to me is: you’re trying to deport grandmothers more professionally. We’ve had more professional versions of ICE before, but we still have the largest undocumented population in the world.

Q. What would make voters trust Democrats to govern on immigration?

A. What I experience regularly is Democrats thinking: we have nothing to gain by ever talking about it, we only have things to lose. Republicans spend so much money and so much time talking about immigration. There are better issues for Democrats — health care, the cost of living — and those should be at the top of the agenda. But you cannot refuse to have an affirmative plan on the president’s top issue.

I support Congressman Gabe Vasquez, in a must-win House district in southern New Mexico. He put out a bill for a care-worker visa that would also legalize some undocumented care workers. It’s an easy concept for the average American to understand: your current care worker doesn’t have a path to citizenship; I know you want to keep them here; here’s an option. That’s solving a problem for an American family.

Q. Why piecemeal instead of comprehensive reform?

A. I worked on the last comprehensive reform. It came through a trade: we’ll do more on the border if you legalize people. But after the Biden administration, Democrats were saying: we want to end asylum, we want to shut down the border. So what are they trading now for a path to citizenship? Most Americans don’t care about the form it takes. And I don’t think it’s been good that we’ve segmented immigration out from other core issues. If Democrats pass a big housing bill, there should be a workforce component in it — a combination of new visas and legalizing current construction workers — because we know you already need those workers. Ideas like a state-sponsored visa could be really smart, because every state has different immigration needs. I think about New Mexico, about [organic food company] Hatch Chile. Allow states to raise their hand and say: these are the immigrants I need.

Q. Why did so many Latinos swing toward Trump?

A. I’m from southern New Mexico. I grew up in a border community, and I was unsurprised. Sitting in the White House in Biden’s first year, all we did was dismiss Latino border communities. We ignored exactly what they were telling us about what was happening at the border. Then you add the mistake of not doing anything about people being bused into cities, and long-time undocumented community members seeing new arrivals receive work permits they had never received. It was the border plus dropping this long-time Democratic promise.

And in the 2024 campaign, you never heard either President Biden or Vice President Harris explain what mass deportation actually is: that it would mean anyone with an immigration violation. Their silence allowed a lot of people to believe: well, he’s going to get these new people out, and that seems fine with me. So Latino voters now feel very betrayed. They say: we thought you meant someone else, not us. We didn’t think you’d stop the DoorDash drivers, the construction workers.

Q. ICE and Border Patrol are funded through 2029. If Democrats win only the House, what can they actually do?

A. It will be very difficult, because giving people legal status is the single most protective thing Congress could do. They could try to claw back resources, but that requires Trump to sign a bill. So their most powerful tool is going to be oversight, to grow the unpopularity of mass deportation. We’ve seen President Trump pull back before: after family separation, he ended the policy. Democrats have an opportunity to link this to the arguments they’re making in other spaces: who is getting rich off of our family members being detained? What was traded to send a long-time U.S. resident to a country on the African continent they have no ties to? They could pass a bill saying ICE cannot make arrests at schools, hospitals, and other sensitive locations. But President Trump would veto it.

Q. He’ll veto anything. So, nothing substantial changes until Trump is gone?

A. This is where I wish Democrats were a little more cutthroat: make him say, “No, I want ICE in schools.” Force him to veto it. People want fighters. I believe what we’re starting is organizing toward the end of the Trump era. But Democrats have to decide they don’t want to be a country where ICE can stop any Latino and ask for their papers. You have to change the law to do that.

Q. What should a Democratic majority investigate first?

A. Some of the more explosive oversight will be around contracting: deals for warehouses being built around the country to detain people, the funding transfer to Florida for Alligator Alcatraz. We still need many more details about the El Salvador agreement. Are they trading natural resources for detention and deportation flights? Congress has been very hands-off with the policies that govern ICE. It has been a norm that ICE doesn’t show up at a hospital, because that’s bad for public health. What this has shown is that the norm is meaningless if a president doesn’t want to follow it.

A few whistleblowers have exposed a rapid hiring process, lowering qualification standards for people to carry a lethal weapon in our streets. My first encounter with Border Patrol as a citizen, I was 12 years old, leaving middle school. Border Patrol has long held very bad and invasive practices, and now there’s a pipeline from Border Patrol to ICE. The agent who killed Renee Nicole Good was a Border Patrol agent, and it was a group of Border Patrol agents who killed Alex Pretti, both in Minneapolis. People didn’t care when those practices were at the border, but now it’s in your street. I’m very curious about which of the president’s friends are getting rich off of mass deportation.

Q. On legalization, who comes first: Dreamers, TPS holders, long-time residents?

A. Where I sit, I still feel like I’m convincing Democrats to put forward legalization again, to even consider going beyond the American Dream and Promise Act, which would protect Dreamers and TPS holders but would leave out a huge portion of the undocumented population. When I think about some of the most painful moments of the past year — the death of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo — he would not be covered by either bill. How do you make the case that someone like Lorenzo, who was American except for the lack of a document — how does this Congress protect him?

When we make it all or nothing, one attempt, like under the Reagan administration, everyone feels we did it once. But we need to do it multiple times, and I can imagine different champions. If there’s a senator who really cares about military families, that person should lead a legalization of military family members. It sounds piecemeal, but what it really is is trying to add on to the base and not leave people out. The easiest thing in the world would be to say: let’s change the registry date. But Democrats aren’t there. This is the same group of Democrats who voted for the Laken Riley Act.

Q. Do the progressive wing and the center approach it differently?

A. They both lack answers and vision. Progressives have been really concrete about their goals on affordability. Then they say things like “Abolish ICE.” And I tell them: I would give anything for you to organize around legalization instead, because you can abolish ICE and it will just be moved into something different, but you’ll still have the undocumented population.

Say you have an American family — I get these calls all the time — and they say: this neighbor who works at our store, whom I’ve known for 10 years, has just been taken away. What can I do? And I tell them there’s nothing you can do. There’s no line for them to get into. There’s no way for you to sponsor them. There’s no way to help your neighbor. If we aren’t responding as a party to that missing piece of the law, we’ve failed to respond to this moment in history.

Q. Can Democrats defend an orderly border and a functioning asylum system without accepting Trump’s approach?

A. We could have built a system that worked differently. I joined the Biden administration to do that. I ran the wind-down of Remain in Mexico, but what it really was was a test of what it would look like to work with the border community and with Mexico to triage the most vulnerable asylum seekers in an orderly process. That process got stopped. What ended up happening was three years of absolute chaos and disorder.

I resigned. We were not trying to prevent catastrophes like 10,000 Haitians showing up at the border one day without the White House knowing it was happening. I didn’t want to be part of pretending we were doing the best we could for my own community. I saw community spaces in Las Cruces, New Mexico, turned into shelters. I fly home through El Paso, and I’d never seen migrants sleeping on the floor all along the El Paso airport. The Biden White House didn’t appreciate that constituency.

Q. Border crossings are near zero. Hasn’t Trump been effective?

A. If you went from 100,000 encounters a month at the worst of it to under 10,000, that’s tangible. Lower border crossings are generally better for everyone involved. But I get nervous when any nation says the border is fixed. Under Biden, we kept Trump’s exact border policy, and in the first weeks of the term, Mexico stopped taking people back in Tamaulipas. All of a sudden, we were in crisis. If Mexico changed its policies, the numbers could go up next week. Trump has the same laws, the same constraints the Biden administration had. That’s why I’m so bullish on Democrats having something else to offer, because I don’t think we can compete with Trump on the perception of the border being closed.

Q. If Latinos prove decisive, how do they turn that into lasting influence?

A. My dream is border communities leading the future of asylum and processing, because they’re the ones who experience it. And I always say you need to show up on the Hill. Something Dreamers were so effective at was getting people to show up and do meetings. Senator Bob Menendez used to say: where are the protesters? Where are the groups pushing us on anything? A big part of developing champions is constituency groups telling them: this was our vote, and this is something we need you to act on. If you look at early press conferences from the future speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, immigration is not on the priority list. That is the signal to all those voters.

Q. According to a May UnidosUS poll, immigration reform ranks fifth among Latinos’ concerns.

A. I’ve never been a proponent of it being any Democrat’s top issue. But Democrats will suffer consequences if they don’t address it, because they’ll find themselves taking over another White House — this is my lesson learned from Biden — thinking opposition to Trump was enough to substitute for a vision on immigration. There are going to be more American citizens impacted. Operation Wetback in the 1950s was a model for what we’re seeing now, but that was more concentrated in the Southwest and California. It’s almost like Minneapolis was an acute emergency-room situation, and now the whole country has a low-grade fever. This White House was okay doing meatpacking raids in Kansas when they may lose a seat there. Democrats are a decade behind on coming up with an answer.

Q. Can you build a majority for legalization without reducing immigrants to their economic usefulness?

A. I find the economic argument more compelling than I did earlier in my career. Do you reduce immigrants to their economic contributions, or do you try to get Americans to see them as the full human beings they are? Right now, because of President Trump’s own actions, there’s a new way to bring people into seeing how the average American benefits from ICE not being in their communities. Jazmine Ulloa of The New York Times told me Latinos say it’s like a second pandemic. People are staying home again and having friends deliver their groceries. That is an economic chilling effect for everyone. Where ICE arrests have exceeded the average for an area, Americans have lost jobs. When you have a president who wants to deport every immigrant in your community, you lose out.

Q. If Democrats win on November 3 and still can’t stop the deportation machine, what would be unforgivable not to even attempt?

A. Not attempting to pass as many legalization vehicles as possible, and not making sure every American knows that you have one party with a plan to protect their neighbor, their employee, and their family member, and another party that is going to keep taking those people from your homes and communities. A path to citizenship is very popular. For Democrats not to add that back as an advantage they actually have over Republicans would be a massive mistake.

title: ICE, inflation and Trump: gen Z readers share their concerns heading into the voting both
description:
Gen Z readers across the country highlighted to the Guardian the issues shaping their views ahead of the election.
Charlie, a 22-year-old library worker in Ohio, pointed to healthcare and affordability as the most important issues shaping their vote.
Emily, a 28-year-old living in central Illinois, identified artificial intelligence, Israel’s war on Gaza and ICE as among the biggest concerns shaping the political landscape.
Similar concerns about the prospect of Democratic underperformance were raised by Connor Long, a 29-year-old remote sales representative in Orlando, Florida.
Long said he was “excited to see how this election is shaping up but am leery of the data we are seeing.”
text:
The 2026 US midterms are approaching against a backdrop of growing political uncertainty, with young voters increasingly mobilizing around concerns about the country’s future.

Although nearly 50 million Americans aged 18 to 29 are eligible to vote in the midterms, almost half remain either unregistered or civically disengaged, according to US Census Bureau data.

Gen Z readers across the country highlighted to the Guardian the issues shaping their views ahead of the election. Among their biggest concerns were the rising cost of living, federal immigration policies, the climate crisis, election interference and the rollback of civil rights.

For Tyler, a 24-year-old working at a community church in Richfield, Minnesota, “ICE, inflation and worries about [Donald] Trump’s military force have been … huge factor[s] in voting this year.”

“I like going to the grocery store but I don’t like seeing the price increase amid this unpopular and illegal war,” Tyler said, adding: “​​Fascism is taking hold and I want there to be some semblance of accountability, and I want to make sure that we actually have a real opposition party that we’re not seeing at the moment, aside from some candidates.”

However, even a Democratic victory would not necessarily ease concerns about election integrity, with Tyler worrying that “there will be some trickery and subversion of results or another version of January 6”.

Charlie, a 22-year-old library worker in Ohio, pointed to healthcare and affordability as the most important issues shaping their vote.

“Advocating against universal healthcare indicates, to me, a deep disregard for the actual wellbeing of the American people. Also, the wealth disparity in the US is astronomical, so advocating for a greater tax on the ultra-wealthy is important to me as well. People who have to work to survive are doing so poorly right now, all I want is to see life become affordable again,” Charlie said.

For a 25-year-old maintenance worker in Connecticut, the financial pressures of everyday life can also make civic participation difficult.

“I do want to vote, but that depends on how accessible it is. If I have the time and energy I go out and vote. I do work a lot. I have a lot of bills to pay (car, car insurance, rent, utilities, student loans, medical bills). It is hard to find time to do just about anything,” they said.

They also expressed frustration with the candidates on offer, saying that a lack of confidence in either party could make deciding how to vote difficult.

“The problem is I am worried that if I vote, I will vote wrong because I don’t really trust any of the people up for office … I don’t want to vote for a Republican, but I also don’t want to vote for [Connecticut governor Ned] Lamont because his track record of doing what he said he would (even trying) is not very good and he has put more money into corporate pockets than into the working class,” they said.

“I am concerned that any meaningfully good legislation will have bullcrap logrolled into it for things that our communities don’t want. I also worry that the almighty American dollar will blind every politician in the race and none of them will have actual integrity,” they added.

Emily, a 28-year-old living in central Illinois, identified artificial intelligence, Israel’s war on Gaza and ICE as among the biggest concerns shaping the political landscape.

“Our refusal to acknowledge the cruelty and absurdity of this administration has normalized it into our culture, if it wasn’t there already. Any attempt to criticize it is shot down with claims of hysteria or wokeness. Our … participation in this modern propaganda will have lasting impacts. I am deeply concerned how the world looks at us, and how we will look back at ourselves,” Emily said.

Looking ahead to the election, Emily said the hope is to see “any politician that looks like they actually have a backbone and won’t just tweet that someone should do something about this”.

The climate crisis and immigration enforcement are also shaping how young voters view the election.

Matthew Doutt, a 26-year-old accountant in Knoxville, Tennessee, said: “This administration has done deep damages to the guardrails meant to defend against climate change, and we need someone – anyone – to get us back on track … Unfortunately, with me being in a conservative state that’s been heavily gerrymandered, no one stands out in my state in a positive way.”

He also raised concerns about the potential presence of federal immigration agents at polling locations.

“Tennessee is one of several states that has partnered with ICE for local enforcement. I’m expecting to see ICE at polling locations to supposedly prevent against undocumented immigrants [from] voting but I expect it to be more about intimidating liberals,” Doutt said.

For Niamh Catterall, an 18-year-old university student from Texas currently studying in Ireland, the election will mark her first time voting. She plans to cast her ballot by mail, with the war, cost of living, protections for minorities and immigrants, and the separation of church and state among her main concerns.

“I am hopeful of a break from party politics and a renewed focus on how a candidate can help a society or individual. In the case of many of the candidates who I support, such as [Gina] Hinojosa or [James] Talarico, their platforms go beyond experience or big picture, federal politics like being aligned with Trump and actually focus on what groups within the state need, whether that is healthcare or cost of living,” Catterall said.

For Nathan, a 21-year-old computer science student in Texas, LGBTQ+ rights and datacenter expansions are key issues amid the performances of Democratic candidates in the state.

“It really excites me to see how well Talarico is doing! The idea of a blue Texas is mind-blowing to me,” Nathan said, adding: “I know that Democratic candidates in southern states almost always lose. I also really wish that more people my age voted.”

However, for Scott, a 29-year-old software engineer in Washington who has already voted, concerns about the future span both sides of the political aisle.

“I’m extremely concerned with the lack of leadership from both parties, but especially with the imminent harm from the Republican party, and Trump in particular. This level of corruption is unprecedented and unacceptable. Although my state is not competitive on the national stage, I felt it was at least something I could do,” Scott said.

He also described a growing sense of economic and political uncertainty among young Americans, alongside frustration with what he sees as a lack of a compelling vision from Democrats.

“My career went from a sure thing to unknown in less than 10 years. I, and many others, especially my age, are not optimistic for the future … I’m emotionally raw, and very tired. My biggest concern is that Democrats won’t rally behind a unifying coherent vision for the future that we can get excited about. I’ve literally heard Democrats say we need a vision for years. They need to get one now … It doesn’t need to be perfect, and it’s OK if there’s unknowns, but it needs to be something that the vast majority of Americans can rally behind,” he added.

Similar concerns about the prospect of Democratic underperformance were raised by Connor Long, a 29-year-old remote sales representative in Orlando, Florida.

Long said he was “excited to see how this election is shaping up but am leery of the data we are seeing.”

text:
Voters heading into Tuesday's midterm elections face a choice that reaches beyond who controls Congress: whether lawmakers should preserve Immigration and Customs Enforcement, dismantle it, or cut off the money supporting detention and deportation operations.

Across House and Senate races, candidates have proposed changes ranging from abolishing ICE to ending immigration detention contracts and allowing civil rights lawsuits against federal officers. Some have introduced legislation; others are campaigning on commitments they would pursue if elected.

The divide extends within the Democratic Party. At its August meeting, the Democratic National Committee approved separate, nonbinding resolutions supporting reform and abolition, leaving candidates to define their own positions. These 15 candidates illustrate how far that debate now reaches.

In Michigan, Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has made abolition an explicit campaign demand. "You can't reform ICE, you can't retrain ICE, you have to abolish ICE," he said during the primary, according to his campaign's account of a debate. He faces Republican Mike Rogers in the race to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters.

Minnesota's Democratic Senate nominee, Peggy Flanagan, calls for dismantling ICE and replacing it with an immigration system built around public safety, due process and a pathway to legal status. Her platform also supports secure borders and investment in immigration courts, staffing and technology. Her position pairs institutional replacement with continued immigration enforcement.

Massachusetts Sen. Ed Markey, seeking reelection, has explicitly called for defunding and abolishing ICE. He opposed a January funding package that temporarily extended DHS funding and has joined Rep. Ayanna Pressley in legislation to end qualified immunity for federal officers. "We must defund and abolish ICE," Markey said in January.

In the House, Illinois Rep. Delia Ramirez, running in the 3rd District, has proposed one of the broadest institutional overhauls. Her Reimagining Safety Act would dismantle DHS, abolish ICE and Customs and Border Protection, and establish a Department of Community Safety. The proposal would preserve functions including disaster response, transportation security, cybersecurity and customs while beginning a separate civil immigration system.

Massachusetts Rep. Ayanna Pressley, running in the 7th District, combines abolition demands with an effort to expand legal accountability. Her Qualified Immunity Abolition Act with Markey would allow civil rights claims against federal law enforcement officers and eliminate the qualified-immunity defense. She also voted against January's DHS funding bill. "There is no reforming this lawless agency," she said.

Michigan Rep. Rashida Tlaib, seeking reelection in the 12th District, is an original cosponsor of Ramirez's restructuring bill. Her record also includes support for a moratorium on government facial recognition and biometric surveillance, including technologies used in immigration enforcement.

Arizona Rep. Adelita Grijalva, running in the 7th District, is another original cosponsor of the Reimagining Safety Act. That places her behind a legislative proposal to eliminate ICE and CBP while transferring or preserving other homeland-security functions, rather than simply changing agency leadership.

Massachusetts Rep. Jim McGovern, running in the 2nd District, also signed on as an original cosponsor. His support puts another senior House Democrat behind replacing DHS with a department organized around community safety.

Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar, seeking reelection in the 5th District, has called for abolishing ICE and introduced the Make ICE Pay Act. According to her office, the measure would redirect $140 billion allocated to ICE and CBP through the 2025 Republican tax-and-spending law into communities affected by immigration-enforcement surges.

New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, running in the 14th District, explicitly supports abolishing ICE in her campaign platform. She reiterated that demand in an October statement responding to an ICE shooting in New York. Her position calls for eliminating the agency, going beyond requirements for cameras, identification or additional training.

Washington Rep. Pramila Jayapal, seeking reelection in the 7th District, has called for dismantling ICE while conducting congressional oversight of detention facilities and enforcement practices. In an October account of her work, she argued that the agency must be dismantled and its violence ended. Her oversight agenda includes hearings, detention-center visits and demands for information about officer-involved shootings.

Pennsylvania Rep. Summer Lee, running in the 12th District, helped unveil the Melt ICE Act with Ramirez and Rep. Yvette Clarke. The proposal would strip immigration-detention authorities, end existing detention contracts within two years and prohibit new contracts. Lee described it as a step toward abolishing the agency.

New York Rep. Yvette Clarke, seeking reelection in the 9th District, is also advancing that legislation. It would require DHS to develop a plan to remove immigrants from ankle monitors within six months and redirect funding toward community services, including housing and health care.

New Jersey Rep. Analilia Mejia, running for a full term in the 11th District after winning April's special election, makes her position explicit on her campaign website: "It's Time to Abolish ICE." The former labor organizer also discussed abolition in a March interview with NJ Spotlight News.

Arkansas Democratic challenger Robb Ryerse, running in the 3rd District, supports abolishing ICE and redirecting enforcement money toward immigration judges and staff to reduce case backlogs. He also supports a pathway to legalization for undocumented residents. Ryerse is challenging Republican Rep. Steve Womack.

The proposals would require different legislative paths. Funding restrictions would limit what the agency can spend; abolishing ICE or rewriting detention law would change its underlying structure. Ending qualified immunity would address civil liability for officers. Winning Tuesday would give supporters an opportunity to advance those measures, but passage would still require congressional approval and a president's signature, or sufficient votes to override a veto.

title: Why Immigration Agents Don't Quit in Protest | The New Yorker
description:
Still, there was a feeling among immigration agents that they were being shackled by the new Administration.
By 2024, the Border Patrol had lost a quarter of its workforce, with many longtime agents opting for early retirement.
The operation was so unpopular with the rank and file that Border Patrol and ICE struggled to find personnel for the deployment.
In a conversation with Vox about why Border Patrol agents obey immoral orders, he warned against placing the moral onus on individuals over institutions.
And yet, the more I learned about Barry’s movement, the more I imagined the possibility of a similar community of former immigration agents.
text:
In the winter of 2018, Joshua Childress was sent to the Yuma Regional Medical Center, in southwest Arizona, to guard a man who’d fallen from a thirty-foot-high border wall. Childress was in his seventh year in the United States Border Patrol and had grown accustomed to doing hospital watch, in which agents monitor recently apprehended migrants to insure that they don’t escape while receiving care. To Childress’s surprise, the injured man spoke fluent English. Childress asked why he had come to the U.S. “Because this is my home,” the man replied.

The man, who appeared to be in his early twenties, had lived in Arizona since he was eight years old—longer than Childress had been in the state himself. A few months earlier, the man had hosted a barbecue at his house, and neighbors had called in a noise complaint. The police came, asked for the man’s I.D., and reported him to immigration authorities, who deported him to Mexico. Childress asked why the man hadn’t sought Dreamer status under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, which provides protection from deportation for certain undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children. The man explained that he had wanted to, but his father had been afraid that the paperwork was a trick meant to entrap them.

Childress listened as the man described the mountain town where he’d grown up, a place that sounded much like the community where Childress was raised, in rural Colorado. “I barely speak Spanish,” the man told Childress. “I don’t know anybody in Mexico. I’ve been down there wandering around for three months, trying to figure out what to do, and I decided, You know what? I’ll take my chances and come back here. And then I fell from the fence and broke my leg.”

The doctor arrived and announced that the man had suffered a complete fracture and recommended that he seek surgery as soon as he was back in Mexico. If the injury went untreated, the doctor warned, it could lead to sepsis. For now, he said, the man would be fitted with a temporary cast and returned to Border Patrol custody.

Like all agents, Childress had come face to face with countless migrants; he was familiar with their struggles. But he was adept at pushing aside stories of misfortune to focus instead on the border crossers who had serious criminal histories—the arrests he felt good about. Increasingly, however, Childress had begun to question whether the vast majority of the migrants he encountered, most of whom had come to the country to change tires or pick lettuce or work in construction, really posed a threat. Once, a man at the Yuma processing center had removed his shirt to show Childress marks on his back, where he had been whipped by smugglers after he refused to carry a bundle of drugs across the border. The lashes, it occurred to Childress later, were “Christlike.”

As Childress transported the man with the broken leg to the Border Patrol station, it struck him that he was about to send someone many people would consider a “model immigrant” to potential doom. Nevertheless, he off-loaded the man in the station’s gated sally port and handed him over to a colleague to be processed for deportation, just as he had done countless times before. This, after all, was the job.

I first heard of Childress in the fall of 2018, when reading an article that he wrote for the Daily Beast titled “Why I Quit the Border Patrol.” “I ultimately realized that I was putting people in cages for non-violent offenses, something I opposed in every other area of the law,” he wrote. “I was impeding the movement of people when I wanted to be able to move freely around the world. I was enforcing the rules of a game I had won simply by being born on the right side of a line.”

Reading Childress’s account was like looking in a rearview mirror. I had quit the Border Patrol for similar reasons in 2012, after nearly four years as an agent, and had spent the next phase of my life trying to make sense of my participation in the militarized violence of immigration enforcement, working as a barista and a bartender while attending school to become a writer and a teacher. Childress’s departure from the Border Patrol came shortly after the implementation of Donald Trump’s “zero-tolerance policy,” under which parents were separated from their children at the border, sparking a national uproar. At the time, it was possible to believe that agents’ understanding of their work might be changing.

That summer, more than a dozen Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents signed a letter to the Secretary of Homeland Security, Kirstjen Nielsen, calling for the agency to be disbanded. In July of 2019, Jenn Budd, who had resigned from the Border Patrol nearly two decades earlier, wrote an “Open Letter from an Ex-Border Patrol Agent,” calling on current agents to demand change or quit in protest of the immoral orders that they were being asked to carry out. The following year, Wesley Farris, a high-ranking member of the Border Patrol’s notoriously hard-line union, spoke out against the zero-tolerance policy, telling PBS’s “Frontline” that separating children from their parents “was the most horrible thing I’ve ever done.” But remarkably few agents followed in Childress’s footsteps; Farris, for example, refused to participate in separations but did not quit, asking his supervisor to assign him elsewhere instead.

Much of the outcry stirred by the harsh policies of the first Trump Administration was quelled by Joe Biden’s promise of a more measured approach. His Presidency saw a record increase in migrant encounters at the border, a fact that is often attributed to lax enforcement. In fact, the Biden Administration left several of Trump’s restrictionist policies in place, and detentions at the border increased twelvefold while total removals tripled. Still, there was a feeling among immigration agents that they were being shackled by the new Administration. By 2024, the Border Patrol had lost a quarter of its workforce, with many longtime agents opting for early retirement. They often blamed the President. “Under Biden, things are the worst they have ever been by far,” one agent told the Washington Examiner, adding, “Agents are afraid of ending up on the news for doing their job or getting in trouble for doing their job. There is no morale.”

With Trump back in the White House, many agents now regard the Administration as once again on their side. But the demands of meeting its overarching goal—deporting a million people a year, per Trump’s top domestic-policy adviser, Stephen Miller—have led to a new form of strain. In 2025, The Atlantic reported that ICE’s workforce “has never been so miserable.” Employees have become burned out and morally conflicted as their focus has shifted from pursuing drug smugglers and human traffickers to apprehending asylum seekers in courthouses and arresting day laborers at their worksites. Another agent said that he was contemplating quitting rather than continuing to spend his days “arresting gardeners.”

In early 2026, after the murders of Renee Good and Alex Pretti during Operation Metro Surge, in Minneapolis, the journalist Ken Klippenstein reported that many immigration agents were “getting seriously paranoid” about the public backlash to the shootings. The operation was so unpopular with the rank and file that Border Patrol and ICE struggled to find personnel for the deployment. By July, morale among immigration officers had dipped below its nadir during the Biden Administration, with agents now complaining of being overextended, inundated with novice recruits, and undermined by inflammatory rhetoric from on high. Agents said that they had previously found motivation in their jobs by “being able to stop bad people and narcotics from coming in,” and expressed frustration that the Administration’s political posturing was distracting from their duty to “protect the public” and to focus on “the very worst of the worst.”

The sociologist Irene Vega, in her 2025 book “Bordering on Indifference,” draws on a series of interviews with Border Patrol and ICE agents to analyze the “moral economy” of the immigration-enforcement workforce. From the moment agents arrive at the federal law-enforcement academy, she writes, they “are trained and socialized as police officers, and taught that their raison d’être is to protect America by preventing the entrance and executing the removal of noncitizens deemed unwanted by the state.” The inherently bureaucratic nature of enforcing immigration law has always been at odds with the paramilitary image that is sold to most recruits. Agents prepare for violent criminal encounters and cultivate a “warrior mentality” despite the fact that they are most often, as Vega writes, “at war with an enemy that does not fight back.”

Many agents who have quit for moral reasons cite this tension. In a 2019 article for The American Scholar, Brendan Lenihan, a former Border Patrol agent, wrote, “The federal government taught me how to shoot an assault rifle from a moving vehicle and how to fast-rope from a hovering helicopter, but never did anyone explain how to go home at the end of a shift and forget about the migrants I’d apprehended and their stories.” As with Childress, the accumulation of nonthreatening encounters eventually made his job untenable. “I left the Border Patrol because I was exhausted by the tragic stories,” he wrote, “and because the more I saw, the less affected I was by events that had once seemed shocking.”

How is it, then, that so few agents seem to arrive at this moral breaking point? Nearly two-thirds of Americans disapprove of the Trump Administration’s immigration crackdown. It has become customary for agents to mask their faces from public view—D.H.S. maintains that this is to prevent doxing, but it is also emblematic of a growing perception of this work as shameful. In off-duty social situations, agents often obscure what they do to avoid awkwardness and scorn, even hiding the nature of their employment on dating apps. “We can’t always support what happens just because it’s one of us,” a Border Patrol agent had told a private group chat in the wake of Pretti’s killing. And yet, even as their work has grown increasingly cruel, there has been no exodus of agents who reject it.

Last spring, I began reaching out to my former co-workers to hear about their recent experiences in the job. The first who agreed to speak with me, an agent who now works for ICE, suggested that we meet at a diner in Arizona. It had been years since we’d seen each other; in greeting, we clasped hands and embraced. Over coffee, we talked about our families, and he asked about my life as a university professor. Gradually, our conversation turned to our old colleagues. He caught me up on who was still in the Border Patrol, who had transferred to the Canadian border, and who, like him, had gone to work for ICE. Many of my former co-workers, I learned, had become fathers; others had succumbed to alcoholism. A few, he told me, had died by suicide.

Eventually, I asked about his work. As he saw it, morale was good, far better than under Biden—his office had more resources and had expanded with new hires, many of whom had backgrounds in law enforcement and were hard workers. There were caveats, of course. He did not like being sent to arrest people at courthouses during immigration and asylum hearings, which felt like a trick. He thought that it had been a bad idea to send border agents to Minneapolis, since they were accustomed to patrolling barren deserts, “where everybody is an illegal,” and not trained to police the population of an inner city. Something was bound to go wrong, he said.

But he quickly shrugged off any misgivings. The politicized nature of the work was unavoidable. He’d learned to take it in stride long ago. Often, when he was processing someone for removal, the person would sit across from him and begin to recount why they had come to the U.S. Maybe they had family here, maybe they even had kids. Everyone has a story, he said, but it was his job to tell them, “Look, I understand. But you can’t be here.”

In the weeks that followed, I connected with more former co-workers. One, a fellow-Latino whom I’d always known to be sensitive in his treatment of migrants, told me that he “agreed with the mission but not the tactics.” An agent who was still working at the southern border said that, in recent years, ICE agents have become increasingly hostile toward the people they are arresting. “The growth in abuse of rank and authority has become so distorted that due process no longer exists,” he told me, adding that standards of agent accountability had reached new lows.

Despite their qualms, none of the agents I spoke to—many of whom were nearly eligible for retirement—disagreed with current policies strongly enough to leave. But one of them mentioned Aaron Veckey, a former agent who, in 2024, gave a series of interviews to the right-wing media personality James O’Keefe. While in the patrol, Veckey had raised concerns about detention conditions with his superiors, who repeatedly dismissed the issue. He filed a whistle-blower complaint with the U.S. Office of Special Counsel and soon received a cease-and-desist order for “reporting sensitive information outside of Border Patrol,” a charge he was cleared of after an internal investigation. With O’Keefe, he spoke of the “dogma of apathy” that prevailed among agents and compared the treatment of migrants at his station to the torture at Abu Ghraib.

As far as I know, Veckey, who was then less than a year from retirement, is the only non-anonymous active-duty agent to publicly blow the whistle on the agency’s inhumane treatment of migrants. Over the phone, he described images from the peak of asylum-seeker arrivals, in 2023 and 2024, that continued to haunt him. As many as six hundred migrants were detained outdoors without shade in his station’s parking lot and sally port, where temperatures reached a hundred and fifteen degrees in the summer and dipped below freezing in winter. He recalled a night when he found sixty migrants piled on top of one another for warmth. Another agent had shown him a photo of a half-dozen migrants jammed in a porta-potty to share body heat. Despite the freezing temperatures, agents confiscated the migrants’ coats and refused to give them blankets. Veckey remembered being ordered to remove jackets from breast-feeding mothers.

The conditions that Veckey described mirror those which have been reported at temporary ICE facilities during Trump’s second term. In Chicago, hundreds of migrants were held for three or more days in facilities not meant for overnight detention; at the Mesa airport, in Arizona, more than seven hundred people were crowded into a deportation staging facility with a maximum capacity of two hundred and three. In downtown Manhattan, as many as eighty-six people were crammed for three or more days at a time into a temporary holding room on the tenth floor of 26 Federal Plaza. It was one of four immigration-detention spaces at the courthouse, which are designed to hold no more than twenty-two people combined. The Washington Post called the room “a closet of humanity that smelled of sweat, urine and feces.”

“Not everyone felt the same way about how people were being treated,” Veckey told me. “But a lot of people did. A lot of agents looked around, like, ‘This is crazy. This is fucking horrifying.’ ” Others, however, were downright malicious. “There was a lot of petty abuse going on,” he said. “They were relishing treating these people like shit, throwing their phones away for no reason, not giving them water.” One day, while taking a family into custody near the border wall, Veckey watched a co-worker snatch a bowl of porridge from a mother who was shooing away a nearby street dog as she attempted to feed her infant. “That’s my fucking dog,” the agent sneered, taking the bowl from the woman and setting it down in front of the stray. Veckey’s heart sank. “I just wanted to throw up,” he told me. Finally, he intervened: “All I could muster up was ‘Nah bro, we ain’t doing that shit.’ ”

Veckey was also alarmed that other agents refused to stand alongside him after he filed his complaint. “Nobody would join me,” he told me. “The best Christian men I know at that station all had their excuses.” In his interview with O’Keefe, he said it was “one of the biggest pains in my career to know that so many good men are sitting on the sidelines on this.” For the better part of two years, he urged his co-workers to file their own reports, but none did. “I told all these guys, ‘Just call this lawyer. You can do it anonymously,’ ” Veckey told me. “But, nah, they won’t do it. They won’t do it. The guys just won’t fucking do it.”

The brutality of American immigration enforcement is nothing new. The U.S. Border Patrol was created with the passage of the Immigration Act of 1924, a piece of legislation championed by nativist politicians and self-professed eugenicists. The act, which imposed strict quotas on legal migration from Europe and banned migration from Asia altogether, exempted Mexico to appease U.S. agricultural interests and created the Border Patrol to police crossings and to insure that workers left the U.S. after the harvests. Early agents were often former enforcers of the Chinese Exclusion Act—“Chinese Inspectors” and “Mounted Guards”—and ex-Texas Rangers, who’d become notorious during the previous decade for terrorizing borderland Mexicans in a lynching campaign known as La Matanza. Many, too, were active members of the Ku Klux Klan.

According to the historian Greg Grandin, the Border Patrol in its earliest years was a “cult of brutality” that transformed the act of border crossing into “a ritual of abuse.” Migrants were required to pay entrance fees, take literacy tests, and submit to delousing protocols, which meant stripping naked and being doused with kerosene, gasoline, or DDT. Their clothes and other belongings were fumigated with Zyklon B, a cyanide-based pesticide later used in Nazi gas chambers.

Five years after the creation of the Border Patrol, Senator Coleman Blease, an outspoken proponent of segregation and lynching, successfully led an effort to pass the Undesirable Aliens Act of 1929, which made crossing the border without authorization a criminal offense. By 1954, the agency was large enough to launch Operation Wetback, a mass-deportation campaign set in motion by the Eisenhower Administration that mobilized what the Los Angeles Times described as “an army of border patrolmen complete with jeeps, trucks and seven aircraft” in an “all-out war to hurl tens of thousands of Mexican wetbacks into Mexico.”

The operation, now understood to be the largest such effort in U.S. history, has been enthusiastically invoked by President Trump. The methods of removal were indisputably harrowing. Deportees were placed in concentration camps and packed onto buses, trains, planes, and cargo boats for transport to the interior of Mexico, enduring conditions subsequently described in reports to Congress as akin to those aboard an “eighteenth-century slave ship.” One roundup, conducted in hundred-and-twelve-degree heat, resulted in eighty-eight deaths.

In the 1983 book “The Tarnished Door,” the investigative reporter John Crewdson detailed a litany of abusive tactics employed by the Immigration and Naturalization Service, the predecessor of ICE and C.B.P., including handcuffing migrants to moving cars, stealing their valuables, extorting them for sex and money, and pushing them off cliffs and then disguising their deaths as accidents. Crewdson described the agency as “shot through with nepotism, incompetence, corruption, and brutality” and recounted incidents of “men with drawn guns knocking on bedroom windows, shining flashlights on couples in bed, climbing in windows and barging through doors without permission, and taking occupants (usually aliens, sometimes citizens) away in various stages of undress.’’ Establishing total control of the border and immigration, he concluded, could never be achieved “short of the establishment of a police state.”

After 9/11, the war on terror wedded immigration enforcement to national security. The I.N.S. was dissolved, and its workforce was split across three agencies under the newly formed Department of Homeland Security: ICE, the Border Patrol, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Along with the bureaucratic reshuffling came a surge in funding and recruitment. Veterans of the conflicts in Afghanistan and Iraq, in particular, found post-deployment work in the new enforcement apparatus. In many cases, they were using the same military equipment and technology that they’d used in the fight against Al Qaeda and the Taliban.

Ever since, the border-industrial complex has thrived on the narrative that immigration is dangerous and out of control. But agents themselves have balked at the characterization. In a 2018 op-ed for the Arizona Daily Star, Chris Montoya, a retired Border Patrol agent, pushed back against agency claims of having “the most frequently assaulted and most frequently injured” federal law-enforcement officers as “outlandish,” citing data that U.S. marshals and personnel at the Bureau of Indian Affairs and the National Park Service faced more attacks. Border Patrol agents, he concluded, “enjoy one of the safest law enforcement jobs in America.”

Montoya’s article was published in response to the killing of José Antonio Elena Rodríguez, a Mexican sixteen-year-old who was shot ten times in the back by an agent who claimed that he feared for his life after rocks were thrown at him over the border wall. The agent in the case was eventually acquitted of charges of second-degree murder and manslaughter. D.H.S. officers remained largely silent about the incident. James Tomsheck, the former head of internal affairs for the Border Patrol, who was forced out of his job in 2014, alleged a culture of rampant impunity and corruption, saying that very few agents are willing to publicly voice complaints. There was, he said, “a clear understanding on the part of the rank and file in the Border Patrol that if they should engage in whistle-blower activities, or do anything to promote transparency, that they would be retaliated against in a way that would likely end their career.”

Perhaps the most salient factor in this silence is agents’ persistent belief that they are simply enforcing the law. “Conflating legality with morality is how agents can face the human suffering produced by immigration law and retain a sense of rightness,” Irene Vega writes. Most of the agents she interviewed maintained that the laws they were enforcing were just, even if their interactions with vulnerable migrants often gave them pause. One agent confessed that, to bury her emotions, she would recite something like a personal mantra. “This is your job,” she often told herself. “You’re just doing what’s legal.”

Joshua Childress and I met on a bright spring morning in a Phoenix café not far from his home. The café was owned by Greek immigrants, he told me, and he’d heard about it at the Eastern Orthodox church where he worshipped and worked as a handyman. We ordered freddo espressos and soon began sharing stories of the low-level abuse and malfeasance we had witnessed in the patrol. Childress recalled how senior agents insinuated that trainees could mount searches and make arrests based on little more than a gut feeling, how a perceived aggression could be used to justify almost any use of force, and how the word of agents was almost always trusted over the testimony of the people they apprehended. “I knew things were messed up as I was doing them, as I was learning them,” Childress told me. “But I was justifying it. You learn during training how to word things so it doesn’t sound like you’re doing what you’re actually doing.”

The Border Patrol began implementing Trump’s zero-tolerance policy in May of 2018. “I kind of wish I had planted my flag at that point and said, ‘No, no more,’ ” Childress told me. But his wife had recently lost her job, and the couple had twin boys starting at a new school. They decided to delay his resignation, and he stayed on for several more months. Driving in and out of the parking lot each day, he noticed that many of his colleagues’ vehicles had Don’t tread on me bumper stickers. Childress recalled thinking, They don’t realize they’re the boot. In the end, he said, “it wasn’t so much that I changed my mind as I started to be honest with myself.”

When I asked Childress why he thought more agents didn’t quit, he quoted Upton Sinclair: “It is difficult to get a man to understand something when his salary depends on his not understanding it.” Indeed, in many ways, there has never been a more lucrative time to be an immigration agent or a more costly time to quit. As part of Trump’s hiring push, new recruits enjoy up to fifty thousand dollars in signing bonuses on top of starting pay that ranges from sixty to ninety thousand dollars. Agents who stay on earn tens of thousands in retention bonuses, and those who rejoin after retirement can receive pension pay along with their salary. Most ICE and Border Patrol agents can expect to make about a hundred thousand dollars after just three years in the job, with many earning nearly two hundred thousand a year by the time they retire.

Especially in border regions, where the median household income is less than fifty thousand dollars, many Latinos see these jobs as one of the best routes to upward mobility. A former colleague confessed that he has long considered leaving and tried for years to lay the groundwork for an exit, even returning to school to earn a master’s degree. “I would have one hundred per cent bounced if I didn’t have a child,” he told me. Another agent I spoke to compared the job to “golden handcuffs.”

The day Childress finally mustered the courage to ask his superiors how to quit, he was met with bafflement. They had never heard of an agent quitting. Childress had no safety net and no backup plan. He found a job doing maintenance for an apartment complex, began publishing think pieces on the side, and made occasional appearances on libertarian-leaning podcasts. In one of Childress’s interviews, the host, Thaddeus Russell, drove home the reality of his choice. He’d just gone from making more than a hundred thousand dollars a year to competing for the same kind of trade jobs sought by the migrants he had been arresting. “You took a tumble in terms of your class status,” Russell told him.

When I asked how Childress viewed the decision now, nearly a decade later, he leaned back in his chair and shrugged. “I sleep good at night,” he said.

What should be expected of agents who have qualms about their work? According to Bernardo Zacka, a political-science professor at M.I.T., the question misses the larger issue. In a conversation with Vox about why Border Patrol agents obey immoral orders, he warned against placing the moral onus on individuals over institutions. “The problem is that we put people in situations where they must either act immorally or act heroically,” he said. “That’s a recipe for disaster.”

To Zacka, immigration enforcement is distinct from other bureaucratic functions in that it requires agents to directly intervene in people’s daily lives. “You know you are separating children from their parents—you can see the tears and hear the screams,” he said. “It’s not that bureaucracy shields you from experiencing morally agonizing situations, but that it exposes you to them so frequently that you must develop psychological coping mechanisms that reduce the strain.” Agents asked to implement new enforcement policies might be outraged at first, he continued, but “how long can you go on living with yourself as someone who routinely does morally repugnant acts?”

According to Vega, one of the primary ways agents rationalize what they do is through denial. They downplay the suffering they cause migrants, minimizing arrest and detention as mere inconveniences or casting them as actually helpful for migrants in the long run. They insist on their own powerlessness, regarding themselves as witnesses to, not architects of, the policies they enforce, and blame migrants for their suffering, contending that they “put themselves in that situation” by violating the law.

Central to such denials is an all-encompassing dehumanization of migrants. Officers are acculturated to see migrants as entirely unlike them, despite the fact that more than half of Border Patrol’s twenty-one thousand agents and nearly a third of ICE’s twenty-two thousand agents are Latinos, many only a generation or two removed from their own family’s migration. They come to think of migrants and asylum seekers as potential gangsters, rapists, or petty criminals, whose asylum claims are almost always suspect, their stories exaggerated to take advantage of the freedoms and generosity of the state.

It’s one thing to theorize about this dehumanization but something else to hear it plainly acknowledged by the people enacting it. One former Latino colleague who still works as an agent told me that, at the height of COVID, “we were deporting everybody, and there was this mother who coughed on me in front of her kids, and I was like, ‘Don’t fucking cough on me!’ ” He shook his head recalling the encounter. “It was like a seesaw battle—I’m yelling, then I’m apologizing, then I’m giving all these people food, then I’m saying, ‘Shut the fuck up.’ ” After a pause, he continued, “You see these people like cattle. So I remember I went home and I cried. You don’t want to treat humans like that.”

In 2021, I attended an online panel co-hosted by the group Veterans for Peace. The event commemorated the fiftieth anniversary of the Winter Soldier Investigation, organized by Vietnam Veterans Against the War, in which more than a hundred veterans spoke publicly about war crimes they had witnessed or participated in. At the time of the panel, Veterans for Peace was connecting the experiences of antiwar veterans with national conversations around police brutality in the aftermath of the killing of George Floyd and the long history of racial violence that preceded it.

Jan Barry, a co-founder of Vietnam Veterans Against the War, has made the point that there are now established pathways for antiwar veterans to speak out and that no similar tradition exists for dissenters within law enforcement. And yet, the more I learned about Barry’s movement, the more I imagined the possibility of a similar community of former immigration agents. There are, of course, obvious differences between soldiers and agents, for whom a readiness to kill on behalf of the state is generally understood to be a more distant prospect. But the lethality of deportation, an agent’s primary tool for punishment, deserves recasting.

Last year was ICE’s deadliest in two decades, with thirty-two reported deaths in custody, a mortality rate nearly four times greater than that under Biden. This year is on track to surpass even those figures. The A.C.L.U. has tallied a total of three hundred and sixty-seven deaths involving Border Patrol personnel since 2010, and, according to the U.N.’s International Organization for Migration, nearly seven thousand people have died or gone missing while crossing the U.S.-Mexico border since 2014. (Most experts agree that the actual number is likely far higher.) Being returned to their native country can have fatal consequences for migrants, too. In 2020, a study by Human Rights Watch found that at least a hundred and thirty-eight of the more than one hundred thousand Salvadorans deported from the U.S. between 2013 and 2019 had died upon returning to El Salvador.

Brittany DeBarros is the organizing director of About Face: Veterans Against the War, which she describes as a support network for post-9/11 veterans who were “disturbed by the gap between what they’d witnessed and what the American people were being told.” About Face offers veterans a way to navigate shame, guilt, and rage by “standing in the truth of the harm you’ve done,” something that DeBarros, a veteran herself, found liberating. The existence of such groups creates what political scientists call a permission structure: a framework that offers people an opening to change their mind or their behavior and to embrace new, or deeply buried, ideals. In About Face, veterans find community in the shared experience and morals that caused them to reject the systems in which they once perpetuated suffering.

I have long believed that there is a kind of cosmic coin that links border agents and migrants. Just as many soldiers speak of being forever tied to the lives they have taken in combat, I consider myself to be eternally linked to the people I helped capture and deport, and to the people who died trying to evade me. But when I asked former agents about the possibility of forming a group like About Face, most of them reacted with apprehension. There was confusion over what such a group would even be: a support group? An advocacy group? A resource for current agents to find alternative employment?

I had no answers to these questions. Each of us had quit without a roadmap, led only by our own conscience—and conscience, as defined by Hannah Arendt in these pages, is inherently unpolitical. “The fear of being alone and having to face oneself can be a very effective dissuader from wrongdoing,” Arendt writes. “But this fear, by its very nature, is unpersuasive of others.” There is a difference, she argued, between “conscientious objectors,” who act privately to keep their hands clean, and “civil disobedients,” who act publicly and therefore become “bound together by their decision to take a stand.”

Without coming together, I realized, former agents like me were leaving little sign for others to follow.

As the heat of summer began to settle over the Arizona desert, I reunited with Joshua Childress for a beer at a dark English-style pub. Ever since our last meeting, he told me, “all these things just keep popping up.” He added, “I never think about it otherwise.”

Of the few agents I know who have quit on moral grounds, Childress is the only one who did so publicly, speaking to the press within weeks of his resignation. He told me that he sometimes questioned the manner of his departure, whether everything he’d said and written had reached only those already inclined to agree with him. “I don’t know that I’ve changed a single mind,” he said. At times, he wondered if he might have made more of an impact by staying in his job and trying “a little harder to be that beacon of light in the darkness, to be that good example.”

His comments brought to mind a friend who works in another branch of D.H.S.—the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services—which oversees asylum, naturalization, and citizenship applications. Under Trump, the agency rebranded its immigration officers as “homeland defenders,” which recently departed officials have said is part of a “strategic demoralization and dismantling of the agency.” (A similar overhaul has been taking place in the Department of Justice, where immigration judges are now commonly referred to as “deportation judges” and those perceived to be granting asylum too freely are fired.) Amid all the turmoil, my friend has persisted. “I don’t know if it’s something we just have to endure, or if being in the right position at the right time in history is going to give us an opportunity to do something meaningful,” he told me.

Such thoughts raise the question of whether enforcement agents and bureaucrats of good conscience who leave their posts are only helping to fulfill the Trump White House’s vision for a hollowed-out, even more violent immigration system. In other words, should lone dissenters stay and carry out orders with as much humanity and subversive resistance as possible, or should they abandon the institution to its cruel designs? The apparent dichotomy fails to account for a third option: that agents, once they leave, might work to change the terms under which the system still functions.

At the pub, Childress and I spoke briefly about ideas of reconciliation and national reckoning, trying to parse where our own actions fit within a larger whole. I explained how I found some solace in taking university students to the border, in working alongside migrant-aid groups, and in visiting asylum seekers in detention. Childress asked if I was religious, and if I thought of these acts as something like repentance. I told him that I wasn’t, and that I understood them to be more like restitution—even though I knew whatever I was trying to redress could never be fully restored.

Childress nodded. He told me that he had recently discussed the very same thing with his priest, wondering how best to atone for the violence he’d participated in. I asked about his church, and he told me that he had been helping with a major renovation project, in which the walls and domes of the sanctuary were being painted with Eastern Orthodox iconography. I was intrigued. As a teen-ager, I had travelled in Eastern Europe and Turkey and seen the painted caves and monasteries of early Christians, who often practiced their faith in secret. Hearing this, he asked if I would like to see the paintings—it was after hours, but he had the keys to the building.

The church was a few miles down the road, and I trailed his car much in the same way, I briefly thought, that I used to caravan behind fellow-agents as we drove down to the border at the beginning of a shift. I pulled up alongside his vehicle in the empty parking lot and followed him through the door into the narthex, standing alone in the dark foyer as he left to turn on the lights. When he reappeared, he crossed himself before entering the nave, gesturing at the gallery of angels and saints above us, their heads ringed with golden halos. He explained that the icons had been painted in Greece to match the exact measurements of the church before being sent across the ocean. He led me to a panel along the wall that depicted St. Kassiani, the hymnographer, and St. Romanos, the melodist, showing me how he had helped paint the colored border.
