text:
Synopsis

In a move affecting green card applications, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services has altered its stance on tax compliance. Unpaid taxes and unfiled returns could jeopardise an applicant's chances of approval, as immigration officers will closely evaluate tax history. This change extends to US citizens sponsoring relatives and has sparked legal disputes about its conformity to existing regulations.

Listen to this article in summarized format

The US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has adopted a stricter approach to green card applications, with unpaid taxes, unfiled returns and outstanding tax payments potentially counting against applicants during the approval process. The policy requires immigration officers to look beyond basic eligibility conditions and examine an applicant's overall circumstances before deciding whether to grant permanent residence.

The change follows a policy memorandum issued by USCIS in May 2026, which treats adjustment of status (AOS) as a discretionary benefit. Adjustment of status is the process through which eligible foreign nationals already in the US apply for a green card without having to leave the country.

Also read: US Supreme Court rejects bid to restore immigration judges’ power to pause deportation cases

Under the revised approach, meeting the basic requirements for a green card may not be enough. Officers must weigh positive and negative factors, including an applicant's compliance with tax laws, before making a decision. The approach could affect people applying for permanent residence through family sponsorship or employment, as well as US citizens sponsoring relatives.

Unpaid taxes could affect green card approval

Immigration lawyers have warned that applicants with unpaid federal, state or local taxes could face difficulties under the revised policy. This may include people who have not yet filed their tax returns because they have obtained an extension, as well as those who are paying outstanding taxes in instalments under a repayment agreement with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) or a state tax authority.

Also read:US Green Card lottery 2027: Court blocks reopening of Diversity Visa programme; what applicants should know

Karin Wolman, a New York-based immigration attorney, has advised people preparing to apply for adjustment of status to review their tax records and settle outstanding liabilities before filing their applications.

"As the policy memo reframes AOS as a rare discretionary benefit, USCIS officers have been routinely denying cases in situations that used to be acceptable. One of these is where the applicant or sponsoring US citizen owes back taxes: if you haven't filed a return yet because it's under extension, or you are making partial payments under a payment plan with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) or the state, that can now result in denial of a green card application. Get your house in order, file the tax return and pay the balance owed. It is best if you can do so before filing the application, but definitely before the interview," she said.

The policy also has implications for US citizens sponsoring their family members for green cards. Such sponsors are generally required to submit an Affidavit of Support to demonstrate that they have sufficient financial resources to support the relative they are sponsoring. Tax returns and payment records are among the documents used to establish their financial position. Outstanding tax liabilities could therefore become an issue during the assessment of these applications as well.

Tax compliance can also affect US citizenship

The stricter approach is not limited to people applying for permanent residence. Tax records can also become important when green card holders apply for US citizenship through naturalisation. Applicants must generally demonstrate good moral character as part of the citizenship process, and USCIS considers failure to meet tax obligations a negative factor when assessing this requirement.

People with overdue federal, state or local taxes may be asked to provide proof that they have filed the required returns and entered into a repayment agreement with the relevant tax authority. This means that obtaining a green card does not necessarily end the scrutiny of an individual's tax compliance when applying for a more permanent immigration status.

Wolman also highlighted the connection between tax payments and citizenship applications. "Timely payment of taxes is also a good moral character factor when applying for naturalisation," she said.

Legal challenge against the policy

The revised approach is facing a legal challenge in the US. A coalition of immigration advocacy organisations, unions and individual applicants filed a lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security and USCIS in a district court in Massachusetts on October 5, 2026.

The plaintiffs argue that the policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act, the Immigration and Nationality Act and constitutional due process protections. They have asked the court to issue an injunction blocking the policy while the case is being heard. The case remains pending, and no court order has been issued to block the policy as of the latest update provided.

“There’s many more officers, agents, whatever you want to call them, running around town right now than there were a month ago,” she added.

The incidents were among several reported across the Sacramento region Saturday just days before the election.

Giselle Garcia, programs director for Sacramento-based immigrant support organization NorCal Resist, said her group has documented at least 83 detainments since Oct. 6 — when advocates say the surge started.

Before October, Garcia said the organization averaged about 21 documented detainments a month. NorCal Resist also recorded 138 dispatches this week, which Garcia notes is not including Saturday’s activity.

But she cautioned against attributing the increase primarily to the election,

“For us, pinning this all on the election is reductionist,” she said.

Garcia pointed to the Trump administration’s increased funding for immigration enforcement, which she said has allowed the agency to hire more agents, acquire additional vehicles and conduct multiple operations simultaneously.

“We do think we might be looking at the new normal,” Garcia said.

An election-related escalation?

UC Davis law professor Kevin Johnson said he sees a connection between the increase in immigration enforcement and the approaching election.

“I think that it’s not a coincidence that Election Day is coming and this administration has pushed and pushed and pushed on immigration enforcement,” he said.

He noted that there have been reports of immigration officers near ballot drop-off locations — including in Sutter County — while the administration has also pursued legal action related to allegations of noncitizen voting.

Johnson acknowledged that the expanded enforcement may represent a longer-term shift.

“The new normal is heightened immigration enforcement and a little twist of that is the non-citizen voting angle and the claim that the election results may be corrupted by immigrant voting,” he said.

Johnson also said the activity could intimidate people who are legally eligible to vote, including people of color and recently naturalized citizens.

Ellen Chapman, an organizer with Indivisible Sacramento, said her group is concerned that increased enforcement could discourage some people from voting.

“Our fear is that that’s what they want,” Chapman said. “That if you increase ICE activity right before an election, of course, it puts a chilling effect on… families that are mixed status.”

Chapman said Indivisible groups are coordinating with a national coalition monitoring potential threats to the election.

The coalition has established what she described as “red lines” — incidents that could trigger a rapid mobilization of protesters. That could include ICE agents appearing at polling locations or other actions that organizers believe threaten the voting process.

“We’re not afraid and we have agency,” she said. “That’s what I want people to know.”

CapRadio reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment but they did not respond.

text:
The most contentious issue of this year’s most contentious local race may be whether the candidates plan to cooperate with Trump’s sweeping deportation regime.

As Albany County Sheriff Aaron Appelhans, a Democrat, battles for reelection against Republican challenger Daron Wyatt, the two have sparred over jail safety, transparency, use-of-force, vehicle pursuits, a highly public false claim and a less-public partisan pledge deriding same-sex marriage.

But for many voters this cycle, making a decision on which candidate to support will likely come down to the their differing attitudes toward Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE.

Trump has supercharged the federal immigration enforcement agency since taking office in 2025. It received a budget boost in that year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act that put ICE on par with some of the world’s most well-funded national militaries. It has made headlines in the time since — most notably when its agents killed U.S. citizens in Minneapolis in January, inspiring protests in Laramie and elsewhere.

But ICE’s actions, and the atmosphere those actions have created in the country, have been felt in more intimate ways too, as some make the tough decision to self-deport rather than risk enforcement actions.

The administration claims it is removing “the worst of the worst” from the United States, but in Wyoming, as in the rest of the nation, most of those deported have not been convicted of any crime.

For county sheriffs in Wyoming, the new landscape of federal immigration enforcement requires they decide how to respond.

Specifically, they must decide whether to enter into legal agreements with ICE that empower local law enforcement agents to enforce federal immigration law. They must also decide how to respond when ICE asks the local detention center to hold individuals beyond their release date — to give immigration agents time to come collect them.

Neither Appelhans nor Wyatt plans to sign what is known as a 287(g) agreement with ICE, though their reasoning is different. They also disagree vehemently about whether or not to honor ICE detainers. Appelhans said he will honor only judicial warrants; Wyatt said he will honor administrative warrants, too.

287(g) agreements

As other Wyoming sheriffs began inking official agreements with ICE in 2025, Appelhans told the Albany County Commissioners that his agency would seek no such contract.

The 287(g) program — named for the section of the federal Immigration and Nationality Act that authorizes it — allows state or local police agencies to carry out immigration enforcement on behalf of ICE. That’s a law enforcement responsibility usually reserved for the feds.

By June 2025, four Wyoming sheriff’s offices had signed such agreements. Today, 14 local agencies and the Wyoming State Highway Patrol participate in some version of the 287(g) program.

Appelhans said he still has no interest in signing any such deal.

“Having a partnership with an agency that’s really trying to forward more of a political campaign than actually policing their communities just isn’t a good partnership,” he told The Laramie Reporter. “We don’t need to terrorize our community here by partnering with ICE and making sure that everybody’s scared. Ethically and morally, we are not in the business of just rounding people up for no reason whatsoever. We’re in the public safety business … Until something changes, then my views on that aren’t going to change.”

Wyatt said he has similar concerns about deputizing local cops to enforce ICE mandates.

“Without any doubt at all, I am not in support of local law enforcement enforcing immigration laws in the community, meaning going door to door, knocking on people’s doors, asking them for their immigration status,” he said. “[Residents] have to be able to trust you, and they have to know that if they’re a victim of a crime, not only can they report it, but you’ll investigate it as fervently as you would if it was a crime committed against a United States citizen.”

The Laramie County Sheriff’s Office, based out of Cheyenne, has arrested hundreds of people under its own 287(g) agreement. Wyatt is closely tied to the LCSO, serving as a reserve deputy and counting its leader, Sheriff Brian Kozak, among his political donors.

Wyatt has said he’s “not in support of a 287(g) agreement” for Albany County and does not plan to sign one if elected, especially as their legality is being challenged. But he’s also not opposed to reevaluating that stance if the courts declare those agreements unambiguously legal and he later feels there is a need for such an agreement in Albany County.

There are actually three distinct agreements agencies can sign with ICE under the 287(g) program — one relating to work in jails, another granting limited on-the-street immigration enforcement powers, and another empowering local agents to serve immigration warrants.

Wyatt said joining one of those could make sense in the future, given what it might offer the jail or what it might offer Albany County deputies out in the community.

By way of example, he said the LCSO’s immigration enforcement along Interstates 25 and 80 has pushed drug traffickers to use Highway 287 in Albany County more frequently.

“Could there, at some point, be a need to do enforcement like that to save lives? There could be,” he said. “But I’m not committing one way or another yet … My whole thing is what’s best for the community, right? And if we can bring in revenue by housing prisoners in a safe, secure, dignified environment, and it’s going to bring revenue in [and] that will then allow us to hire more deputies, that will then allow us to be more effective and have a safer jail — would I look into that? I’d certainly look into it, and again, weigh the options as to what’s best for Albany County.”

ICE detainers

Appelhans and Wyatt are sharply divided on the question of whether to honor “immigration detainers.”

These are requests made by ICE to hold arrestees suspected of being in the country illegally for up to 48 additional hours beyond their release date. The goal is to give the federal agency time to come collect them. But the practice raises questions about what that additional jail time means for the civil rights of the people being held — some of whom have already paid bail and would otherwise get to go home.

The legality of ICE detainer requests is being challenged, including in a high-profile case out of Wisconsin wherein the state’s ACLU chapter has argued ICE detainers don’t give sheriffs the authority to hold arrestees longer than the court says they can.

For sheriffs like Appelhans, who oppose the detainers and do not honor them, the crucial detail is that ICE’s requests are not binding. They are “administrative warrants” rather than judicial warrants, meaning they are neither reviewed nor approved by a judge.

Appelhans said it’s his job to honor judicial warrants, but he’ll reject administrative requests.

“Those aren’t real warrants,” he said. “They’re not signed by a judge, and so it’s a bad deal for us to essentially break the law and trample on people’s constitutional rights to hold them longer, just for another federal agency. We don’t bend over backwards or do that for any other federal or local agency, and so we won’t as long as I’m still here.”

Appelhans said he is also hesitant to cozy up with a federal agency that regularly infringes on people’s civil liberties.

“ICE has shown pretty consistently and pretty regularly that they’re not a professional, legitimate law enforcement agency,” the sheriff said.

By contrast, Wyatt said he plans to hold arrestees for ICE if elected. He said it’s a matter of public safety.

“I would immediately start honoring ICE detainers,” he said. “I think that what you’ve seen in Minneapolis and all these other areas where they’re involved in these significant uses of forces and shootings … they’re doing it only in those areas where the county sheriff or local government is not honoring ICE detainers, and/or is creating a sanctuary city or a sanctuary county or a sanctuary state.”

Wyatt said if ICE can pick up the people they’re looking for at the county jail, they won’t need to engage in the large-scale manhunt-style enforcement actions that can result in violence. He said this makes it “counterproductive” to oppose ICE detainers if you want to keep ICE out of your community.

“If you honor that ICE detainer and you hold them only for up to 48 hours … it’s a transfer of custody in a controlled environment where there’s not going to be use of force, there’s not going to be interference, there’s not going to be fearmongering in your community,” Wyatt said.

This is the same rationale ICE itself provides on the agency’s FAQ page:

When jails, prisons or other confinement facilities agree to honor immigration detainers, ICE officers can take custody of removable aliens in a safe, controlled environment instead of at-large in the community.

At-large arrests are unpredictable and can be dangerous to the public, aliens and federal law enforcement officers. It’s safer to assume custody of removable aliens in a secure, private environment.

Appelhans rejects this argument.

“I don’t think that’s steeped in reality,” he said. “We have plenty examples of us not honoring those administrative holds … and those folks have been released, and we don’t have a large presence of ICE terrorizing our community.”

Disputed history

In his interview with the Reporter and later that same day during a debate against Wyatt, Appelhans said he had received and rejected four detainer requests from ICE during his time in office. He said then, and has reiterated since, that he has never honored ICE detainers.

Wyatt said that’s a lie.

During the debate, the challenger said he had information from ICE showing Appelhans had received far more than four requests and had honored many of them — especially before Trump took office in the winter of 2025.

Wyatt provided the results of a Freedom of Information Act request he filed with ICE: a spreadsheet purporting to show 44 detainer requests made to the “Albany County Jail” since Appelhans took office in December 2020. A column labeled “Honord Y/N” includes a “Y” on 27 of those rows.

The Reporter presented the sheriff with this spreadsheet. Appelhans said he doesn’t believe the document is accurate.

“As I mentioned in the debate, we don’t have a way of tracking detainers as such, and answering the question involves a lot of sorting through records kept for other reasons, but I’m sure I’d remember if we had a significant number of detainers and whether we honored them,” he said. “What’s more, I don’t know what goes into how ICE makes a record of what it calls a detainer. I remember at least one case where the inmate was released to the [Wyoming] Department of Corrections to serve a prison sentence. Does ICE mark that down as ‘honored’? I want to be very clear that no one has been released until the judicially-determined sentence has been served, and that judicial warrants always will be honored.”

Wyatt doesn’t doubt the accuracy of the ICE records he received. He said Appelhans choosing not to honor ICE detainers under the Trump Administration is an example of putting “politics over public safety.”

Appelhans accused Wyatt of the same.

“Wyatt has tried to turn a constitutional question into a political question, which I think is disturbing,” he said. “It’s not a question of who is president, it’s a question of what the law is. But I would also say that ICE is not the agency it once was when it was the Immigration and Naturalization Service. I hope others feel the same shock I feel when I see law enforcement agents who are masked, who have no personal identification on the uniform, who snatch people and put them in unmarked vehicles, and worst of all, who shoot people on the street.”

Lingering questions of legality

During the debate last month, Appelhans reiterated his belief that ICE detainers are not legal requests.

“We only honor holds from any department — local, state or federal — that provides a warrant for them to extend that hold,” he said. “We follow that law. We don’t honor [ICE detainers] because they’re not legal.”

Wyatt said they’re not mandatory but they are legal.

“The Albany County Sheriff’s Office is the only sheriff’s office in the state of Wyoming that does not honor ICE detainers,” he said. “I think it would be a far cry to say that 22 other sheriff’s offices across the state and the chief executives of those organizations are violating the Constitution and the law.”

Wyatt said if ICE detainers are declared illegal, he would stop honoring them.

“I believe that it will ultimately go to the U.S. Supreme Court for a decision, and when the ruling is made, I will follow the law,” he said. “If they say it’s lawful, I’ll uphold ICE detainers. If they say it’s not, we simply won’t do it.”

text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP) — Alaska's Republican-run state government on Saturday urged a federal judge to dismiss a lawsuit filed at President Donald Trump's direction to stop the certification of a possible Democratic win in that state's pivotal U.S. Senate race, writing that there is "no reason for this Court to entertain this meritless lawsuit any longer."

READ MORE: Justice Department seeks to isolate Alaska ballots as criminal probe underway over Senate candidate

The scathing filing from the state's attorney general's office comes as U.S. District Court Judge Sharon L. Gleason set a deadline of Saturday for arguments over whether she should dismiss the lawsuit without even a hearing. The complaint from the U.S. Department of Justice has been roundly criticized by election law experts and demands that the judge halt certification of a possible win by Democrat Mary Peltola until it is determined whether voters were confused by the presence of a second candidate on the ballot with the same name as her main rival, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

The Department of Justice on Friday added a request that the judge separate all ballots showing votes for the second Dan Sullivan until it can be determined whether voters were fooled into wasting their votes for a spoiler candidate. In its Saturday filing, Alaska said this was "both disturbing and impossible." It added there would be no way to do that without violating voter privacy.

Trump also demanded that Peltola be prosecuted after The New York Times this week reported that internal texts and posts appear to show the Democrats' campaign was involved in recruiting the second Sullivan, a retired school teacher in the remote fishing village of Petersburg, onto the ballot. But the state filing notes that the two Sullivans are distinguished from each other on the ballot — the senator is listed as a Republican and the incumbent, while the other simply as "Daniel J. Sullivan Jr."

"State officials carefully designed the ballot to minimize voter confusion," Alaska officials wrote. "The Court should immediately dismiss this lawsuit with prejudice and allow state officials to conduct the general election — including ballot counting and certification — free from unwarranted federal interference."

The Trump administration argued that a preamble to the 1990s law governing voter registration gave it the responsibility for ensuring states maintained the "integrity" of federal elections. It has said it's simply trying to combat fraud by preventing the Democrat from being declared the victor in a race that could determine which party controls the U.S. Senate.

The Department of Justice issued a wave of subpoenas and announced it was conducting a criminal investigation in the case as the administration has stepped up its use of its legal powers to support Trump's side in the midterm election.

Peltola has denied involvement in the presence of the second Sullivan on the ballot. The Times report was based on interviews with her former campaign manager, texts and contributions from a political group backing Peltola to an out-of-state Democratic consultant who recruited the second Sullivan.

WATCH: Republicans seize on controversy in Alaska's closely watched Senate race

Alaska's Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, who announced a state probe into the situation after the Times story, has condemned the placement of the second Sullivan on the ballot. The Alaska Supreme Court ruled this summer that the second candidate fulfilled all legal requirements to stay on. The state government's filing on Saturday says that the new revelations about the possible role of Peltola's campaign don't change the fact that he's legally on the ballot.

"Not every wrong can be righted in federal court," the state wrote.

Peltola's campaign and voting rights groups also have urged Gleason to dismiss the case, putting them in unusual alignment with Alaska state officials.

"Imagine if the federal executive could pluck a few words like 'election integrity' from some statutory preamble and, on that basis alone, bend the machinery of state elections to his will, preemptively blocking certification of a U.S. Senate election to protect his preferred candidate from defeat and then subjecting voters to a law-enforcement-led inquest about who they 'really' supported," the American Civil Liberties Union wrote in a filing urging the lawsuit's dismissal. "Imagine that world and ask whether it is what the Framers wanted or precisely what they most feared."

text:
Vernellia R. Randall, “Weekly Racial Justice Update: October 25–31, 2026,” Race, Racism and the Law (November 1, 2026).

Racial justice depends on whether people can secure housing, obtain medical care, practice their religion, and elect representatives who can act on their priorities. This week’s developments show how government and institutional decisions restrict those opportunities—and how communities organize to challenge those restrictions.

The Census proposal is the immediate priority. Comments are due November 2. Removing racial and ethnic questions would weaken the information communities need to document discrimination and demand accountability. The other stories connect that struggle to voting, housing, healthcare, education, and Indigenous rights.

1. Census: Submit Comments by November 2

The Census Bureau has extended the public-comment deadline on its proposed residence criteria and restrictions on demographic questions to November 2, 2026. Comments should identify Docket USBC-2026-0628.

The proposal would prohibit questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation on the decennial census short form and other questionnaires used to enumerate the population. It would also exclude foreign citizens who are neither U.S. citizens nor lawful permanent residents from congressional apportionment. Other provisions would change how usual residence is determined.

The restrictions would not prohibit demographic questions on the American Community Survey and other surveys that do not enumerate the population.

Why it matters:

We cannot challenge racial discrimination effectively without information that documents it. Removing racial and ethnic questions would weaken that evidence. Excluding residents from apportionment would also change whose presence counts toward congressional representation. Both proposals threaten accountability and fair representation. Submit comments opposing them by November 2.

Take action:

Explain how your community, organization, research, or civil-rights work depends on accurate population and demographic information. Identify the provisions you oppose and describe their consequences. Visit Regulations.gov and search USBC-2026-0628.

U.S. Census Bureau, “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions,” Federal Register, September 10, 2026. https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-09-10/html/2026-18481.htm (last visited November 1, 2026).

U.S. Census Bureau, “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions; Extension of Comment Period,” Federal Register, October 5, 2026. https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-05/html/2026-20328.htm (last visited November 1, 2026).

↑ Back to Top

2. Alaska Senate Election: Federal Intervention Threatens Certification in Race Involving Mary Peltola

Alaska asked a federal court to dismiss the Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking to delay certification if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses under circumstances the department attributes to confusion with another candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan. The state argued that the lawsuit lacks a legal basis and threatens election integrity.

During the week, federal officials confirmed related investigations. Associated Press reporting published October 31 describes DOJ’s request to preserve and segregate ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for possible examination of voter confusion. That was a government request, not a court order granting the requested relief or a finding that voters had been deceived.

Why it matters:

Alaskans have the right to choose their senator and have their votes counted under lawful procedures. Federal officials should not use their authority to obstruct certification because their preferred candidate loses. Courts must scrutinize the government’s asserted justification and protect voters’ choices. The stakes include Alaska Native representation and equal treatment of candidates.

Liz Ruskin, “State of Alaska Says DOJ Lawsuit over Senate Race ‘Has No Legal Basis,’” Alaska Public Media, October 27, 2026. https://alaskapublic.org/news/politics/elections/2026-10-27/state-of-alaska-says-doj-lawsuit-over-senate-race-has-no-legal-basis (last visited November 1, 2026).

James Brooks, “As Alaskans Vote, State’s Top Federal Prosecutor Confirms Criminal Investigation of Dem Groups,” Alaska Beacon, October 30, 2026. https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/10/30/as-alaskans-vote-states-top-federal-prosecutor-confirms-criminal-investigation-of-dem-groups/ (last visited November 1, 2026).

Associated Press, “Justice Department Seeks to Isolate Alaska Ballots amid Criminal Probe over Senate Candidate,” carried by NPR and Maine Public, October 31, 2026. https://www.mainepublic.org/npr-news/2026-10-31/justice-department-seeks-to-isolate-alaska-ballots-amid-criminal-probe-over-senate-candidate (last visited November 1, 2026).

↑ Back to Top

3. Asian American Communities: Texas Organizers Respond to Racist Attacks

American Community Media reported October 27 on hostility directed at Indian American, South Asian, and Muslim communities in Texas. Community leaders described residents questioning whether they could safely celebrate their cultures and religions in public. They also said the hostility was motivating people to organize and vote.

Organizers identified limited language assistance and inadequate outreach as additional obstacles. They emphasized reliable information and practical help, while warning against circulating unverified reports that might frighten eligible voters away from the polls.

Why it matters:

People should not have to hide their cultural or religious identity to feel safe in their communities. Texas organizers are confronting that intimidation while helping residents obtain reliable voting information and make their voices heard.

title: More Than 627,000 Venezuelans Could Regain Deportation Protections in the United States
description:
The Trump administration appealed, and in October 2025 the Supreme Court acted through its emergency shadow docket, temporarily blocking the district court's order while litigation continued.
That stay is scheduled to expire November 6 — the same date TPS protections would resume if no new court order is issued.
Real Lives Behind the Legal Numbers TPS grants two concrete benefits: protection from deportation and authorization to work legally in the United States.
Any emergency application to the Supreme Court must be filed before the existing stay lapses on November 6.
A DHS spokesperson had previously characterized similar lower-court orders as "lawless and activist," signaling the administration's intent to contest any unfavorable outcome at the Supreme Court level.
text:
A federal appeals court on October 30 refused to keep Venezuelan deportation protections suspended, setting November 6 as the date when Temporary Protected Status could snap back into force for hundreds of thousands of immigrants — unless the nation's highest court moves to block it again.

The ruling places the Trump administration on a tightening clock: fewer than seven days to persuade the Supreme Court to intervene, or watch a program it dismantled more than a year ago quietly return to life.

A Year-Long Legal Fight Reaches Its Sharpest Moment

The dispute traces back to a decision by then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem to cancel Venezuela's 2023 TPS designation rather than allow it to run its course — a move a federal district court in California ruled exceeded her statutory authority. That ruling in National TPS Alliance v. Mullin sided with immigrant advocacy groups who argued that Congress never granted the secretary power to void an existing designation mid-cycle.

The Trump administration appealed, and in October 2025 the Supreme Court acted through its emergency shadow docket, temporarily blocking the district court's order while litigation continued. That stay is scheduled to expire November 6 — the same date TPS protections would resume if no new court order is issued.

The legal landscape then shifted significantly. In June 2026, the Supreme Court issued a 6-to-3 ruling in Mullin v. Doe, a separate immigration case the government argued stripped federal courts of jurisdiction over challenges like this one. The justices subsequently vacated the Ninth Circuit's earlier judgment in the Venezuelan case and returned it for reconsideration under the new standard — a maneuver known as a GVR: grant, vacate, and remand.

The Appeals Court Rejected Both Government Arguments

On remand, TPS holders contended that Mullin v. Doe left intact courts' authority to assess whether the secretary had exceeded the boundaries Congress set on her power — a far narrower question than a broad policy challenge. The Ninth Circuit agreed, declining on October 30 to issue a new stay as the Supreme Court's hold nears expiration.

The three-judge panel also turned down the government's fallback position: a 21-day administrative buffer that would have pushed any restoration well past November 6. Both denials were unanimous.

Jessica Bansal, TPS Counsel with the National Day Laborer Organizing Network and counsel for the plaintiffs, was direct about what the ruling means: the Ninth Circuit's order will "restore TPS for Venezuela" starting November 6, barring further Supreme Court action.

Real Lives Behind the Legal Numbers

TPS grants two concrete benefits: protection from deportation and authorization to work legally in the United States. For the more than 627,750 Venezuelans enrolled in the program, losing that status last year created immediate legal exposure and, for some, catastrophic consequences.

Evidence placed before the Ninth Circuit included sworn declarations from Venezuelan beneficiaries describing what happened after protections were stripped. Carlos Ernesto Sanchez Villa testified that he was deported to Liberia — a West African nation with which he had no prior connection of any kind. "It felt like something out of a horror movie, but unfortunately, for me it was real," he said in his court declaration. Another beneficiary described being transported across Mexico by bus and dropped near the Guatemalan border without shelter, money, or assistance. Advocacy groups say that in the period since the Supreme Court first froze the district court's protections, thousands of Venezuelan TPS holders have been detained, deported, or killed.

Restoring TPS would not be instantaneous. Advocacy groups note that the practical rollout depends on how U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services structures the reinstatement — a process that in previous TPS litigation cycles has moved through formal agency notices and updated guidance on the USCIS website.

Six Days Left — and One Court That Could Change Everything

The legal window is closing fast. Any emergency application to the Supreme Court must be filed before the existing stay lapses on November 6. Legal analysts tracking the case note that the justices' own June ruling hands the administration a sharper jurisdictional argument than it carried into the first emergency appeal — making intervention a genuine possibility rather than a long shot.

A DHS spokesperson had previously characterized similar lower-court orders as "lawless and activist," signaling the administration's intent to contest any unfavorable outcome at the Supreme Court level. Whether the justices act — and how quickly — will determine whether hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans regain their legal footing in the coming week.

"Our struggle continues," the National TPS Alliance said in a statement following Friday's ruling.

title: 'It left me in shock': St. Cloud immigrant speaks about trauma after ICE re-arrest - MPR News
description:
Over the last month, MPR News has uncovered a new Immigration and Customs Enforcement tactic: the re-arresting of ICE detainees.
Yader Cortez and Jennifer Cortez, his U.S.-born wife, live in St.
U.S. District Judge Jerry W. Blackwell ordered the immediate release of Yader Cortez from ICE custody on Oct. 1.
His wife, Jennifer, a U.S. citizen, reached out to state lawmakers.
His re-arrest on Oct. 2 left Yader believing there is no respect for the law in the United States, he said.
text:
Over the last month, MPR News has uncovered a new Immigration and Customs Enforcement tactic: the re-arresting of ICE detainees. Recently, one man on the cusp of securing U.S. residency was detained again just three minutes after a judge’s order freed him.

Yader Cortez and Jennifer Cortez, his U.S.-born wife, live in St. Cloud with their 17-month-old daughter Arianna and Jennifer’s three children from a previous relationship.

U.S. District Judge Jerry W. Blackwell ordered the immediate release of Yader Cortez from ICE custody on Oct. 1. Blackwell called the warrantless arrest back in June “illegal.”

Yader, a Nicaraguan immigrant, had been held at Sherburne County Jail since the beginning of July. He was picked up by federal agents one day after he agreed to a plea deal for a fourth-degree misdemeanor DWI. The agreement said Yader would serve probation, not incarceration. Yader said agents picked him up six blocks from his house.

On Oct. 2, Yader was transferred from the jail to Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building to sign papers and be released. As soon as he walked outside the rear of the building, he was immediately re-arrested.

Shortly after he was freed, he said three men dressed in civilian clothing approached him and asked him if he was Yader. In an MPR News interview conducted in Spanish, he said he answered yes.

“Then he tells me, ‘You’re being arrested by ICE.’ I ask, ‘Why? The judge is letting me go free, isn’t he?’” Yader asked the official. “Then he said, ‘The judge doesn’t know what he’s doing. He made a mistake in your case. He’s fed up.’”

The Department of Homeland Security said it is within the law to re-arrest immigrants in this way.

“When an illegal alien is ordered released by a judge, that does not immunize the alien from immigration enforcement for all time. Instead, if ICE does not appeal the ruling, it may seek to rearrest the alien in a way that complies with the judicial decision. To suggest that ICE cannot do this is nothing short of sabotage,” a DHS spokesperson told MPR News.

Yader said he is traumatized from the whiplash he endured on the day of his re-arrest.

“I had never experienced anything like that — going from being free to suddenly being imprisoned again — and it left me in shock,” Yader said.

He said he remembered the start of that day when he was supposed to be released. Yader recalled how “friendly” the ICE officers were. When he was detained again, Yader said it was a different story.

“His expression changed — much like the wolf’s before devouring Little Red Riding Hood — and his tone was different,” Yader said in Spanish. “He spoke to me in a way meant to instill fear and dread.”

The 40-year-old said he knows what he experienced that day.

“I felt sad seeing so much hatred from that person who works for ICE, because that is what I would call racism—I can’t think of any other word for it,” he said.

Yader is now released again — after his lawyer and his wife spent the weekend using every tool in their respective boxes to free him. His lawyer Danielle Oxendine Molliver made phone calls and wrote up a motion to file in court.

His wife, Jennifer, a U.S. citizen, reached out to state lawmakers. She also turned to social media to share their story with others.

“I want to shine a light that this is happening because nobody's talking about it,” she said.

Jennifer said she’s grateful that her husband didn’t experience the physical violence associated with ICE in Minnesota.

“That doesn't mean that they are not going at it a different way. If that makes sense, they are hurting us just the same. You know, psychologically, emotionally,” she said.

His re-arrest on Oct. 2 left Yader believing there is no respect for the law in the United States, he said.

“They are acting against the law, much like in countries ruled by dictators who wield the same power — controlling the police and inflicting harm upon their own people,” he said.

The weekend after his re-arrest, his wife said she found out from another lawyer the couple had retained that Cortez had been approved for U.S. residency.

Jennifer said she called him that Sunday. She told him he would be released. And that he was now a U.S. resident.

“Gloria al Señor Jesus Cristo,” Cortez remembered saying. “Gracias a Dios.” (“Glory to the Lord Jesus Christ. Thank you to God.”)

He said he barely slept that night in his cell.

text:
Shabana Mahmood will announce sweeping new rules on Monday on how long legal migrants must wait for settlement in the UK, with most likely to wait a decade and some up to 15 years.

Ministers – including the housing secretary, Angela Rayner – had raised concerns about the effect the rules would have on care workers already in the UK who would be likely to face a 15-year wait for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain (ILR).

The government’s response to the consultation on the reforms, which will be put before MPs on Monday, is expected give some exemption to care workers already in the UK, though most other professions will face the lengthy waits for settlement.

Mahmood, the home secretary, has proposed that the settlement wait could be reduced if legal migrants showed they had contributed to their local communities via a “points based system” or if they were earning higher incomes.

She is expected to meet union general secretaries on Monday – some of whom have raised alarm at the changes – to map out the final details.

The Guardian first reported in July that the prime minister, Andy Burnham, was considering exempting hundreds of thousands of care workers from the reforms to relieve pressure on the social care sector. The Home Office has granted about 200,000 health and care worker visas in the last five years, with many more people coming as their dependants.

Under the plans published for consultation, the standard qualifying period for settlement would double from five to 10 years, while some workers in occupations below graduate level, including care workers, could face a 15-year qualifying period, subject to proposed exemptions and reductions.

In June, Rayner described making care workers already in Britain wait up to 15 years for permanent residence as “un-British”. In September, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said the plans would have been “tough” for her family, who came to Britain as refugees.

In a letter to Mahmood and the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, seen by the Guardian, parliamentarians and organisations representing migrant workers, racial equality campaigners and health professionals describe the proposals as “an iteration of Windrush era policies”.

The Windrush scandal, exposed by Guardian reporting in 2017, involved mainly Black Britons being wrongly detained, deported and denied access to work and essential services, despite having the right to live in Britain.

In their letter, dated 29 October, the signatories urge ministers to “stop history from repeating itself” by abandoning the proposals or, at a minimum, introducing extra safeguards.

Signatories argue that changing the rules for people who have planned their lives around existing settlement requirements would be unfair and could encourage essential workers to leave the country.

They warn that proposed exemptions for some public-service workers may fail to protect staff employed by independent health and social care providers, as well as workers’ family members.

The letter urges ministers to follow the recommendations of the Windrush Lessons Learned Review, conducted by Wendy Williams, which called for improvements in the development and scrutiny of immigration policy, including greater consideration of its impact on affected communities.

The Labour MPs Bell Ribeiro-Addy, Diane Abbott, Clive Lewis and Rachael Maskell are among the signatories, alongside the Green MPs Ellie Chowns, Carla Denyer, Siân Berry and Hannah Spencer. Organisations backing the letter include the Work Rights Centre, Action for Race Equality, Care England and the Society of Radiographers.

The signatories write: “Windrush was a scandal borne from racist immigration policies … this situation is not historic when this same wrong persists, and the same groups are targeted by current immigration proposals.”

The signatories warn the health and care sector is already “dangerously under-staffed” and that the proposed changes risk “worsening the health and wellbeing of everyone in the UK”.

The letter argues that the government could struggle to meet cancer treatment and NHS waiting-list reduction targets without retaining and expanding the workforce, particularly in professions heavily reliant on internationally trained staff, like radiography.

It raises particular concerns about adult social care, adding: “International workers are essential to maintaining current levels of care. Without them, services will contract, and unmet need will increase.”

Launching the consultation on earned settlement last year, Mahmood described Britain as a “multi-faith, multi-ethnic democracy” that demanded “contribution and integration”. She added: “To become a part of this country, permanently, is therefore not a right but a privilege – and one that must be earned.”

text:
Federal immigration authorities have asked the U.S. Supreme Court to consider Jaciel Cirrus Rojas’s case, which raises a question about bond access for people arrested inside the United States after entering without authorization. The Department of Homeland Security has also asked the justices to pause Rojas’s case while they consider a related dispute involving a Brazilian national arrested in Massachusetts, according to Wisconsin Watch.

The legal question reaches beyond one case

The dispute concerns a 1996 federal law that requires detention without bond for people found crossing the U.S. border without authorization. Earlier administrations generally applied that requirement to border cases, leaving many people arrested in the country’s interior able to seek bond hearings. In July 2025, ICE Director Todd Lyons adopted a broader interpretation requiring detention without bond regardless of where someone was arrested; the Board of Immigration Appeals later endorsed that view, Wisconsin Watch reported.

The justices have already agreed to review a separate mandatory-detention case, Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha. The Catholic Legal Immigration Network reports that the court granted review on Oct. 1, 2026. The case asks whether federal immigration law requires detention during removal proceedings for people in the United States who have not been formally admitted.

Appeals courts have reached opposing conclusions about the detention policy. Courts based in New York, Cincinnati, Denver, Atlanta and San Francisco have rejected it, while the Eighth Circuit has joined the Fifth Circuit in upholding it, according to Bloomberg Law. Its analysis also counted more than 9,300 district-court rulings rejecting the government’s policy and three petitions pending at the Supreme Court.

Rojas’s appeal and custody status

The Seventh Circuit ruled 2-1 for Rojas on July 30, 2026, finding that he was not subject to mandatory detention and could receive a bond hearing. The ACLU of Wisconsin, which represented him, says the court reversed a district court’s denial of his habeas petition. Judge Joshua Kolar wrote for the majority; Judge Diane Sykes dissented. Wisconsin Watch reported that Sykes said the Supreme Court was needed to settle the issue uniformly.

Rojas’s case began with an ICE arrest at his Racine apartment in June 2025. Agents had gone there looking for a prior tenant, but arrested Rojas, a Mexican national who had entered the United States in 2018 without a visa, Wisconsin Watch reported. The outlet also reported that Wisconsin court records showed no criminal convictions under his name and that he spent nearly nine months in ICE custody at the Dodge County Detention Center in Juneau.

The available custody reports describe different points in time. In December 2025, the Wisconsin Examiner reported that Rojas remained in detention. Wisconsin Watch later reported that he had left custody earlier in 2026 after a California federal judge vacated the mandatory detention rule nationwide; the Ninth Circuit stayed that ruling less than a month later. Wisconsin Watch also reported that federal authorities planned to detain Rojas again, a development relevant to why the case remains active.

What a ruling could change

A decision against mandatory detention could let thousands of detainees in circuits that have upheld the policy ask for bond hearings, but it would not compel immigration judges to grant release, Wisconsin Watch reported. The legal dispute has also reached Wisconsin’s federal courts: the state’s Western and Eastern District courts received more than 100 habeas petitions over the past year from people challenging ICE detention, the outlet reported.

authors: Cybele Mayes-Osterman, Jack Brook, Associated Press
description:

text:
A federal immigration officer charged with aggravated assault after he ran over a Mexican man with his car in Houston will turn himself in on Monday, according to his attorney.

Mario Alberto Morales, a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer, struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, a 48-year-old construction worker, with his unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as he chased Parra Hernandez through a parking lot. A grand jury indicted Morales on Friday on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

READ MORE: An ICE officer is charged with assault for striking a man with a car in Houston

Morales is planning to turn himself in at a courthouse sometime on Monday, David Lindenmuth, his attorney, told The Associated Press. Lindenmuth previously told the AP that the incident was "clearly just an accident" and that local officials had "invented a crime out of thin air."

Parra Hernandez broke his leg and is recovering at a rehabilitation facility while in federal custody, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told reporters on Friday.

ICE has said Parra Hernandez ran in front of Morales' car.

Previously released surveillance camera video shows Morales' vehicle drive over a median and strike Parra Hernandez as he runs away.

Teare played footage from Morales' body camera on Friday that showed the agent making sharp turns with his steering wheel. He then stops and exits the vehicle and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is lying on the ground, screaming.

"I was coming in, and I hit him with the car," Morales can be heard saying after another ICE agent arrives.

Parra Hernandez told deputies that he fled the traffic stop when Morales started pulling on a mask, and Morales "threw the car" at him, according to a Harris County Sheriff's Office incident report reviewed by the AP. Morales told deputies that he did not brake before he hit Parra Hernandez, but that he did not intentionally strike him, according to the report.

ICE said after the incident that the target of the operation was a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who the agency said was seen getting into a car with Parra Hernandez. Mendoza-Cervantes' daughter told the immigrants' rights group FIEL that her father has been dead for nearly a decade.

READ MORE: ICE officer appeared to intentionally hit a man with a vehicle in Houston, Texas, prosecutor says

Morales is among a small handful of federal agents who have been criminally charged for wounding people during the Trump administration's aggressive immigration crackdown. ICE agent Christian Castro pleaded not guilty last month to charges that he lied to the FBI after he shot and wounded a Venezuelan man as immigration agents swept Minneapolis earlier this year.

Many other ICE shootings, including some that were fatal, have not ended in charges for the agents involved.

Morales, 33, has served as an ICE agent for a little over a year, according to Lindenmuth.

Teare said on Friday that authorities have a "significant amount of information" on Morales, and that, in his experience, law enforcement agencies would not hire someone with his background. He did not elaborate.

Morales was charged with a misdemeanor in 2013 for stealing four DVDs, according to Harris County Court records. Those charges were dismissed after he paid a $270 fine and struck a plea deal.

Morales unsuccessfully ran to represent Texas' 34th congressional district in this year's election cycle under the name "Bam Morales," which Lindenmuth confirmed. Morales served in the U.S. Army's 82nd Airborne Division and later as a corrections officer and law enforcement officer, he wrote in a Ballotpedia candidate survey. He wrote that his top priorities were veterans' rights, economic issues and service guided by the Christian principles of "compassion, integrity, service, and accountability." He listed illegal immigration as one of the country's greatest challenges.

Morales also wrote in the survey that he was endorsed by an organization called "Make America Godlier Again."

Morales appeared at a 2024 Christian conference held by televangelist Johnson Suleman. In video of the conference, Morales appears to act as a Spanish translator as Suleman serves free food and "extends his touch of love to migrants."

"I want to pray for the immigrants," Suleman said, as Morales translated those words into Spanish. "I bless you. May the lord grant your request and open your doors."

Mayes-Osterman is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

text:
Note to readers • This story is jointly published by nonprofits Amplify Utah and The Salt Lake Tribune to elevate diverse perspectives in local media through student journalism.

By the time Chief Matthew Johnson learned about the woman, she was gone.

Johnson, who has led the Spanish Fork Police Department since 2022, heard about her from the city manager, but only in vague detail. She was Hispanic, and she was nervous.

It was unclear what she wanted or needed when she arrived at City Hall — but staff members there said it seemed evident that she was distressed. They directed her to report her concerns to the Police Department.

That’s what Johnson wants the residents of his city to do when they’re in trouble. That’s what police need from residents in every community.

After being told to go to the police, though, the woman left without another word. The city manager said she seemed fearful that police would question her about her immigration status.

“We’re not into immigration enforcement,” Johnson later lamented. “But the fear is real.”

The result of this fear and distrust: Crimes can go unreported and unsolved.

Johnson is among many law enforcement leaders across Utah who worry about how to build or rebuild trust with victims and witnesses in a world in which the perception — and sometimes the reality — is that cooperating with police can lead to entanglements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Take, for example, a Sept. 30 enforcement measure ICE conducted alongside the North Valley Police Department in Sanpete County.

ICE agents who rode around with officers in the small central Utah towns of Moroni, Mount Pleasant and Fountain Green that night ended up taking five people into custody after police made routine traffic stops.

It was the result of what’s called a 287(g) agreement, a formal pact that authorizes local officers to perform immigration enforcement functions. About 10% of Utah’s roughly 140 law enforcement agencies have such agreements with ICE.

After the arrests in Sanpete County sent a ripple of fear through the community, the North Valley department’s chief apologized and said he would reevaluate the accord.

While several major municipal departments — including Salt Lake City, Ogden, West Valley City and Provo — have declined to work with ICE, police leaders and legal advocates have said worries across the state persist.

ICE did not respond to requests for comment on this story, but the Department of Homeland Security, which houses the agency, has said 287(g) accords are “critical” to giving ICE the resources it needs to make arrests across the country.

“When local law enforcement refuses to work with DHS,” the department said, “our law enforcement officers have to have a more visible presence so that we can find and apprehend the criminals let out of jails and back into communities.”

Johnson, the Spanish Fork chief, explained that his department decided not to formalize a relationship with ICE over concerns that a pact would discourage residents from engaging with police.

Utah County, where Spanish Fork sits, does have an agreement in place, but Johnson said the sheriff’s office uses it largely at the corrections level — meaning deputies check immigration status when someone is booked into jail. That’s not the approach Spanish Fork officers take.

“We’re not here to inquire about anyone’s status,” Johnson said. “If they’re a victim of a crime, that’s our job to investigate.”

Johnson said Spanish Fork “hasn’t implemented anything specifically” to ease the fear, but he noted that people who are still concerned can use a tip line in which residents can report criminal activity anonymously.

“We hope,” he said, “this would alleviate any fear of reporting due to legal status.”

Logan resident Fabiola Perez understands why immigrants lacking permanent legal status might be wary of that sort of contact with police. She was brought across the border from Mexico at age 11 and lived without documentation for years before earning a green card, and, earlier this year, her U.S. citizenship.

“I’m legal. I have everything. I never committed a crime,” Perez said. “But I still feel guilty to be here — because the community, or a lot of people, make you feel guilty to be brown, to be different.”

She said the feeling of being watched — of being suspected — never fully disappears.

“I learned at a really early age what it is to be afraid of the police,” Perez said. “Instead of feeling safe, to this day when I see them, I worry. I’m a little bit scared.”

Calls for service drop by the hundreds

Early this year, West Jordan Police Department Deputy Chief Richard Bell said he had begun noticing a troubling trend.

In recent years, his department has usually fielded about 6,500 calls for service a month. But that number, he said, has dropped by several hundred a month.

“It’s purely speculation on my part as to the why,” Bell said. But in a city in which 40% of the population speaks a language other than English at the dinner table, he said, “I wonder if there’s a concern about calling.”

West Jordan has not signed a 287(g) agreement, and Bell said the department does not intend to do so. But the lack of agreement does not stop ICE agents from learning in other ways about people who have pending cases, including minor traffic violations and civil matters that are handled in a city’s municipal court.

Bell said his department’s approach to every resident — regardless of status — comes down to an unofficial slogan: “You matter like I matter.”

“Whether they’re victims, whether they’re suspects, whether they’re witnesses,” he said, “we expect our officers to treat others as they would want themselves or one of their family members to be treated.”

That expectation isn’t just a slogan; it is something the department has built into training. When concerns about immigration enforcement began rising among staffers, he said the department sent guidance to all employees outlining expectations, then folded the topic into quarterly training.

Either the chief or Bell himself attended each of those trainings, the deputy chief said, “making sure that we had an actual conversation about our expectations.”

Still, West Jordan police also can’t stand in the way if ICE agents make an arrest that appears to be lawful. Those lawful arrests don’t just include hardened criminals.

While President Donald Trump has framed his administration’s staunch immigration policies as a way to help communities that “are being ravaged by migrant crime,” the nonprofit Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse has estimated that roughly 70% of current immigration detainees have no criminal convictions.

The nonprofit National Immigrant Justice Center, meanwhile, is among the organizations that have filed lawsuits alleging that ICE has arrested people who have come to the United States seeking asylum from persecution, which is allowed under U.S. law.

Courthouse arrests stoke fear

Skyler Anderson, an immigration attorney in Taylorsville who has practiced for 16 years, said the pattern police chiefs describe — an increased hesitancy for immigrants, whether documented or not, to work with police — is consistent with what he sees in his caseload.

“Police departments, jails and courts in Utah have increased their cooperation with ICE in the past year, leading to more arrests of noncitizens,” Anderson said. “This creates a fear of appearing in court for even minor offenses, which undoubtedly fosters a fear of any police interaction, even for victims.”

Kendall Moriarty, an immigration attorney who has practiced in Utah since 2018 and now works primarily in deportation defense, said it also impacts the willingness of people to do something that police and prosecutors need everyone in a community to be willing to do: Act as witnesses.

One of Moriarty’s clients, a woman who had witnessed domestic violence involving a family member, was subpoenaed to testify about what she saw.

She didn’t respond.

“She was so scared,” Moriarty said, “because of courthouse arrests.”

At a February meeting of the Salt Lake County Council, Sheriff Rosie Rivera expressed concerns about the increased presence of ICE agents in Utah’s 3rd District Court, where her office manages security.

“Part of the problem is ICE is showing up in court,” she said at the meeting. “They have no identifiers. They’re in plain clothes. They’re wearing masks. We don’t know who these people are either, so it has become a problem.”

Moriarty has seen this fear affecting her clients in other ways.

She described a client who has stopped attending church altogether because ICE has conducted operations in her neighborhood and near her congregation. Another client, she said, no longer leaves her house to go grocery shopping after her husband was detained and deported. She fears her children would be left without a parent if she were taken, too. Moriarty said the woman’s oldest child, about 15, stopped attending school to work instead after the family lost income.

“It is absolutely affecting everyone’s lives,” Moriarty said.

Visa for victims in short supply

When he was a young man in The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, Jeff Simmons served a Spanish-speaking mission to Panama and Costa Rica. Then, as a member of the Air Force and Air National Guard, he worked as an Arabic-language linguist.

That multilingualism wasn’t the only reason Simmons was selected to lead the Logan City Police Department in 2023 but, in a city with a quickly growing immigrant population, it certainly helps.

Now, Simmons said, some of the immigrants in his community appear to be pulling back. “Do I think maybe some in the Hispanic community have withdrawn? Yeah, I think so,” Simmons said. “And that’s unfortunate, because we’re not the immigration police.”

Simmons said he and his officers try to communicate that message as much as possible, accepting invitations to speak with community groups. But it can be hard to explain the difference between local police and federal immigration forces — not to mention the nuances of whether a department has an additional agreement to help ICE.

“We certainly try to get as many Spanish speakers as we can,” he said.

Logan also has not signed a 287(g) agreement. “That’s not our purview,” Simmons said. “That’s the federal government’s job.”

Federal law recognizes that sometimes, for police officers to do their jobs, an immigration enforcement action might need to be paused. That’s why, once or twice a week, Simmons signs onto what’s called a U visa application — an agreement that is intended to offer some protection to undocumented victims of crimes who are willing to cooperate with law enforcement in the investigation or prosecution of criminal activity.

“We don’t care if they’re documented or not,” Simmons said. “We want to know if they’re victims of a crime.”

Simmons said the number of those applications demonstrates how many undocumented residents are still engaging with police.

But the visas aren’t a guarantee. Over the past few years, NBC News reported, people who have been approved for a U visa — but who are in the process of waiting for that protection to be confirmed at the federal level — have been detained and deported. And, in February, the federal Board of Immigration Appeals officially ruled that a removal case doesn’t need to be paused to allow time for a U visa decision.

Congress caps U visa approvals at 10,000 a year. That leaves tens of thousands of applications in a federal backlog.

Anderson, the Taylorsville immigration attorney, said all of these factors send a message that the government isn’t interested in protecting people who are cooperating with police if those people are at risk of deportation.

“So,” he said, “it is no surprise to me whatsoever that there is an increased fear of interacting with the police and reporting crimes.”

Targets for crime

Police chiefs from Brigham City in the north to redrock country in the south have reported similar findings: People are more afraid of the cops now.

St. George Chief Kyle Whitehead said his department’s assurances to protect all people, regardless of status, haven’t stopped a yawning trust gap from forming between immigrants and police. And that, he said, extends beyond just unreported crimes.

In his department’s experience, undocumented residents are sometimes targeted specifically because perpetrators know they are less likely to call the police.

“There are victims in our community that are victimized because they are illegal immigrants,” Whitehead said. “They’re extorted, people steal from them — we even have kidnappings, trafficking situations. And they’re basically threatened: ‘If you don’t go along with this, I’m going to call ICE on you.’”

Whitehead said the consequences fall on everyone.

“If we put barriers in place that may cause them to hesitate,” he said, “to not want to come forward — it’s not good.”

Whitehead said his department’s response to the ICE expansion is to stay out of immigration enforcement entirely. St. George hasn’t signed a 287(g) accord, but Washington County, where St. George sits, has.

To help residents understand what his department will and will not do when it comes to immigration enforcement, Whitehead said, the best bet is ongoing outreach.

“The main thing we try to do is to seek out opportunities to connect with all people in our community,” he said, “whether it be through social media or community events.”

Fear still lingers

The question of whether to engage with ICE has left many Utah departments caught between competing pressures — and Kaysville Chief Sol Oberg said stepping back from cooperation comes with its own cost.

Oberg said departments that limit cooperation with ICE have removed themselves from having any meaningful influence over federal enforcement operations within the community.

“When you can’t work with ICE, you’ve taken yourself out of the equation,” Oberg said. “You have no more influence on what’s going on.”

Oberg’s office has also not signed a 287(g) agreement, and he figures it might not need to take that step. “Right now,” he said, “we don’t really have an illegal immigrant community in Kaysville or much of a presence here.”

He said his department also hasn’t taken any specific steps to ensure residents who may lack legal status feel comfortable reporting crimes to the police.

Even law enforcement leaders who have signed 287(g) agreements have sought to be very clear that the agreements aren’t all-encompassing.

“Our deputies will not participate in immigration sweeps or workplace raids,” Utah County Sheriff Mike Smith said in a statement in July, “and any immigration-related action occurs only after an individual has been arrested on separate criminal charges.”

Despite assurances from police, the proliferation of federal agents across the country has stirred an unnerving feeling, even for people like North Logan resident Dulce Cortez.

Though her mother was undocumented for years, Cortez was born here. She’s a citizen, but she feels her anxiety rise when she sees a police car on the street.

She still is afraid when an officer simply drives behind her.

“It makes me question if I were to seek help from police enforcement,” she said, “would they believe me right away, or would they question me?”

description:

But the judge dismissed the case without prejudice and gave Trump an opportunity to file an amended complaint addressing those shortcomings.

text:
A federal judge on Saturday again dismissed President Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal over its reporting on a lewd birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein bearing Trump’s name.

For the second time this year, US District Judge Darrin P. Gayles ruled that Trump failed to plausibly allege that the Rupert Murdoch-owned newspaper acted with “actual malice” when it published the story.

Gayles rejected the president’s argument that The Journal should have withheld its story after he denied writing the letter, saying such a requirement would violate the First Amendment.

“Were that the law, any time a public figure or his team denies an accusation, journalists would be immediately blocked from publishing negative or contradictory press,” the judge wrote.

The ruling is another stinging defeat in the president’s legal crusade against the American news media and is sure to be celebrated by the press freedom groups that have denounced Trump’s suits.

Gayles previously dismissed the $20 billion lawsuit in April, ruling that Trump’s original complaint relied on “formulaic” assertions of malice that came “nowhere close” to the legal standard for a public figure.

But the judge dismissed the case without prejudice and gave Trump an opportunity to file an amended complaint addressing those shortcomings.

In Saturday’s ruling, Gayles found that Trump’s revised complaint still failed to resolve those issues and dismissed the case with prejudice.

“We’re pleased with the court’s decision,” a spokesperson for Dow Jones, the Journal’s parent, told CNN.

Trump’s legal team signaled that it plans to appeal the ruling.

A spokesman said Trump “will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants.”

Trump sued The Journal, its parent companies, Murdoch and two reporters in July 2025 after the newspaper reported on the sexually suggestive letter. Trump denied writing it and accused The Journal of knowingly publishing a false story.

The case was especially unusual because Trump brought it while serving as president. Legal analysts who spoke with CNN said they could not recall another instance of a sitting president suing a news outlet over a story.

However, it was also part of a recognizable, long-running pattern for Trump — using the courts to pressure news organizations over unflattering coverage of him.

During his second term, Trump has also filed a $15 billion defamation case against The New York Times over its coverage of his 2024 campaign. A judge dismissed the original complaint last year but allowed Trump to refile. In July, the judge deferred a decision on the Times’ motion to dismiss and directed Trump to revise his complaint again, which he did in August.

Late last year, Trump sued the BBC for $10 billion over its editing of his January 6, 2021, speech in a documentary about the Capitol attack. The British broadcaster has vowed to defend the case in court.

One month before taking office, Trump sued Iowa pollster J. Ann Selzer, her polling company, The Des Moines Register and its parent company, over a poll released days before the 2024 election showing him trailing Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in Iowa. A judge dismissed that lawsuit with prejudice in September.

Legal experts have deemed these lawsuits frivolous and full of holes, but warn that winning may be besides the point for Trump: The publicity and threat of protracted litigation can pressure news outlets and chill aggressive reporting.

This story has been updated with additional information.
