Will the indictment lead to changes on the ground?

Harris County Precinct 2 Commissioner Adrian Garcia, a former Harris County sheriff, said during a virtual news conference that Morales’ work history should have been a red flag from the onset.

Teare’s office told the Chronicle that Morales could not land a job with U.S. Border Patrol several years ago and had been working as an ICE contractor before he was hired as a removal operations officer during ICE’s hiring surge last year.

“You could expect a great deal of rhetoric from ICE leadership or from the president. But if you have agents that should never be given this authority, then we can only imagine that they will run with impunity or at least try to,” Garcia said. “So, I have no hope that the actions taken here will translate into some reform in the department.”

U.S. Rep Al Green, D-Houston, said President Donald Trump would likely thwart any efforts to overhaul how ICE operates. He cited how the president in July stepped in after ICE agents announced a temporary pause to vehicular pursuits in the aftermath of the deaths of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston and Durán Guerrero in Maine.

“After ICE was indicating that they would cease and desist with these operations in the vehicles, the president came out and he very strongly indicated that this was a tool that was necessary,” Green said. “He went on to commend the officers for what they were doing, and this was after the deaths of persons at the hands of ICE.”

U.S. Rep. Christian Menefee, D-Houston, struck a more optimistic tone.

“Hopefully this indictment will make ICE agents in Houston stop acting with impunity,” he said. “President Trump has no power to pardon state law crimes. And he won’t be president forever. These agents need to know they will be held accountable when they break the law and harm people in our communities.”

Kim Bruno, the immigration attorney representing Parra Hernadez, thanked the district attorney and said that her client’s story hasn’t changed since the incident happened, which was proven by the newly released footage.

“From the beginning the video told a different story than what was offered by the agency. The video shows Mr. Parra running from the vehicle and not in front of the vehicle,” she said during a news conference Friday at the FIEL offices. “The released footage of the body camera shows the officer intentionally jerking his wheel into Mr. Parra, the same story that has remained consistent.”

Bruno added that aside from his physical ailments, Parra Hernandez has also dealt with mental health issues.

“He has struggled with anxiety and depression,” she said. "All he wants is accountability. He wants assurances that this will not happen to anybody. He is so sympathetic and all he cares about are the other people. But he's the one in the bed suffering.”

Bruno also said that Parra Hernandez lamented that her client was allegedly assaulted by a fellow Latino.

“His exact words were: ‘They wanted to kill me. There is a lot of racism, even among Hispanics. And this is why I believe he wanted to kill me,'” she said.

Here's what other Houston-area leaders and advocates had to say about Friday's indictment.

Cesar Espinosa of FIEL Houston: ‘A glimmer of hope’

Cesar Espinosa, the executive director of advocacy group FIEL Houston, said the indictment is a positive development when immigrant communities live in daily fear under Trump’s immigration crackdown.

“We want to commend District Attorney Sean Tiere for and Sheriff Ed Gonzalez for having a steadfast commitment to justice and following through what is what is supposed to happen,” he said. “I think today brings a glimmer of hope to a very devastated and beaten community.”

EXCLUSIVE:Body camera video shows ICE agent's chilling response to running over Houston immigrant

U.S. Rep. Sylvia Garcia: 'No one is above the law'

U.S. Rep. Sylvia Garcia, D-Houston, celebrated the indictment as a reminder that everyone, including law enforcement officers, should be held to account.

“Today, Miguel Parra Hernandez is one step closer to receiving the justice he deserves. The grand jury's decision sends a powerful message to our community,” she said in a statement. “Even at a time when so much feels out of control, when our communities feel under attack, we are reminded that no one is above the law.”

But Garcia added that the “fight is not over” and the Houston community is still waiting for justice to be served after the July 7 fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican immigrant killed in the East End, and others who have been killed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers across the country. Teare's office also continues to investigate that case, which remained before a grand jury as of Friday morning, he said.

“We must continue demanding justice for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, Renée Good, Alex Pretti, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, and so many others whose families and communities are still waiting for answers,” she said. “ICE must be held accountable and officers who break the law must face justice in the court of law, just like anybody else. A badge does not place anyone above the law and accountability.”

Good was shot and killed during an ICE surge operation in Minnesota in January; Pretti was killed that same month during a protest in Minnesota and Durán Guerrero was killed in Maine during a traffic stop.

Garcia also praised Teare for pursuing accountability in the Parra Hernandez case.

Espinosa cautioned against making a comparison to the Morales indictment and the investigation into Salgado’s case.

“It's just a whole different set of circumstances,” he said. “We want the community to be aware that these two cases are separate. In one case, you have very clear video. In the other case, you have almost no video.”

MORE: Who is Mario Alberto Morales? What to know about ICE agent accused of hitting Houston immigrant with car

State Sen. Molly Cook: A challenge to the narrative

State Sen. Molly Cook, D-Houston, said the indictment could challenge the narrative ICE officials usually offer when an ICE agent injures a person during an operation.

“It won't bring back the loved ones that we've lost but I think it really has the potential to turn the tide of this conversation,” she said. “There are lies after lies after lies on the record from the Trump administration but now we have the opportunity to see the truth and to see justice.”

Espinosa said the indictment could also lead to ICE officers changing their tactics during operations.

“I think it's going to send a shockwave or at least it'll make agents think twice before using excessive for force or using any force,” he said. “For a lack of a better term, the ball is now in the Trump administration's court. They have to make changes so that these things don't happen. I make no mistake about it. You and I should not be talking about Lorenzo Salgado Araujo or Mr. Miguel Hernandez Parra.”

Harris County Precinct 4 Commissioner Lesley Briones: Communities 'terrorized' by ICE enforcement

Harris County Precinct 4 Commissioner Lesley Briones, whose district includes Clay Road where the incident happened, also praised Teare for his efforts and said Trump’s unchecked power has “terrorized” communities.

“I commend Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare for his pursuit of justice following the dangerous use of force against Miguel Parra-Hernandez,” she said. “The Trump administration's extreme, reckless immigration enforcement has terrorized our communities, harmed our families, and undermined the rule of law. We cannot allow this abuse of power to continue unchecked. Our community deserves justice, transparency, and an end to the fear and chaos.”

US Attorney Aaron Reitz : 'A political prosecution'

Aaron Reitz, the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas, said Morales’ indictment amounted to a “scalping” of a federal agent by a local prosecutor.

“Disappointed in his inability (to) swiftly bring charges in the tragic Salgado shooting in July, the Harris County District Attorney now appears determined to put a different federal agent’s scalp on the wall,” he said in a statement. “This time he’s pursuing what looks like a political prosecution of an ICE agent for doing his job – exactly what his allies have been agitating for.”

Reitz added that his office was not consulted about the indictment and said that as of Friday, his office sees no basis to pursue federal charges.

“We will, of course, continue to evaluate any relevant evidence and legal issues within our jurisdiction,” he added.

Houston Mayor John Whitmire's office did not respond to a request for comment on the indictment.

Harris County Precinct 1 Commissioner Rodney Ellis

“Every person in Harris County deserves safety, dignity, and equal protection under the law, regardless of immigration status,” Harris County Precinct 1 Commissioner Rodney Ellis said. “An ICE officer striking Mr. Parra Hernandez with a vehicle and breaking his leg is deeply disturbing, as are District Attorney Sean Teare’s reports that federal officials have failed to cooperate with county investigators. Mr. Parra Hernandez and his family deserve answers, and our community deserves a full accounting of what happened.”

U.S. Rep Lizzie Fletcher, D-Houston

“This incident was not an accident. It was the predictable result of an agency that rushed thousands of people into the field without the training this job demands,” U.S. Rep. Lizzie Fletcher said. “Our neighbors keep paying the price for that recklessness, here in Houston and across the country. In this case, body camera footage made the truth clear, and every ICE officer in the field should wear one.”

text:
A federal appeals court has left in place restrictions on part of the Trump administration's voter fraud investigations in nine states through Tuesday's midterm elections, rejecting another attempt to lift an order limiting federal agents' field operations and interviews involving actual or suspected U.S. citizens.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit on Friday declined to have a larger group of its judges reconsider a three-judge panel's refusal to stay the preliminary injunction. Seven judges dissented from the decision not to rehear the matter, arguing that the lower court had improperly constrained the executive branch's authority to investigate suspected illegal voting.

The restrictions apply in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. According to the seven-judge dissent, six of those states were identified in the record as part of the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) enforcement campaign, while three others were identified through media reports.

Read More on News

The decision is one of several recent legal setbacks for the administration's escalating push against alleged noncitizen voting in the closing days before the midterms. The Department of Justice (DOJ) has brought election-related charges around the country, while federal immigration agents have been sent to homes to investigate suspected illegal voting.

Newsweek reached out Saturday to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for comment on the ruling.

Ninth Circuit Leaves Trump Administration Restrictions in Place

The case, California Nurses Association v. Mullin, was brought in September by the California Nurses Association, National Nurses United, Voto Latino Foundation, Santa Clara County and the City and County of San Francisco against DHS, immigration agencies and federal officials.

The nursing organizations said U.S.-citizen members feared being wrongly identified, investigated or detained under the federal initiative and had curtailed election-related activities as a result. The district court found at this preliminary stage that the organizations likely had standing to sue on their members' behalf.

The plaintiffs argued that the administration's investigation of potential noncitizen voters could wrongly target U.S. citizens and amount to voter intimidation prohibited by Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act.

On October 21, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín granted a preliminary injunction. The order bars the government in the nine states from conducting certain election-related field operations and interviews involving people whom officials know, suspect, or reasonably should know or suspect are U.S. citizens. It also restricts election-related field operations based wholly on certain federal records when those operations involve people officials know, suspect, or reasonably should suspect are U.S. citizens.

The Trump administration appealed and sought to put the injunction on hold while the appeal proceeds. A Ninth Circuit panel denied that request Friday, concluding that the government had not demonstrated the irreparable harm required for a stay.

A Ninth Circuit judge then requested a vote on rehearing the panel's decision en banc, meaning before a larger group of judges. A majority of the court's nonrecused active judges did not vote to rehear the order, according to the court's October 30 filing.

The result leaves the injunction intact during the final days of voting.

How DHS Is Investigating Suspected Noncitizen Voters

The court filing provides additional detail about an enforcement program previously reported by Newsweek, in which armed Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents have visited homes to question people about citizenship and voting.

According to the court record, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) identifies potential illegal voters by comparing voter information from state and local governments and publicly available sources against DHS and commercial databases. USCIS then manually reviews potential matches, with the stated goal of excluding U.S. citizens before cases are referred to HSI.

Appearing on Fox News on Saturday, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin put the scale of the administration's effort at more than 300,000 investigations.

“We’re investigating over 300,000 cases,” Mullin said during a discussion of alleged noncitizen voting. The figure refers to cases under investigation, not confirmed instances of illegal voting.

If USCIS concludes that someone likely voted illegally, it creates a record for that individual in TECS, a federal law-enforcement database. HSI then decides whether further investigation is warranted, and field offices independently review records before deciding whether to act. One possible step is an interview with the suspected voter.

DHS previously told Newsweek that federal agencies used government and commercial data to supplement voter-registration information, verify identities and eliminate false positives.

A DHS spokesperson also previously defended the door-to-door operations to Newsweek, saying HSI would "continue to investigate election fraud."

"HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders," the spokesperson said.

Critics have challenged both the reliability of the government's data and the decision to send federal agents to people's homes shortly before an election.

Wendy Weiser, vice president for democracy at the Brennan Center for Justice, previously told Newsweek that the approach was "highly irregular and inappropriate," arguing that the tactics risked intimidating legitimate voters.

Beau Tremitiere, counsel at Protect Democracy, which represents the plaintiffs in the case, told Newsweek on Saturday that the latest court decisions mean eligible voters in the affected states "can cast their ballots without fear of armed immigration agents showing up at their door."

"The courts have been clear that these limits don't impact legitimate law enforcement efforts," Tremitiere said. "All these rulings do is block DHS from sending armed agents after U.S. citizens based on data it knows is wrong days before an election."

Asked about what could happen next in the case, Tremitiere said: "We can't predict the future, but wherever this goes next, we'll be ready to defend the voting rights of every eligible American."

Seven Ninth Circuit Judges Dissent

Friday's Ninth Circuit order drew a 33-page dissent from Judge Eric Tung, joined by Judges Consuelo Callahan, Ryan Nelson, Daniel Collins, Daniel Bress, Patrick Bumatay and Lawrence VanDyke.

Tung argued that the district court had gone too far in restricting legitimate law-enforcement activity.

"By enjoining the government from even investigating illegal voting, the district court departed from its limited role," Tung wrote. He argued that the district court had confused investigations of suspected illegal voting with the voter intimidation prohibited by federal law.

The dissent argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing, that private parties could not bring a lawsuit to enforce Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act and that the government's investigations did not violate that provision in any event.

Tung also argued that the injunction was vague and overbroad, writing that its language could effectively prevent the government from conducting lawful election investigations whenever officials had reason to think an investigation could involve a U.S. citizen.

"The many errors in this case warranted en banc review," Tung concluded. "The district court allowed abstract fear to substitute for concrete injury. It invented a right of action where Congress supplied none. It equated investigation with intimidation."

The dissent represents the views of the seven judges and does not alter the injunction, because a majority of the eligible active Ninth Circuit judges did not vote to rehear the panel's ruling.

Trump Steps Up Voter Fraud Push Before Election Day

The court fight comes as President Donald Trump and his administration have made alleged voter fraud and noncitizen voting a major focus in the closing stretch of the midterm campaign.

The Justice Department has announced scores of election-related criminal investigations in recent weeks, including cases accusing noncitizens of voting, falsely claiming U.S. citizenship while registering and committing related offenses.

Trump also announced Monday that anyone reporting voter fraud in past elections or the 2026 midterms would receive $1 million if the information resulted in an arrest and conviction. The White House did not provide Newsweek with details about how the proposed reward would be funded or administered when asked earlier this week.

In a separate case Friday, U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson temporarily barred DOJ and DHS officials nationwide from threatening state and local election workers with prosecution for processing or counting ballots in compliance with governing election laws. The order also restricts federal demands that states remove specific people from voter rolls or treat their ballots differently based on the administration's allegations that they are ineligible.

Thompson wrote that the administration's actions were likely to interfere with election administration and disenfranchise lawful voters. The ruling is temporary and does not resolve the underlying lawsuit.

In California, the administration is separately fighting state officials over roughly 20,000 registered voters it says are likely noncitizens. A federal judge this week refused the DOJ's request to require election officials to segregate ballots associated with people on that list, and the Ninth Circuit on Friday also rejected the government's request for emergency relief in that separate dispute.

The administration maintains that heightened enforcement is necessary to protect election integrity. Critics counter that noncitizen voting is rare and that unreliable citizenship data can wrongly flag eligible voters.

The litigation will continue, but Friday's action leaves the restrictions on DHS field investigations in force across the nine states through the close of polls Tuesday.

The statement followed Stevens' latest attempt to suggest that El-Sayed's candidacy has threatened Jewish communities, by tying him to an anti-Rogers ad by an outside group, Rebellion PAC, that addressed how the billions of dollars and political support the US provides to Israel each year costs Americans. The Trump administration has publicly said the US launched its illegal war on Iran after being pushed to do so by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu—a decision that has markedly worsened the affordability crisis for Americans.

El-Sayed's campaign has said the digital ad does not "speak for" the progressive candidate, while others have pushed back on the claim by the vehemently pro-Israel Stevens and pro-Israel groups that the video is antisemitic, noting that it says nothing about Jewish people.

In his statement Friday evening, El-Sayed appeared to have little interest in engaging with Stevens further regarding persistent accusations by corporate Democrats who have claimed he hasn't done enough to reach out to Jewish communities, whom his campaign has been speaking with extensively about fighting antisemitism and their views on Israel at "deep canvassing" events.

"Our campaign is and has always been focused on addressing the most critical challenges Michiganders are facing: skyrocketing gas prices, unaffordable groceries, and the inability to see a doctor," said El-Sayed, noting that his message had allowed him to win the primary in August despite "a historic $70 million in outside spending by big corporations" and the pro-Israel lobby on behalf of Stevens.

Two sources told Politico that El-Sayed's campaign was asking Stevens not to campaign with him in the final weekend, which the congresswoman had begrudgingly said she planned to do in her statement demanding an apology from the candidate.

But El-Sayed himself was applauded by progressives for "holding firm and ignoring the whines and threats of extremists," as art director Lindsay Ballant said.

"For those folks demanding that El-Sayed condemn that ad, he isn’t playing your stupid game," said another observer. "He understands that whatever he does, it won’t be enough. There will always be another demand. So take your cudgel somewhere else."

Even if El-Sayed took time away from the statewide door-knocking tour he had planned for the weekend to address Stevens' demand, podcaster and former Obama administration staffer Tommy Vietor asserted that "people would then say he didn't condemn it firmly enough."

"The guilt by association shit is endless," said Vietor. "Meanwhile, Abdul is literally being called a jihadist by the president of the United States!"

Rep. James Clyburn (D-SC) and Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), and Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) are set to join El-Sayed at the "Knock Out the Vote" canvassing event from Saturday through Monday.

Thompson ordered officials with the Trump administration to stop demanding that election workers remove voters from rolls, sequester ballots cast by people the White House has claimed are ineligible to vote due to being noncitizens, and refuse to issue ballots to people who have been included on the administration's error-riddled lists of residents whom it says have voted illegally.

"Because the public has a paramount interest in ensuring that election officials and workers are able to carry out their work in accordance with federal law and election procedure, and the official day of the elections is only a couple of days away, the balance of the equities and public interest weigh in plaintiffs’ favor," said Thompson.

The ruling was handed down in connection with a lawsuit filed by the Service Employees International Union (SEIU), the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME), and other groups.

Protect Democracy, part of the coalition that sued, called the threat "yet another attempt designed to shake Americans’ confidence in the election results and undermine our electoral process."

Patrick Moran, president of AFSCME, said Thompson's ruling and the temporary restraining order she issued were "a resounding win for the election workers who make our democracy happen and for all Americans’ freedom to vote."

"We applaud the court for granting a temporary restraining order protecting election workers from unlawful prosecution simply for following the law and forbidding the administration from interfering with the lawful administration of elections," said Moran. "Now, our nation’s nonpartisan election workers, many of them AFSCME members, can continue to do their jobs, and our elections can continue to proceed freely and fairly.”

With President Donald Trump's approval rating at an historic low and Republicans facing widespread disapproval of the illegal war on Iran they've supported, healthcare cuts they voted for, and violent mass deportation operations they've funded, the White House has approached the midterms with a laser focus on sowing doubt about the results before the elections are completed.

The DOJ demanded confidential voter roll data from states across the country last year, pushing the baseless claim that the lists were rife with the names of noncitizens who would be illegally permitted to vote. The administration has been rebuffed by dozens of officials.

In response, the Department of Homeland Security and DOJ have used commercially available data and federal records to cobble together their own lists of voters they say have cast ballots illegally. The results of the effort have included a list of 185 people in Nevada, all of whom were proven to be citizens, and a list of 28 immigrants in California whom federal officials said were suspected of voting before they became naturalized citizens—representing about .0001% of all registered voters in the state.

The administration has also pushed for the certification of Alaska's election results to be blocked, citing the presence of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot—one clearly labeled as the incumbent Republican senator, the other not—and on Thursday, sent the threatening letters to election officials across the country.

Earlier this week, Judge David Carter in the US District Court for the Central District of California said that the administration's threats "must stop," throwing out the DOJ's attempt to force the state to sequester ballots cast by 20,000 people officials claimed were not citizens.

"DOJ tried to bully election workers with threats and intimidation," Norm Eisen, co-founder of Democracy Defenders Action, said Saturday. "Last night, a federal court shut it down. We and our partners are fighting to protect elections in the court of law."

The conference produced about $1.8 billion in nature-finance agreements, including a commitment of $500 million from the Netherlands to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, which rewards countries for protecting their tropical forests. Six contributors also pledged $60.13 million to the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund, which supports the Global South in implementing the 2022 framework.

However, "overall spending on biodiversity remains far short of the $200 billion per year target in the Kunming-Montreal framework," wrote John Cannon at Mongabay, while the framework's demand to reform "damaging subsidies remains largely unmet."

Experts say $700 billion in additional annual spending is needed to protect and restore ecosystems damaged by mining, drilling, and other industries, pollution, and other human activities.

Governments committed to reducing subsidies by at least $500 billion per year by 2030, but about $2.4 trillion "is still estimated to flow annually toward subsidies that can harm nature," said Sustainable Business Services.

Daudi Sumba, chief conservation officer at World Wildlife Fund International (WWF), said that the Global Review that came out of the summit was “a strong signal to countries that they must do better when it comes to action for nature."

"But without clear scaling of the funds to be able to deliver, I fear finance will remain the key issue that continues to haunt the UN biodiversity summits," said Sumba. "Negotiators returning home must now turn the Global Review into clear dedicated action, scaling nature’s recovery by transforming the most damaging sectors and activities across our food and finance systems.”

The Cali Fund, a mechanism that came out of COP16 in Colombia and is designed to share digital sequence information on genetic resources, is also falling short of the goals set for it by last year's conference. The fund aims to raise at least $1 billion annually from companies that access DSI from genetic resources for pharmaceuticals and other products, but "with only $10,000 pledged at the close of [COP17]," said WWF, "follow-up work at intersessional meetings will be important."

“Back when the UN Convention on Biological Diversity was first adopted in 1992, one of the main pillars was ensuring the fair and equitable benefit-sharing from biodiversity, especially from provider countries and local communities,” said Vishaish Uppal, director of governance, law, and policy at WWF-India. “Almost 35 years later, we’re still not seeing the companies that profit off nature sharing their benefits with the Indigenous peoples and local communities that act as the custodians of much of the biodiversity that their businesses rely upon. It really is about time that countries iron out these differences, so that funding can reach the people and places that need it the most.”

An Lambrechts, a biodiversity politics expert at Greenpeace International, said that "giant corporations did everything they could to keep the Cali Fund voluntary two years ago, and then did everything they could to stop the fund from working in Yerevan."

"It is unacceptable that big multinational corporations are turning massive profits from what they take from nature while contributing very little to its protection and leaving people across the world to face the impacts of the biodiversity crisis," said Lambrechts.

"It is unacceptable that big multinational corporations are turning massive profits from what they take from nature while contributing very little to its protection and leaving people across the world to face the impacts of the biodiversity crisis."

Negotiators also established a permanent body for Indigenous peoples and local communities under Article 8(j) of the Convention on Biological Diversity, but Sustainable Business Services warned that "questions remain over institutional status, representation, and the extent of their participation in decision-making."

COP17, said the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS), "put forth a clearer picture of the global biodiversity crisis and the gaps that must be closed to meet the world’s 2030 targets."

But Susan Lieberman, vice president for international policy at WCS, said that "the negotiations themselves ended up weak on ambition."

“This meeting should have been a turning point, not just a stocktake. Success required governments to commit the political will and financing needed to reverse biodiversity loss," said Lieberman. "That means protecting and restoring ecological integrity, respecting the rights and leadership of Indigenous peoples and local communities, and reducing the drivers of decline. With just four years until 2030, we cannot afford another conference that diagnoses the crisis without accelerating the cure."

Twenty-two of the 23 targets set by the Kunming-Montreal framework are behind schedule, and Lieberman said that COP17 "has clarified the challenge" of ensuring they are met.

"Now governments must summon the political will, resources and resolve to meet it," she said. "We applaud the Armenian government, the [Convention on Biological Diversity] secretariat, and many governments and partners for keeping the momentum moving toward achieving the 2030 goals and targets. But ‘good enough’ should never be acceptable.”

Friends of the Earth International (FOE) also said the two weeks of negotiations had "ended with weak decisions and many unanswered questions," pointing to "the capture of this space by transnational corporations" and the "greenwashing and false solutions like biodiversity offsets and credits" that it said would continue.

Along with calling out harmful subsidies, FOE helped launch a campaign during COP17 highlighting how "business sectors contribute to biodiversity destruction and related human rights impacts," such as in the pulp and paper and biomass industries.

"In Indonesia, the expansion of industrial plantations and biomass production continues to drive forest loss and biodiversity decline," said the Environmental Paper Network, which joined the initiative.

With the Yerevan Pathway, said Nele Marien, coordinator of the forest and biodiversity program at FOE, "the structural drivers of biodiversity loss remain an elephant in the room: the financial and legal systems that undermine biodiversity need to be addressed."

Wilmer Lucitante, member of the Kofan nation and spokesperson for the Union of People Affected by Texaco and FOE Ecuador, said that COP17 is "a turning point, as the ways of operating of the Indigenous body of the convention were established."

"Yet the measures are voluntary, and do not alter the power transnational corporations wield in our territories," said Lucitante. "In the Kofan territory, from the time of Texaco and until now, fossil fuel companies have contaminated our lands and violated our rights. Voluntary measures are clearly not enough."

WCS said the overall outcome of the summit, just before countries meet in Türkiye for the 31st UN Climate Change Conference, where climate finance is expected to be a major topic, was "too timid."

"The COP17 decision merely encourages countries to begin applying a set of voluntary guidelines, which will be negotiated further before COP18," said the group. "This 'kicking the can down the road' falls far short of what is needed at a time when climate change poses a significant threat to biodiversity ecosystems, and the loss and degradation of ecosystems is driving emissions and reducing the capacity of people and nature to adapt."

The administration reportedly intends to send the Afghans to Pakistan, whose government would then expel them across the border into Afghanistan, where the Taliban has ruled since the US withdrew from the country in defeat over five years ago.

According to the Times, those slated for deportation include relatives of people who aided the US military invasion and occupation and at least one gay man. Both categories of people would face possible execution or severe persecution by the Taliban.

"Five years ago, Americans watched Afghans cling to planes to escape the Taliban. On Monday, our government plans to charter one back to their persecutors' hands," Krish O'Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of refugee resettlement organization Global Refuge, said in a statement Friday.

"For the people on that manifest, the consequences could be prison, torture, or worse," she added. "For their families here, some of whom served alongside US servicemembers, it means losing a loved one without knowing whether they'll ever hear from them again."

Vignarajah implored the Trump administration to halt or reverse the plan before the flight departs.

"Pakistan is patently unsafe for Afghans," she said. "Its own government has made that clear by hounding them out of the country by the millions. Deporting Afghans into that crackdown is a deliberate decision to put them in harm's way."

Since 2023, Pakistan's government has expelled more than 2.7 million Afghans, according to Global Refuge, and has vowed to remove approximately 1.5 million who remain in the country regardless of their immigration status. The United Nations has documented killings, arbitrary detention, and torture of people associated with Afghanistan's former US-backed government and security forces.

The Taliban has also systematically stripped Afghan women and girls of the rights they gained during the US invasion, banning them from secondary schools, universities, and most employment, while imposing sweeping and draconian restrictions on their lives.

"Individuals returned to Afghanistan face grave, systematic dangers, including arbitrary detentions, executions, public flogging, and retaliatory violence," the group Human Rights First said Thursday. "Women and girls face severe restrictions on basic freedoms, including systematic denials of education, employment, and public speech."

Several Democratic US lawmakers, including Democrats on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, decried the planned deportations.

"We made a promise to our Afghan allies—that after aiding and protecting our troops during the conflict in Afghanistan, America would not abandon them," said Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.). "This administration is betraying that promise, deporting them to potential torture and death."

Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) posted: "While he hopes nobody is watching, Trump greenlit the expulsion of more than 150 Afghans back to Taliban rule, where they will face almost certain persecution, torture, or worse. Accountability for Trump’s cruel immigration agenda cannot come soon enough."

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) also weighed in, writing on social media, "Our Afghan allies risked everything to help the United States."

The Michigan race could determine which party holds control of the Senate—and whether Democrats are able to rein in Trump in the last two years of his presidency.

Mehdi Hasan of Zeteo News emphasized that while the congresswoman was happy to condemn a fellow Democrat who "has nothing to do with an ad that isn’t racist," she has ignored "the endless actual racist abuse the candidate has had to endure."

text:
Deportations via Pakistan

The Trump administration plans to deport dozens of Afghan migrants via Pakistan, with ABC News describing a court filing that shows a deportation flight expected next week would take the deportee to Pakistan and then onward to Afghanistan. Shane Vandayour of Afghan I-OK described some of those facing deportation as relatives of people who worked alongside American forces, and the BBC said the Donald Trump administration plans to deport dozens of Afghan migrants via Pakistan. NBC News said a senior administration official told it the proposed deportation flight could take place as early as Monday, and it said the deportees could include relatives of Afghans who worked with the U.S. military in its 20-year war against the Taliban.

ABC News said advocates and families previously told it that hundreds of Afghan immigrants are being held in Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention in Louisiana, from where many international deportation flights depart. Shawn VanDiver, founder and president of AfghanEvac, told ABC News that families of those detained are "terrified."

Fear of Taliban return

Shawn VanDiver told ABC News that if removed to Afghanistan, some families fear those removed will face torture or persecution from the Taliban, and he said, "Anybody from Afghanistan is in danger if they get sent back."

Human rights defenders warned that some migrants may be targeted due to their ethnic or racial background, and the BBC said the U.S. Department of Homeland Security declined to comment on potential deportation operations in the future and cited security considerations.

The administration’s position is, ‘These individuals do not have status in our country, therefore we don’t really care what happens to them,’ and NBC News quoted a senior administration official as saying it while it said the official declined to be identified because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

Reuters said the deportations are via Pakistan because Washington, lacking diplomatic ties with the Taliban government, cannot directly arrange their return to Afghanistan, and the BBC reported that.

NBC News said the legality of so-called third-country deportation agreements is set to be debated by the Supreme Court in December.

Lawmakers and advocates react

Democratic Rep. Scott Peters said in a statement that "Afghans who stood with American troops, and their families, are being quietly loaded onto a plane to Pakistan" and he called the decision "absolute cruelty" that needs to be reversed.

Senator Chris Coons of Delaware wrote on X that "While he hopes nobody is watching, Trump greenlit the expulsion of more than 150 Afghans back to Taliban rule" and he said they will face "almost certain persecution, torture, or worse."

The BBC said the U.S. Department of Homeland Security would not comment on potential deportation operations in the future and cited security considerations, while it also reported that Vandayour urged the U.S. Congress to pass a law granting temporary protected status to Afghans residing in the country.

Shawn VanDiver told NBC News that AfghanEvac had confirmed that in recent days, at least 80 Afghans have been moved to Louisiana from 34 other ICE facilities around the country, and it said 19 of them were without legal representation.

A State Department spokesman reaffirmed that "all countries must be able to manage their borders and immigration processes in a manner that ensures the safety, security, and prosperity of their citizens."

The city contracts out garage management to a private entity, IMCO Parking, that in turn subcontracts it to the federal General Services Administration, which supports logistics for other federal agencies.
“Any use of city garages to stage ICE enforcement activity is not in line with the SFMTA and city values.
And that agency in turn assigns parking spaces to ICE.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have parked their vehicles in a downtown garage owned by the city, and allegedly staged enforcement operations out of the structure — a possible violation of San Francisco’s sanctuary city ordinance.

The San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency confirmed Friday that the immigration agency is assigned parking spaces inside the Golden Gateway Garage at 250 Clay St.

“We are aware that the [General Services Administration] has assigned parking spaces to the Federal Immigration Customs and Enforcement Agency in the SFMTA’s Golden Gateway garage, as it is located on Clay Street in very close proximity to the ICE field office,” wrote spokesperson Parisa Safarzadeh, director of communications for SFMTA.

The city contracts out garage management to a private entity, IMCO Parking, that in turn subcontracts it to the federal General Services Administration, which supports logistics for other federal agencies.

The city said it is investigating the issue. “We are working with our City Attorney’s Office to explore all options related to our contractual agreement at this time,” Safarzadeh wrote.

“Any use of city garages to stage ICE enforcement activity is not in line with the SFMTA and city values. We are working with IMCO Parking, our parking garage management vendor, to understand and ensure any use of our city garage adheres to our local laws.”

The ICE agents have been working out of the garage for at least a year, said activists who have tracked ICE activity in and around the federal building at 630 Sansome St. This site was the epicenter of immigration arrests — and heated protests against them — last year. Immigrants are still arrested at that building.

During those protests, ICE agents and activists clashed repeatedly and violently on downtown streets. Several ICE vehicles were involved. In a July 2025 confrontation, an ICE SUV drove through a crowd of protesters, and a woman holding onto its hood was thrown off onto the street.

The use of a city-owned parking lot for immigration enforcement purposes may violate city and state sanctuary laws, which prohibit collaboration between local municipalities and federal immigration agencies, said Angela Chan, the assistant chief attorney in the San Francisco public defender’s office. She helped to draft some of those laws.

“SFMTA is responsible for overseeing city-owned garages and ensuring they are not used to facilitate ICE operations, directly or through private contractors,” Chan said.

The arrangement involves at least three layers. The city contracts a private firm, IMCO, to operate the garage. IMCO then subcontracts a portion of the lot to the General Services Administration. And that agency in turn assigns parking spaces to ICE.

Safarzadeh said that the SFMTA was aware of its operators’ subcontract with the federal government when it was signed, but said that contract “does not specify which federal agency the GSA assigns to the property.”

It is unclear if the SFMTA knew about ICE’s use of the parking lot before Mission Local’s inquiries on Friday.

Mission Local visited the garage Friday afternoon and observed a barricaded section filled with unmarked cars with federal government license plates, including a row of white vans. No ICE officers or other federal officials could be seen.

But video footage of a violent arrest of an immigrant outside the Concord Immigration Court in October of last year, reviewed by Mission Local, shows a blue Nissan SUV used by ICE with the same license plate as one parked inside the garage.

Activists say they have seen agents inside the lot standing in uniform. They also said a vehicle involved in a recent violent Oakland arrest that left an immigrant hospitalized was observed leaving the lot.

Supervisor Bilal Mahmood, who authored legislation that prevents immigration enforcement on city property, was not aware of ICE’s presence at the city-owned garage until Mission Local raised the issue.

text:
This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune. The Texas Tribune is a nonprofit, nonpartisan media organization that informs Texans — and engages with them — about public policy, politics, government and statewide issues.

Texas ICE agent indicted for striking fleeing Houston pedestrian with vehicle

HOUSTON — A Harris County grand jury indicted a federal immigration agent Friday after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer was filmed on video running over a fleeing pedestrian during an Oct. 10 vehicle pursuit in Houston.

District Attorney Sean Teare said his office launched a criminal investigation of the ICE agent after his office reviewed footage showing an unmarked patrol vehicle striking Miguel Parra-Hernandez, 48.

Teare said ICE agent Mario Alberto Morales faces a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon — the agent’s vehicle. If convicted, Morales could face between two to 20 years in prison, Teare said.

“The evidence that we have in this case is as clear as any that I've prosecuted or investigated,” Teare said at a news conference at the Harris County criminal courthouse.

Surveillance footage captured from a nearby business depicts two men getting out of a white pickup truck and running in different directions through a parking lot. The footage shows a black SUV driven by Morales pursuing one of the men from behind as they ran.

“What happened next shocked our entire community,” Teare said. His office shared ICE body camera footage that showed Morales swerve his vehicle toward Parra-Hernandez at the moment of impact. The agent’s car is jostled — authorities say the vehicle ran over Parra-Hernandez — and the pedestrian can be heard crying out in pain.

Morales stopped his SUV and exited the vehicle. The agent’s body camera shows Parra-Hernandez on the ground, writhing in agony. Morales grabs one of his limp legs and moves it.

“Give me your hand,” Morales told Parra-Hernandez as he turned him face-up. “My leg!” Parra-Hernandez yelled.

“I was coming and I hit him with the car,” Morales told another ICE agent nearby.

Teare also released a recording of a 911 call Morales made.

“I tried to get around him, and he hit my car,” Morales told a 911 dispatcher, according to the audio. The dispatcher asked Morales if he was near Parra-Hernandez.

“Yeah, he’s fine, he’s just complaining of pain,” Morales responded.

He later told the dispatcher that Parra-Hernandez was handcuffed, and Morales planned to put him in the ICE agent’s vehicle. The operator advised the agent not to move him.

A “very concerning” pursuit

Harris County Sheriff Ed Gonzalez, who was also at the news conference, said that there were two other handcuffed people in the backseat of Morales’ vehicle before the crash occurred.

That is “very concerning,” Gonzalez said.

“I know of no law enforcement agency that would deem that to be acceptable,” he added. “To the contrary, it's very unsafe.”

Teare agreed, saying, “No law enforcement officer would have two people in custody in the back of their vehicle who are not wearing seatbelts and engage in another pursuit.”

ICE said that agents were searching for a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who had a deportation order, and believed that man was in the same truck as Parra-Hernandez.

But Mendoza-Cervantes’s daughter later told the New York Times that her father died nearly a decade ago.

An unnamed ICE spokesperson responded in a statement defending Morales, saying that the indictment “is nothing more than a political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians.”

“Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are reckless and false,” the unattributed statement says.

Aaron Reitz, the top federal prosecutor for the Southern District of Texas, said in a statement that he wasn't consulted by Teare's office about the investigation. He called the indictment a "political prosecution" of an ICE agent who was simply doing his job.

Reitz said he's conducted a preliminary review of the case and sees no need to pursue federal charges. He said his office will continue to evaluate the evidence.

"Federal agents should not be turned into political trophies for doing the difficult and dangerous work of enforcing federal laws," Reitz said. "We stand with ICE and all our federal law enforcement partners."

Hiring standards at ICE

Since returning to the White House, President Trump has made immigration enforcement a priority. Congress approved a $75 billion budget for ICE — making it the highest-funded U.S. law enforcement agency — to hire more deportation officers and carry out street-level operations. Morales is one of the surge hires in the agency that occurred in 2025, Teare said.

“Without going into detail of his prior work history and the rest of it, I can unequivocally tell you that I've reviewed thousands of job applications and resumes for law enforcement officers from around this state, and I'm not familiar with a single agency that would have hired this person based on his past,” Teare said.

Teare said he has significant concerns based on the four months of ICE activity in Houston about the background of surge hires, along with their length of training.

Teare added that two immigrants who were detained and were witnesses in this case have since been deported by ICE. He added that one of his office’s investigators had to fly to Port Isabel Detention Center to attempt to talk to a witness “hours before they deported him, less than a week after this crash.”

The district attorney said Parra-Hernandez is currently in a rehabilitation facility and is still facing deportation, regardless of being a “victim of a second-degree felony.”

At least three ICE officers, including Morales, have been criminally charged in connection with immigration enforcement operations during Trump’s second term.

Christian Castro, 52, faces five counts, including second-degree assault and filing a false police report, in connection with the wounding of a man during an immigration operation in Minnesota.

Gregory Donnell Morgan Jr., 35, is facing two felony counts of second-degree assault in connection to a Feb. 5 ICE operation in Minnesota when prosecutors say he pointed a gun at the occupants of a vehicle.

Teare’s office is also investigating the fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who was killed by ICE agent Gregory Feathers after agents tried stopping the construction foreman’s van in Houston while he was on his way to a job site with his employees. Teare said the same grand jury that indicted Morales will also decide whether to indict Feathers.

“In all honesty, this was not even in the back of my mind that I would be having to investigate multiple instances of federal officers harming our community members,” Teare said.

Evidence in the Morales case

Teare said he credits the quickness of the indictments in the Morales case to the availability of body cameras and surveillance cameras. No ICE agents were wearing body cameras when Salgado was shot — but ICE changed its policy after Salgado’s sons and Democratic lawmakers such as Sylvia Garcia, D-Houston, demanded more transparency from the agency.

“I credit the advocacy of the Salgado family that they were wearing body cameras,” Teare said.

Teare said ICE has been more cooperative in this case compared to Salgado’s case.

“We are still working with laser focus on the Salgado case,” he said, mentioning his office is preparing to finish its investigation before Thanksgiving and present it to a grand jury afterwards.

Teare said his office is in contact with the agent’s attorney but doesn't know if the agent is still located in Houston.

Teare said that fewer crimes are being reported to police in Houston because victims are scared ICE will arrest them — or worse.

“They are just driving around our city, grabbing people,” Teare said of ICE agents. “That's what's happening. And they are not exercising any normal law enforcement tactics while they're doing it.”

The community is living in fear, Teare said, and it’s making everyone less safe.

“An ICE badge doesn't give you free rein to violate the constitutional rights of anyone,” he said.

text:
President Donald Trump has his favorite riffs during campaign rallies.

He’s recently complimented the physique of Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio. He still calls out former President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris.

But in recent weeks, the president spun Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., into heavy rotation on his playlist. The Department of Homeland Security and Justice Department are now probing Omar for alleged immigration fraud and financial disclosure reports.

TRUMP SAYS ILHAN OMAR COULD GO TO JAIL OR BE DEPORTED, CALLS HER ‘A DISGRACE TO OUR COUNTRY’

"What she did was use a fake name and other things that are fake," the president groused about Omar. "She used the fake name to be sworn in. I assume she must immediately resign from Congress."

Trump argued that Democrats "just conceded her seat."

They didn’t.

And the president declared that "she will not be legally allowed to be a member of that august body of politicians."

Not accurate.

The president doesn’t decide who gets to sit in Congress. Article I, Section 5 of the Constitution grants that power to the House and Senate. It charges both bodies with authority to "be the Judge of the Elections, Returns and Qualifications of its own Members." The Constitution goes on to say that the House and Senate may "punish its Members for Disorderly Behavior; and, with the Concurrence of two thirds, expel a Member."

We bring up those responsibilities because it’s possible that the House may need to tangle with the "qualifications" of Omar. Especially since the New York Times reported that the Minnesota Democrat faced scrutiny by the Obama-era Justice Department in 2016. Moreover, that inquiry says the feds found evidence that she may have entered into a fraudulent marriage.

If that’s the case, there could be questions about Omar’s citizenship. And thus, whether she’s even permitted to serve in Congress. Especially if it’s found she was naturalized as a citizen via bogus means.

Republicans have been after Omar for years. Across the aisle, Democrats are concerned this could be a distracting headache. Especially if they seize control of the House after the midterms next week.

THE HITCHHIKER'S GUIDE TO WHY REMOVING ILHAN OMAR FROM CONGRESS COULD BE HARDER THAN TRUMP EXPECTS

The inquiry into Omar began in 2016 when she ran for the state legislature. Former President Barack Obama was in office. The investigation continued into the Biden administration. The feds terminated the inquiry in 2021.

After the Trump administration raided Omar’s home in October — seizing electronics and documents — Obama defended the congresswoman.

"It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say," the former president said. "But that’s exactly what the Trump administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar."

Obama said the current inquiry flipped her life "upside down" and characterized it as an effort to "intimidate someone."

Controversial influencer and livestreamer Hasan Piker asked Omar about how her week was going amid the investigation.

"It tracks for me," replied Omar. "That’s kind of what I’m used to."

A spokeswoman for Omar said that she "has repeatedly and unequivocally denied this baseless, disgusting conspiracy theory."

But indications that Omar faced scrutiny ten years ago make it harder to characterize this as wild, right-wing conjecture emanating from the blogosphere.

"Who ordered [the investigation] closed?" asked Fox contributor Paul Mauro. "Reportedly, both administrations had opened cases into this. We now know how much smoke there is."

Omar campaigned for the state legislature in 2016. Her campaign released a letter from the U.S. attorney saying it "wasn’t investigating" nor requesting an inquiry into Omar.

So was she cleared? Or does word of the old probe pour petrol on the flames?

"Omar will talk about and say, ‘They've looked into this. Nothing came about it,’" said University of Minnesota political science professor Kathryn Pearson. "But I think it's also a talking point that Republicans will use. So I think sort of both sides will try to use that to their advantage."

John Nagel is Omar’s Republican opponent on the ballot next week. Nagel views the new investigation as a political wedge.

"With the raid on her home, people should keep this in mind. It's a very serious accusation," Nagel said. "As far as I'm concerned, Somalia comes first in her life. And we are nothing more than a piggy bank for her."

TRUMP PUSH TO OUST OMAR FACES HISTORIC SUPREME COURT TEST, BUT LEGAL EXPERTS SEE ‘UNCHARTED’ TWIST

At least one Republican is ready to bounce Omar from the House.

"If the evidence shows that she is not an American, she has to be removed immediately and probably put in prison," said Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla. "I think the idea that a foreigner might be actually serving in Congress should be terrifying to Americans."

But another House Republican urges caution.

"We just need all the facts," said Rep. Chris Smith, R-N.J. "I hope that the investigation is thorough, fair, and absolutely aboveboard."

And then there is the question of due process.

"The Ethics Committee should commence an investigation. It takes two-thirds of the House to expel a sitting Member. I would highly doubt the Democrats would agree. And certainly not without findings," Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., told Fox. "I think at a minimum, the Ethics Committee should move forward with an investigation immediately upon our return."

This could develop into a real hornet’s nest for the House when lawmakers descend on Washington after the midterms. That’s to say nothing of questions about seating Omar when the new Congress starts in January. If Democrats win the House, would House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. — perhaps as speaker — be forced to grapple with the question of seating Omar if Republicans move to exclude her?

In fact, such a motion to exclude comes right before the new speaker swears in the entire House on Jan. 3. The speaker would swear in 434 members. Then takes votes related to the potential member in question. If Democrats win the House, new, moderate House Democrats might take their first formal floor vote on whether to seat Omar.

Voting against Omar might be good for some of these new members, considering the political nature of their battleground districts. But would the Democratic brass pressure new members to vote with the caucus on such a nettlesome issue?

Democrats who vote to seat Omar give Republicans an immediate opportunity to build a case against newly-christened members representing swing districts. A vote to exclude or expel Omar would go down as one of the most important roll calls of the entire two-year Congress.

We haven’t even explored how progressives and Democratic Socialists — new to the House — might rage at moderate Democrats for not supporting their colleague. That could produce a serious schism among Democrats.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

This isn’t going away. Omar is a lightning rod. The GOP believes it can continue to milk this. President Trump has his favorite riffs about Omar. And it’s possible that House Republicans may as well.

text:
An ICE agent has been indicted by a grand jury in Texas after hitting a Mexican construction worker with his car last month.

The US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer was charged on Friday with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, accused of intentionally ramming the car at the man, prosecutors said.

The officer, Mario Alberto Morales, was driving an unmarked SUV in Houston on October 10 when he struck and ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez, who was running away during a pursuit through a parking lot, according to the Harris County District Attorney's Office.

Parra Hernandez broke his leg and remained in federal custody at a rehabilitation facility, said District Attorney Sean Teare, who announced the indictment at a news conference that included body camera video of the encounter and a recording of Morales calling 911.

ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, an account that Mr Teare said was contradicted by video.

"The evidence we have in this case is as clear as any that I've ever prosecuted or investigated," he said.

Morales's attorney, David Lindenmuth, said his client did not commit a crime.

He and ICE both said Morales did not intentionally strike Parra Hernandez and accused the Democratic district attorney of indicting Morales for political reasons.

"Mr Morales is truly a good man, a former member of our military, that has given his entire life to public service either for his country or in or adjacent to law enforcement," Mr Lindenmuth told The Associated Press.

"To have him charged for what was so clearly just an accident, the DA's office, the DA himself, has invented a crime out of thin air."

Morales had worked as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Mr Lindenmuth said.

Morales, charged with a second-degree felony, was not in custody on Friday and a warrant would be issued for his arrest, according to Mr Teare.

Body camera footage shows ICE car's sharp movements

Parra Hernandez has lived in Harris County, Texas, for more than 30 years and did not have a deportation order or criminal background, according to Mr Teare.

He was in a vehicle that ICE tried to stop.

He jumped out and was followed by Morales, who was in a Jeep Cherokee.

Previously released surveillance video shows the Jeep speed over a median and drive toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away.

Morales's body camera footage that Mr Teare played on Friday shows the officer making a few sharp moves with the steering wheel before the SUV shakes.

In the video, Morales stops the vehicle then gets out and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is several feet away.

Parra Hernandez is on the ground and grabbing his leg, yelling in pain.

Morales is heard saying, "He got hit with a car, bro." It is not clear to whom he is talking.

"I was coming in and I hit him with the car," Morales says after another ICE officer arrives.

In a 911 audio recording in which Morales requests an ambulance, Parra Hernandez can be heard yelling.

Morales tells the operator, "He's fine. He's just complaining of pain."

Parra Hernandez told deputies that he believed a police officer was stopping the vehicle he was in but got scared and fled when the man started putting on a mask.

He repeatedly told deputies that Morales "threw the car at me", according to a Harris County Sheriff's Office incident report reviewed by the AP.

Morales told deputies he did not intentionally hit Parra Hernandez.

He acknowledged that he did not brake before hitting Parra Hernandez and said he was trying to avoid another truck in the parking lot.

Body camera video indicated that Morales had two other suspects in custody in his back seat, according to the report.

But the deputy wrote that Morales told them there was no-one else inside.

"From the beginning, the video told a different story than what was offered by the agency," Parra Hernandez's attorney, Kim Bruno, said on Friday.

She said her client has suffered not just fractures in his leg, but nerve damage and chronic pain.

Family says ICE was looking for a dead person during operation

Other aspects of ICE's account have also been called into question.

After Parra Hernandez was taken into custody, ICE released a photo of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, and said he was the target of the operation that day.

ICE said he was seen entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez.

Family members of Parra Hernandez said they had never heard of him.

FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston that has been working with the family, said Mendoza-Cervantes's daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017.

Mr Teare's office has previously said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE's statement.

ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for years

Morales is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, although other encounters have come under investigation, including a separate fatal shooting by an ICE officer in Texas.

WASHINGTON, D.C. (UM News) — A U.S. federal appeals court ruled Oct. 20 that United Methodists and other faith groups can move forward with their lawsuit to stop a Trump administration policy that allows immigration enforcement within houses of worship.

A divided three-judge panel for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit found that the coalition of Christian and Jewish groups has grounds to sue over the enforcement change.

The faith groups have demonstrated under the new policy, “their members face a ‘credible threat’ of enforcement that will likely cause imminent, if not immediate, injury,” Judge Florence Pan wrote for the majority.

Judge Robert Wilkins joined the majority, and Judge Neomi Rao dissented.

The ruling in “Mennonite Church USA, et. al., vs. U.S. Department of Homeland Security,” revives the lawsuit after a lower court in April 2025 denied the organizations’ bid for early relief. The appellate court has reversed that denial of a preliminary injunction and sent the case back to the lower court.

At issue in the suit is the U.S. Department of Homeland Security guidelines that permit federal agents to carry out immigration raids in “sensitive locations,” such as schools, hospitals, synagogues and churches.

Homeland Security instated the new policy in January 2025, soon after President Trump’s second inauguration. The move put an end to the longstanding practice of restraint in such locations.

The faith groups’ suit, filed Feb. 11, 2025, seeks to prevent Immigration and Customs Enforcement from intruding on ministry without a judicial warrant or special circumstances. The suit contends that the new policy violates both the Religious Freedom Restoration Act and the religious freedom protections in the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution.

The United Methodist Commission on Religion and Race as well as the denomination’s New York, North Georgia and Western North Carolina conferences are among the groups bringing the legal action.

More United Methodist ministries wanted to join the case, but the constraints of the lawsuit limited the number of plaintiffs. Each United Methodist body is a separate legal entity under federal law.

United Methodist leaders, meeting at the Leadership Gathering in Calgary, Alberta, cheered the ruling while noting this is only one step in a long legal battle.

“It’s inherent in our Wesleyan DNA to fight for justice for those that are marginalized and those that are oppressed, and this is an accentuated case,” said Bishop Thomas Bickerton, who leads both the New York and New England conferences. “This was the right thing to do because there are people that are suffering great, great injustices.”

The United Methodist Church’s Social Principles, based on multiple passages on Scripture, have long affirmed “the dignity, worth, and rights of migrants, immigrants and refugees, including displaced and stateless people.” United Methodist congregations don’t check to see if people have the right documentation before welcoming them to worship.

Bickerton added that United Methodist churches in New York have a long history of receiving immigrants into their membership. After all, New York City historically has been where multiple waves of immigrant populations first came ashore in the U.S.

“They are our people, and we’re standing with them at all costs.”

A big source of contention in the case is whether the faith groups involved have shown that the new policy endangered their members and whether reinstating the previous sensitive-location policy would provide relief.

The appellate court’s ruling sided with the faith group’s arguments on both counts.

“Plaintiffs point to several specific examples of the government engaging in enforcement activity at or near their members’ houses of worship,” Pan wrote.

In fact, shortly before the appellate court held oral arguments in the case in February, ICE agents arrested a member of North Hills United Methodist Church Hispanic Mission in Los Angeles, while the church was distributing food. United Methodist Carlos Chavez, an undocumented immigrant from Mexico, was deported shortly after — leaving behind his wife and children. He was not accused of any crime.

“The trauma that the church had to go through is incredible,” said California-Pacific Conference Bishop Dottie Escobedo-Frank, whose area includes Los Angeles.

“We’ve seen it happen in several churches that people won’t come to church if ICE is going to come in,” she said. “Why would they? And so, it affects our ability to gather as worshipping communities because people are afraid to go to church.”

Last year, armed ICE agents also staged an operation in the parking lot of a Charlotte, North Carolina, United Methodist church during preschool pickup.

Western North Carolina Conference Bishop Ken Carter, whose area includes Charlotte, said the conference’s cabinet and trustees decided to join the lawsuit precisely to ensure churches could be safe from such intimidation tactics.

“Sanctuaries are set-apart places that protect human dignity and the image of God,” Carter said. He added that sanctuaries are supposed to provide places “that value people, where they can worship God and trust God.”

The 27 plaintiffs also include the Christian denominations of the Mennonite Church USA, the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church, the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), the Episcopal Church, the Friends General Conference (Quakers) and the Presbyterian Church (USA). The Unitarian Universalist Association is another plaintiff.

Also joining the suit are three Jewish branches — Union for Reform Judaism (the largest Jewish movement in the U.S.), Reconstructing Judaism and the United Synagogue of Conservative Judaism.

They all share a common belief that God calls the faithful to welcome the stranger.

“Immigrants are our siblings, neighbors, pastors, and fellow members of the body of Christ,” said the Rev. Giovanni Arroyo, the top executive of the United Methodist Commission on Religion and Race.

“When fear keeps people from gathering for prayer, receiving pastoral care or participating in congregational life, the whole community suffers,” he said. “We remain committed to accompanying immigrant communities, confronting racism and xenophobia, and equipping congregations to put their faith into practice through solidarity, care and advocacy.”

Bishop Robin Dease, who leads the soon-to-unite North Georgia and South Georgia conferences, shared a similar sentiment.

“Somebody has to stand in the gap. Somebody has to speak out when injustice is taking place,” she said. “I’m excited about the ways that our churches are protecting immigrants.”

text:
According to international media reports, the US government is planning to deport more than 150 Afghanistan citizens to Afghanistan.

Reuters reported on Friday, October 30, that the first flight carrying these migrants is expected to depart on Monday, November 2, via Pakistan.

According to the report, the US government detained these asylum seekers in the state of Louisiana and has made plans to deport them to Afghanistan.

text:
The Kabul Tribune (KT) — Dozens of Afghan immigrants detained by U.S. authorities, including possibly relatives of Afghans who worked alongside American forces, are expected to be deported early next week, ABC News reported, citing lawyers, advocacy groups and families of detainees.

A court filing reviewed by ABC News in the case of one Afghan immigrant indicates that a deportation flight scheduled for next week is expected to take detainees to Pakistan, with further transfers to Afghanistan.

Hundreds of Afghan immigrants are currently being held in Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities in Louisiana, according to advocates and family members previously interviewed by ABC News. Louisiana is a departure point for many international deportation flights.

Charlotte Moyal told ABC News that her husband, who has been in immigration detention for more than a year, was recently transferred from a facility in Pennsylvania to Louisiana. She said he had been notified that he could be deported as early as next week.

Shawn VanDiver, founder and president of AfghanEvac, a nonprofit organization supporting Afghans evacuated during the U.S. military withdrawal from Afghanistan, said families of detainees were terrified about the possible deportations.

He warned that Afghans returned to their home country could face persecution or torture under Taliban rule.

"Anybody from Afghanistan is in danger if they get sent back," VanDiver told ABC News.

A State Department spokesman told ABC News earlier this week that the department maintained its position that all countries must be able to manage their borders and immigration systems while ensuring the safety, security and prosperity of their citizens.

Democratic Rep. Scott Peters, a longtime supporter of Afghan refugees, criticized the reported deportations and urged the administration to reverse the decision.

"Afghans who stood with American troops, and their families, are being quietly loaded onto a plane to Pakistan, where they will very likely be pushed to the Taliban-controlled Afghanistan," Peters said in a statement.

He warned that returning vulnerable Afghans to Taliban-controlled Afghanistan could expose them to mortal danger, calling the reported decision "absolute cruelty."

text:
The US administration is preparing a charter flight to deport dozens of Afghan migrants and asylum seekers to Pakistan. According to NBC News, this could be the first such flight, and, according to human rights advocates and relatives of detainees, it could depart as early as Monday.

A senior US administration official who spoke to NBC News on condition of anonymity said that the plane could not land in Pakistan without the knowledge and approval of Pakistani authorities. At the same time, it is unknown what formal arrangement between Washington and Islamabad could govern this flight.

Risk of return to Afghanistan

Among those facing deportation are relatives of Afghans who worked with the US military during the 20-year US war against the Taliban. Human rights advocates fear that Pakistan may return the deportees to Afghanistan, where the Taliban is in power.

Pakistan, which hosted millions of Afghan refugees for decades, launched a large-scale campaign in 2023 pressuring Afghans to leave the country and forcibly deported some of them. AfghanEvac president Shawn VanDiver said Afghans sent from the United States would face a high risk of being subsequently returned to Afghanistan, where they could face persecution, imprisonment, or worse consequences.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Detainees and agencies' positions

According to VanDiver, at least 80 Afghans have been transferred to Louisiana from 34 other US Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities in recent days. Nineteen of them have no legal representation. He also suggested that hundreds of Afghans may be held at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center.

According to NBC News' administration source, the flight may include people with deportation orders, those denied asylum, and individuals whose temporary protected status the administration has terminated. Some Afghans sought asylum after crossing the US border from Mexico, while some of their cases are still under review.

The White House referred a request for comment to the US Department of Homeland Security. A department spokesperson said they could not confirm removal operations for operational security reasons. ICE did not respond to a request, while the State Department said it was not planning any announcements.
