title: How Trump and his allies seek to interfere in the US midterm elections - The Guardian
description:
The Trump administration’s efforts to interfere began last year with an effort to collect detailed voter roll information from nearly every state.
Trump said he ordered the justice department to file the lawsuit.
US district judge David O Carter ruled against the justice department on Wednesday.
Despite the aggressive approach from the justice department, there’s reason to be skeptical of their list in California.
“We’ve had disputes over Senate elections, like Coleman versus Franken in Minnesota in 2008, but they never determined which party is the majority,” Foley said.
text:
Donald Trump is waging a brazen effort to interfere with voting in this year’s midterm elections, escalating concerns that the federal government will try to slow down certification of election results – a strategy that could create chaos when the new Congress is seated next year.

Experts are certain the administration’s efforts to subvert America’s elections will not work. And some have bemoaned “fearmongering” about far-fetched scenarios that are unlikely to go anywhere in court.

But after the attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021, voting lawyers and other democracy groups aren’t dismissing the possibility of anything.

The potential for interference is related to how close the contest winds up being, said Ned Foley, a professor at the Ohio State University and an expert on disputed elections.

“The more it looks like a blowout or a ‘blue tsunami’, the harder it’s going to be for any attempt to make mischief to get any traction,” he said.

“I put the probability of these impactful nightmare scenarios materializing at under 50%, so I’m not expecting them to make a difference,” he added. But, he said there are “risks of weird things happening, and you need to pay attention to them even if the risk is rather low”.

The Trump administration’s efforts to interfere began last year with an effort to collect detailed voter roll information from nearly every state. And it has continued into the final days of the election, in which the government has sought to sequester ballots in California and filed a legally thin lawsuit to try to stop the certification of election results in Alaska, where there is a hotly contested US Senate race.

The US constitution gives the states, not the federal government, authority to run elections. And it gives the president no power when it comes to voting.

“The type of conduct we have seen from the administration right now is unlike anything we have ever seen as far as federal attempts to interfere with the elections,” said Danielle Lang, a voting rights attorney at the Campaign Legal Center, a watchdog group. “It’s amounting to relatively little because the federal government is just not in charge of the levers of election administration and it can’t force itself to be involved in those levers of election administration.”

Here are some of the main ways Trump and his allies have sought to interfere with the election process – or could.

Using emergency power

Some of Trump’s allies on the right have encouraged him to invoke emergency powers to exert influence over elections, including potentially seizing voting equipment and sending troops to the polls. Trump has refused to rule out such ideas.

The move would be illegal – the president has no power, emergency or otherwise, over elections. Courts would likely quickly step in and stop such efforts.

But even if courts do step in to prevent things like ballot seizures, it could still cause chaos, confusion, and delay in a post-election period where there is uncertainty about the election results.

Stopping certification

The Trump administration’s most aggressive judicial effort to interfere in the election so far has come in Alaska, where it has taken the extraordinary step of asking a federal court to step in before election day and block certification if the Republican candidate loses.

Alaska has an extremely competitive US senate race this year between Republican Dan S Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola, and the outcome could determine which party controls the chamber. In a complicated twist, there is also a Dan J Sullivan on the ballot. The Alaska supreme court allowed Dan J Sullivan to stay on the ballot earlier this year in response to a ruling from the Alaska division of elections disqualifying him.

On 23 October, the justice department sued Alaska and asked a judge to block certification “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan”. It’s unclear how such an investigation would take place after an election, since U.S. voters cast their ballots secretly. Trump said he ordered the justice department to file the lawsuit.

The saga got more complicated days later when the New York Times reported that operatives aligned with Peltola were behind the effort to get Dan J Sullivan on the ballot as part of an effort to siphon votes away from the Republican candidate. Democrats had denied being behind the effort. Trump reacted angrily to the report. “Mary Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done, A FRAUD ON THE AMERICAN PUBLIC, and Dan Sullivan should be allowed to run without either Mary Peltola or FAKE Dan Sullivan on the Ballot,” he wrote on Truth Social.

The justice department’s legal argument for stopping certification is also extremely thin. In its lawsuit, the justice department pointed to broad language in the preamble to the 1993 National Voter Registration Act that says one of the purposes of the law is to “protect the integrity of the electoral process”. Election experts have said it is not possible to hang a legal case on such vague language.

The justice department knows it is going to lose the Alaska lawsuit, but may have another goal in mind, Richard Pildes, an election law scholar at New York University, wrote in a blog post.

“Even if DOJ loses in the federal courts, as it will, the litigation will give ammunition to anyone in the certification process, particularly the Lt. Gov., who might seek to delay or deny certification to the Democrat, Mary Peltola, if she wins, based on the claim that voters who voted for Daniel J. Sullivan (and perhaps ranked no other candidate) meant to vote for in the incumbent Republican Senator, Daniel S. Sullivan,” he wrote. In Alaska, the governor and Lt. Gov sign the certificate for the winning candidate that is sent to the US Senate.

Noncitizen voting

A key element of the Trump administration’s efforts to interfere in the election is a push to create the false impression that there are large numbers of noncitizens on the rolls who are voting – and perhaps to use that argument to mount post-election legal challenges. Studies have shown that noncitizen voting is exceedingly rare and that when it does occur, it is because of confusion.

The administration’s push to find noncitizen voters began last year, when the justice department filed lawsuits across the country seeking to have states turn over their voter rolls – each state is in charge of its own list of registered voters and there is no single federal voter database in the United States. In an extraordinary rebuke, more than two dozen different federal judges – including some appointed by Trump – rejected the requests from the government, saying they were unlawful.

Unable to get voter lists directly from the states, the Department of Homeland Security obtained public voter roll information and began running it against its own records to hunt for noncitizens. It has not been transparent about its methodology, and many experts have been skeptical of its accuracy.

On 13 October, the justice department delivered a USB drive with a password written on a Post-it note to election officials in Los Angeles county purporting to contain the names of 20,000 noncitizens on the voter rolls (there are more than 23 million registered voters in California). It gave the state 48 hours to review the names and sequester ballots cast by anyone whose citizenship had not been confirmed.

The state refused, citing concerns about cybersecurity and the administration’s methodology. On 15 October, the justice department sued California, asking a judge to order the state to sequester the ballots. As the justice department pushed the claims, they also announced the arrest of 28 noncitizens who allegedly had voted at one point in the state. US district judge David O Carter ruled against the justice department on Wednesday. The government is appealing that decision.

On 26 October, the justice department made a similar demand in Washington state, asking election officials to investigate the citizenship of 400 voters and sequester ballots for those whose citizenship it could not confirm.

The justice department has also threatened to prosecute election officials who process ballots from noncitizens.

Despite the aggressive approach from the justice department, there’s reason to be skeptical of their list in California. When local election officials sampled 200 names from the list they provided, they found many of them had already been canceled. Election officials also said a “high percentage” of those flagged appeared to be born in the United States. Washington secretary of state Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, responded to the justice department on Wednesday, saying it believed the list the government provided was inaccurate.

While the justice department’s efforts to get ballots segregated before the election are unlikely to succeed, they could offer a pretext for a post-election effort to challenge the results.

“There will be an argument – I can almost guarantee it – that a bunch of ballots in California should be thrown out because they didn’t segregate them,” said Ben Berwick, an election lawyer at Protect Democracy, a nonprofit that works on democracy issues. “I think this will be laughed out of court if they try to bring this past post-election.”

“That doesn’t mean we shouldn’t be worried or we don’t need to prepare for it,” he added.

Justin Levitt, a former justice department and White House official who worked on voting rights issues, said the government’s case was so weak it would have little chance of succeeding before or after election day. The administration’s lawsuits, he said, are best understood as press releases masquerading as legal complaints.

“There’s no part of the administration’s file that is designed to operate in a fashion where a court will make any meaningful ruling,” said Levitt, who is a professor at Loyola law school in Los Angeles. “There are ways in which the law works where a good claim today that cannot be brought just because it’s too early becomes a viable claim tomorrow. But time does not transmogrify crap into gold.”

Efforts to delay certification at the local and state level

After the 2020 election, Trump and allies put pressure on little-known officials at the local and state level to try and halt the certification of election winners. None of that worked, but election deniers have gained a foothold on local election boards throughout the country – positions from which they could try and slow down the certification process.

Election lawyers are well prepared for this possibility and are confident that judges would quickly end such efforts and order officials to certify the valid winners of elections. In the past, courts have stepped in to force election officials to certify.

“Ultimately, you cannot pull a contested election out of thin air, and there are processes here and you can’t just manufacture contests where they aren’t real,” Lang said. “I don’t imagine it looking all that different than it has in past election cycles where we’ve seen some issues with certification that ultimately come to a resolution. We’ve had counties that don’t want to certify; we’ve dealt with that before.”

Shenanigans on 3 January 2027

Efforts to delay or halt certification could be aimed at 3 January 2027, the date when the new Congress convenes. There’s concern that the Trump administration could use its various legal and rhetorical challenges to the results as a basis to try and block new members from being seated. The US constitution says: “Each House shall be the Judge of the Elections, Returns and Qualifications of its own Members,” giving both the US House and Senate leeway to handle disputed elections.

Federal law requires the governor and secretary of state to sign a certificate certifying a senator-elect’s win and send it to the Senate. In the past, when there has been a post-election dispute about the winner of a Senate race, the candidate who has the certificate gets seated provisionally while the Senate rules committee investigates. In cases where the margin of the race is close and there is no certificate, no senator has gotten seated until the dispute is resolved at the state level. After the 2008 elections, for example, a US Senate seat from Minnesota remained vacant for months while Norm Coleman and Al Franken battled in a close recount for months (Democrat Franken was eventually certified the winner).

“We’ve had disputes over Senate elections, like Coleman versus Franken in Minnesota in 2008, but they never determined which party is the majority,” Foley said. “If partisan control over the Senate hinges on something like Coleman verses Franken, it will be a politically consequential and fraught moment as the dispute remains unsettled. It also depends on how irresponsible the rhetoric is around the dispute.”

There have been lengthy post-election disputes over US Senate seats before. Pildes, the NYU election expert, suggested that the justice department’s efforts to interfere in Alaska may be aimed at bringing such a long-shot challenge in the US Senate.

Trump himself has suggested that Republicans refuse to seat Peltola if she wins.

“You’re going to have to see what happens. It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run. Frankly, I don’t know how you could allow somebody like that to run. It’s so unfair when you look at that,” Trump said on Thursday.

In the US House, there is also the possibility of maneuvering, though it is more complicated.

Unlike the Senate, the House is not a continuing body and ceases to exist at noon on 3 January. That means that any challenge to a member-elect would be heard by the new House – one where Democrats are expected to have a majority.

There’s worry about another longshot strategy. A single bureaucratic official, the clerk of the House, is responsible for putting together the roll of new members. There’s some speculation that Mike Johnson, acting under pressure from Trump, could fire the current clerk of the House and replace him with a loyalist willing to exclude some Democratic members-elect from the roll. Republicans could then theoretically move to hold a speaker vote and try and maintain their majority without the seated Democrats – a strategy that would require the support of the other Republicans in the House.

Democrats would assuredly go to federal court to stop such an effort.

Many scholars are skeptical it would work. Derek T Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, has described the speculation about replacing the clerk of the House as “sophisticated disaster porn”. Johnson has also pledged to seat Democrats who win.

“It strikes me as quite unlikely, to me, at least, that this group of Republicans–the one that takes days to choose a speaker and that regularly cannot maintain order in its ranks–is going to have the cohesion and coordination to pull off this kind of activity, which, to emphasize, can be thwarted by other means, either politically or judicially,” he wrote earlier this year.

But Brian C Kalt, a professor at Michigan State University who has written about contested house elections, said: “I think it’s very hard after January 6th to just write off concerns like this.

“It’s reasonable for people to study the issue, think about the issue, worry about the issue. But I don’t think that it’s some imminent threat,” he added. “If there are going to be any shenanigans, there will be initial steps, signs that will be available. This isn’t just something they can spring.”

Interference at the polls

The Trump administration has refused to rule out the possibility of immigration agents being at the polls, a move that would violate federal law. Speaking in September, DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin refused to categorically rule it out. DHS agents were also canvassing houses earlier this year, inquiring about people’s citizenship and whether they had voted. (A federal court blocked the government from continuing to do this in October). Federal law prohibits armed troops from being at the polls.

“The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” Mullin said. “ICE’s job is immigration, customs enforcement. That’s their job … if we’re serving a warrant we will be where we need to be,” he said. Asked about the possibility of ICE agents at the polls, Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the justice department’s civil rights division, told 60 Minutes recently that “there is no plan to do that.” The justice department, which plans to conduct a significant poll-monitoring operation on election day, has also said it will not use ICE or FBI agents as poll monitors.

Still, election officials are planning on what to do if immigration officers do show up at the polls and there are several lawsuits seeking to block them from being deployed. Democrats are also planning on sending their own monitors to the polls to ensure voters aren’t intimidated or interfered with.

Ballot seizures

One of the Trump administration’s most aggressive efforts to intervene in elections came in January, when FBI agents descended on an election warehouse in Fulton county, Georgia, and seized all ballots from the 2020 presidential election.

Trump lost Georgia in 2020 by 11,779 votes – a result that was confirmed by both recounts and audits. Trump has been obsessed with overturning the result ever since the election and he and allies have pushed several conspiracy theories since 2020 to argue that he didn’t lose. Those theories have all been debunked, which is why it was stunning that a federal magistrate judge signed off on a warrant to seize the ballots in January based on the same theories. (As is customary, the judge did not give a reason for why she felt there was enough probable cause).

Now, there is concern that the Trump administration could try a similar approach elsewhere and convince sympathetic judges to approve warrants to seize ballots. Such an effort could be done with an eye towards making it harder for election results to be certified at the local and state level, Berwick said.

“There’s a big leap between what happened in Fulton county, which was a magistrate being willing to sign a warrant for materials that were over five years old, and a magistrate being willing to sign a warrant for live ballot materials,” Lang said. “Everybody is preparing for every worst-case scenario, but I am very hopeful that we are unlikely to see a warrant signed for live materials.”

text:
What goes on inside Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention centers across the US happens behind closed doors and high fences.

Personal accounts of lengthy detention, misery and sickness and allegations of abuse rarely reach the public directly while people are still behind bars.

But a group of men detained in Texas found a new way to communicate what they are going through in custody, despite being shuttered from the outside world. They compiled hundreds of pages of handwritten testimony and some hand-drawn art, and mailed it from inside the privately run ICE jail.

One man even wrote two protest songs and sang them over a crackly prison pay phone to the Guardian. In a solemn and defiant tone, he sang from the perspective of one detainee to another: “We are the people, raising our voice. You are my brother, brother I am. Today as you find yourself in this prison, give me a hug, I give you love.”

Others’ stories were scribbled on notepaper, between July and September this year.

“We are immigrants, we are not criminals,” one wrote. Distraught, the men blame their situation on “nothing more than the result of racist policies” by the Trump administration.

“Why is it that a simple migrant, who one day leaves for work, can end up not seeing sunlight nor breathing pure air for days, simply due to a status adjustment?” one writes, nodding to Donald Trump’s actions of detaining immigrants despite them having temporary legal status or ongoing cases.

The men find themselves “behind bars, living an experience that marks a ‘before’ and ‘after’ for the detainee and his family”, another testimony says.

The detainees are at the T Don Hutto detention facility in Taylor, on the outskirts of Austin, a place nicknamed “la perrera” – Spanish for “the dog pound” – to reflect harsh conditions.

The package of writings and art was mailed to a detainee’s relative and shared with the advocacy group Center for Popular Democracy, which shared it with the Guardian.

Many tens of thousands of people are detained by ICE across the country – the majority without criminal histories – amid the anti-immigration crackdown. The men’s reported experience is common, but their way of communicating it is not.

The Guardian received testimonies from at least five detainees after months of detention, but is withholding most identifying details for their safety.

They add up to almost 200 pages of narratives in Spanish, drawings and documents. The T Don Hutto facility is run for ICE by the private prison company CoreCivic. The men wrote that the facility makes them feel not like people but like “inventory”.

One explained that they wanted to “alert, denounce and affirm what is seen, lived and felt daily, while being detained”.

One series of drawings depicts a man waving to his family as he leaves for work, but then being arrested by ICE officers swooping outside a grocery store and locking him up. Other, sparely drawn sketches show the detention center’s bleak cells, hallways and communal areas, along with an immigration court.

The fiery testimonies make allegations of abuse by CoreCivic guards, and substandard food and medical care.

“CoreCivic plays a limited but important role in the immigration system,” a company spokesperson said in a statement. “We do not decide who is detained, for how long, or whether someone is released. Our job is to care for the people at our ICE-contracted facilities safely, humanely and with dignity while their cases proceed.”

“The safety, health and well-being of the individuals entrusted to our care is our top priority. We do not dismiss the concerns of the people in our care, and we respond to legitimate issues through established processes,” the spokesperson added.

The detainees also sent out a list of demands, including calls for their immigration cases to be processed more quickly, to be reunited with families, the release of children from other immigration centers and of detainees with developmental disabilities. They also called for investigations into the rising number of immigrant deaths in ICE detention.

“These first-hand accounts reveal more than what is happening inside a single detention facility. They expose an entire system that strips people of their dignity, separates families and treats fundamental constitutional rights as optional,” said DaMareo Cooper, co-founder of the New York-based Center for Popular Democracy, a progressive advocacy organization. “What is equally powerful is the extraordinary courage of those risking so much to speak out. Behind every testimony, every piece of artwork and every story is a human being enduring unimaginable pain.”

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said that “any allegations of subprime conditions or misconduct at the T. Don Hutto Detention Center are FALSE”.

“All detainees are provided with 3 meals a day, clean water, clothing, bedding, showers, soap, and toiletries,” a DHS spokesperson added. “Illegal aliens also have access to phones to communicate with their family members and lawyers. Certified dietitians evaluate meals.”

However, the men, who regard some of the testimonies as a collective appeal, write: “Being an immigrant does not mean you do not have rights.” They go on to say that their notes and drawings were done “for those who will be here, for those of us who are here, and for those who left”.

The Hutto facility is relatively small and detains only men. In late September, there were 497 total detainees – almost reaching full capacity, according to a review of a daily roster page. Most people were booked into the facility in 2026, with many others in 2025. Two men have been detained for more than three years, since September 2023, according to the roster.

“We know some community members in there right now – we get a lot of information about how bad it is,” said Alejandro Caceres, an organizer with the Austin Sanctuary Network, an immigrants rights group in Texas. Caceres said he had also heard repeated complaints about alleged retaliation by guards, substandard medical care and food, and the use of solitary confinement in the facility.

A Honduran father describes in his testimony how he was arrested by ICE in San Antonio, Texas, in August, after seven years in the US. He says he does not have a criminal record. He worked at a mechanic’s shop, and cycled to a convenience store during break to get coffee and cigarettes, but as he was leaving, he says, he saw a black vehicle speeding towards him.

“I thought it was someone driving drunk or under the influence of drugs, or someone who wanted to kill me,” he writes.

He described his fear as the people in the vehicle jumped out and pepper-sprayed him. He lost consciousness and woke up to officials splashing water on his face, he said.

“It was exactly at that moment that I discovered they were ICE,” he writes. The Guardian was unable to confirm his account.

Detainees also accuse guards of abuse. In late September, a detainee described how he saw a Cuban man attempt to take a piece of bread from the cafeteria back to his cell to later eat it “alongside his coffee”. The guards would not allow it, so he quickly ate it in defiance. According to the written account, the confrontation escalated, with guards beating him to the floor, bleeding. Other detainees “only saw through glass how they beat their companion”, the detainee wrote.

In a statement, CoreCivic said that incident “was reviewed in coordination with ICE, and it was determined that excessive use of force was not used”.

DHS did not respond to any of the specific allegations of abuse, with a spokesperson saying the department “are not going to entertain unnamed allegations from the Guardian”.

One of the men detained in the facility who chose to be named is Julian Osorio Garcia, an asylum seeker from Colombia who spoke by phone from inside and is the man who wrote the protest songs and sang them over the phone.

“I do not know why migrants are treated in such an inhumane way,” he said. “We have so many stories here. I have heard some situations that are extremely difficult.”

Osorio has requested asylum in the US and received a work permit while waiting for his case to be decided. But he was arrested in Texas in May, after he and a friend were pulled over by local law enforcement working with ICE – an increasing trend – according to him and a cousin, in separate phone interviews.

Osorio came to the US in 2023 with a legal tourist visa and about one year later requested asylum after being threatened by criminal groups in Colombia, he and his cousin both said. According to a Colombian judicial document shared with the Guardian, a Colombian magistrate with the country’s special jurisdiction of peace found Osorio to be an “indirect victim” of the country’s decades-long civil conflict.

Osorio’s attorney filed a habeas petition with a US federal judge in June, requesting his release while he fights his case. A federal judge in Texas denied Osorio’s petition in late October, meaning he cannot be immediately released from detention.

“It’s a migratory process that is costing tears, the separation of families, the loss of so much money for families [trying to fight their cases] – it’s leading to death,” said Osorio.

“And how can a private company profit from all this?” he asked, referring to CoreCivic.

DHS wants to deport Osorio. A spokesperson said he entered the US legally in 2023 “but chose to violate our nation’s laws by refusing to depart by the required date”.

“This administration is not going to ignore the rule of law just because the Guardian would like us to,” the spokesperson added. “Osorio Garcia will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending the outcome of his removal proceedings.”

The DHS did not respond to follow-up questions about this. Records show Osorio’s asylum case has not been decided.

In its statement, DHS also said that Osorio had been arrested in 2023 in Texas for driving while intoxicated. Court and arrest records accessed by the Guardian show that he was never convicted in connection with the charge and that the case is “inactive”. DHS did not respond to follow-up questions about the case.

The writings suggest strong solidarity among the detained immigrants. Osorio sang over the phone: “They persecute us, they arrest us, they put chains on us … Let’s all take to the streets, let’s go out en masse, we are Hispanos Free.”

One testimony says that when individual immigrants are released from the facility, the other detainees say goodbye by clapping and shouting as loudly as they can.

“Because, from here, no one leaves that easily,” one piece of testimony said.

text:
A recent legal ruling against an effort to fire the star-prosecutor daughter of a former FBI chief targeted by Donald Trump could send a strong message about politicized firings – and influence other judges weighing similar cases, legal veterans said.

Judge Jesse Furman ruled this week that the Department of Justice’s firing of assistant US attorney Maurene Comey without cause was unlawful. Comey, the daughter of former FBI director James Comey, successfully litigated numerous high-profile cases during her tenure at the southern district of New York, including guilty verdicts against Ghislaine Maxwell and Sean “Diddy” Combs.

“It looks as if Judge Furman has completely vindicated her and rejected just about all of the arguments made by the government,” said Carl Tobias, Williams chair at the University of Richmond School of Law. “And so it’s really important to have this because of the way she was essentially summarily fired, and so it sets a valuable precedent.”

The Department of Justice, which fired her without cause, had argued thatarticle II of the US constitution, which defines presidential power, imbued Trump and his attorney general with a right to fire line prosecutors – who are not political appointees.

But Furman this week rejected the department’s position, ruling Comey’s firing was not greenlighted under any law and in fact, violated the Civil Service Reform Act.

The justice department’s claim “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent”, Furman said. “It is also without merit. Indeed, to accept Defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.”

For legal observers, Furman’s decision is cause for optimism – even if optimism of the cautious sort – amid the Trump administration’s alleged repeated attacks on the rule of law. While one judicial opinion does not a panacea make, they said, such a ruling can send a strong message and be considered by other judges weighing similar cases.

“One thing I would caution is that it’s very clear the government will appeal this,” Tobias said. The justice department would do this via the second circuit court of appeals.

“I expect that Furman would be affirmed by that court, and then I assume the administration would then appeal to the US supreme court,” he added.

Then, it would up to the US supreme court to decide whether they even want to hear the case – and if they decline, the lower appeals court decision would stand.

“You are seeing the courts step up and stop and prevent the administration when they are violating the rule of law,” said Neama Rahmani, founder of West Coast Trial Lawyers and a former federal prosecutor. Just this Monday, Los Angeles federal court judge David Carter rejected Trump’s attempt to set aside 20,000 ballots in California, Rahmani noted.

“Whether it’s the supreme court and birthright citizenship, or even individual cases like this, there have been limited, I would say, rulings by the court that have limited what President Trump can do.”

Like Tobias, Rahmani said the justice department can fight federal district and appeals court decisions. And, this kind of case does contain legal issues that might pique the supreme court’s interest – especially if different federal appeals courts were to reach different conclusions.

If the supreme court did decide to hear arguments on Comey’s case, it would by no means guarantee a check on Trump’s power.

“There are a lot of the justices on the supreme court that really don’t believe there should be much of any restrictions on what the president can do,” Rahmani said. “So this is far from the silver bullet.”

For now, though, Furman’s decision can prove influential.

“The decision can be used by other folks who do believe that they were terminated lawfully,” Rahmani said, adding, “It is not binding at all, but it’s certainly something that judges look to with similar or exact same facts.”

Elizabeth Wolstein, a partner at Schlam Stone & Dolan LLP and former Manhattan federal prosecutor in the civil division, said that a judge’s decision in one case could potentially affect how other judges’ weigh similar issues.

“It doesn’t have any binding effect on another judge, even in the same district, as opposed to how a second circuit or US supreme court case would be binding,” Wolstein said. But, “if it’s well reasoned and persuasive, it is definitely going to be persuasive to another judge faced with a similar issue.”

Comey filed suit over her ouster in September 2025. Comey said she neither received notice nor explanation of her firing. Instead, Comey on 16 July 2025 got a letter that stated “your employment with the Department of Justice is hereby terminated, and you are removed from federal service effective immediately.”

When Comey asked the then Manhattan US attorney, Jay Clayton, about this notice, he allegedly said “all I can say is it came from Washington. I can’t tell you anything else,” per court papers.

The Department of Justice has said Comey’s firing was directed by the former US attorney general Pam Bondi and subsequently “ratified” by her successor, Todd Blanche.

Comey’s lawyers and critics of the US president have claimed that she was fired because her father is longtime Trump foe James Comey. Trump’s justice department has repeatedly tried prosecuting James Comey, this week making public its third case against him; one prior proceeding was dismissed, another is pending.

The department had defended the idea that someone’s familial relations could be considered in termination proceedings.

Maurene Comey’s legal team viewed Furman’s ruling as a positive development in protecting the rule of law. Comey’s attorneys are Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron and Deepa Vanamali at Clarick Gueron Reisbaum, as well as Margaret Donovan at Koskoff Koskoff & Bieder.

“The Court’s decision is a complete rejection of this administration’s sweeping claim to unchecked executive power, and it demonstrates that our constitutional system of checks and balances is alive and well,” the team said in a statement.

The justice department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Furman’s decision or claims of politically driven firings. In a statement, the White House rejected allegations that Trump’s justice department is trying to punish opponents.

text:
COLEBROOK, N.H. —

A man who was driving to Canada to start a new life was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in New Hampshire.

Jessie Laurel Tepler-Mujambere, a 28-year-old originally from Burundi, had been living with his adoptive family in Maine for the past decade.

Tepler-Mujambere had a pending asylum status in the United States, and earlier this week he received the paperwork for his Canadian citizenship.

"His car was packed, completely packed, totally ready to go. He's like, I'm moving to Canada. I'm 28 years old now to start my life," his adoptive mother, Denise Tepler, said.

On his way to Canada, Tepler-Mujambere was pulled over by police near Colebrook.

According to the Department of Homeland Security, Tepler-Mujambere was pulled over for speeding, and it was determined he was illegally present in the U.S.

Tepler-Mujambere's family said he was not told why he was pulled over.

DHS said that "Tepler-Mujambere first entered the United States at the Dulles International Airport on November 10, 2014, with permission to stay until May 5, 2015. Against our nation’s laws, he overstayed his welcome and failed to depart once his legal permission expired."

In that same statement to News 9, a DHS spokesperson said, "A pending application does NOT confer legal status in the United States," a DHS spokesperson wrote in a statement to News 9.

Tepler-Mujambere's family told News 9 his work permit was not renewed by the federal government in June.

They said his Canadian citizenship was approved in July, but the paperwork came the last week of October.

Tepler-Mujambere was detained by ICE until he was eventually brought to Canada.

During that time, his family said he was driven from Colebrook to the Strafford County Jail in Dover to spend the night. The next morning, they said he was brought down to Manchester, then back up to the Strafford County Jail for a second night. On Friday morning, his family said he was driven by officers to the Canadian border in Vermont, where he was ultimately released.

His adoptive mother, Denise Tepler, is a state senator in Maine. She called this situation a waste of time, energy, and American taxpayer dollars.

"He almost was in Canada, and he had his Canadian citizenship papers with him," she said. "And yet they put him in jail for two nights. That means we're paying to house him and feed him for two nights."

Tepler said that her son's car was towed to a New Hampshire garage with a $150 towing fee and a $100 per day fee.

The Department of Homeland Security is encouraging people who are not in the United States legally to self-deport.

description:
Federal immigration agents detained the adopted son of a Maine lawmaker for two days this week after New Hampshire police stopped him just 10 miles short of Canada, which had just granted him citizenship.
Police in Colebrook, New Hampshire, stopped him that afternoon and turned him over to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the Teplers said.
The taxpayers paid for his last two nights in a county jail in New Hampshire,” Denise Tepler said in a Friday interview.

text:
Federal immigration agents detained the adopted son of a Maine lawmaker for two days this week after New Hampshire police stopped him just 10 miles short of Canada, which had just granted him citizenship.

Jessie Laurel Tepler-Mujambere, 28, set out on Wednesday, shortly after his citizenship paperwork arrived in the mail, according to his adoptive mother, Sen. Denise Tepler, D-Topsham, who took him in as a teenager when his biological father brought him to Maine from Burundi and abandoned him at a shelter. She and her husband, Sheldon Tepler, a lawyer in Lewiston, later adopted him.

Police in Colebrook, New Hampshire, stopped him that afternoon and turned him over to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the Teplers said. He spent the next two days in custody in different locations across New Hampshire. An agent drove him to a Vermont border station on Friday afternoon.

The case comes as immigration advocates criticize President Donald Trump’s crackdown for sweeping up nonviolent immigrants who are following legal paths to status. In Maine, that has included working asylum seekers who entered the country on visas. The Teplers said their son’s detention accomplished nothing except costing taxpayers money.

“This is ridiculous. The taxpayers paid for his last two nights in a county jail in New Hampshire,” Denise Tepler said in a Friday interview. “They are paying for this transfer to Vermont.”

The family will cover the rest, she said, including hundreds of dollars in fees after his car was towed.

An ICE spokesperson said in a statement Friday that Tepler-Mujambere had overstayed the visa he used to enter the country in 2014 and had detained him “pending his removal to Canada.” It referred to federal incentives offered to immigrants like Tepler-Mujambere’s who were willing to “self-deport now,” including a free airline ticket and $3,000.

The Colebrook Police Department did not respond to a message seeking comment.

When Tepler-Mujambere first arrived in the U.S., he unsuccessfully sought legal status through a program for abused and neglected immigrant children, his family said. He then applied for asylum, which allowed him to get a work permit. He earned an associate degree and worked in health care.

Sheldon Tepler was born in a refugee camp in Montreal after his parents fled the Holocaust. When he obtained Canadian citizenship a few years ago, he realized his adopted son could also get it through him.

“The lights went on: This kid can live in Canada,” he said.

Canada approved Tepler-Mujambere’s citizenship on July 22, according to a photo of the certificate his adoptive sister, Maya Tepler, shared with the Bangor Daily News. The official document did not arrive until Wednesday.

By then, his work permit had expired and the federal government had not renewed it. He spent the months of waiting mostly exercising and reading the Bible, Denise Tepler said.

“I gave him a hug and kiss goodbye and he was excited,” she said.

She thought he planned to cross in Jackman. But at 4:37 p.m., he texted her that Colebrook police had arrested him.

Colebrook is about 10 miles south of the U.S. Customs and Border Protection port of entry in Canaan, Vermont, which is typically used by Mainers traveling toward Montreal. Its police department takes part in a federal program that gives local officers some immigration enforcement powers. (Maine lawmakers banned such partnerships last year.)

“I told them I’m waiting on my asylum but I wa[s] heading to Canada and I have documents to show,” he texted his family, according to a screenshot.

He spent the next two days moving between the Strafford County Jail in Dover, New Hampshire, and an ICE field office in Manchester. Staff for U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, a Democrat from Maine’s 1st District, helped the family keep track of his case, a Pingree spokesperson confirmed.

ICE accused him of overstaying the visa he used to enter the country as a teenager, the Teplers learned. The agency offered him voluntary departure, which is sometimes called “self-deporting,” according to Pingree’s office.

“What, exactly, did this accomplish? New Hampshire police and ICE put him through this ordeal, tied up personnel, and spent taxpayer dollars to accomplish absolutely nothing. This was nothing more than a colossal waste of resources, manpower, and taxpayer dollars,” Pingree said in a statement.

By Thursday evening, officials seemed likely to simply release him. On Friday, an agent drove him to the Highgate Springs border crossing in Vermont’s northwest corner.

He arrived in Canada around 4 p.m. Friday, Maya Tepler said. His car was still sitting in a Colebrook lot more than 100 miles away, packed with his belongings.

text:
A court temporarily halts the resumption of Green Card lottery.

A three-judge panel of the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals Thursday blocked an order that required the Trump administration to reopen the Diversity Visa lottery. The temporary block means the Diversity Visa program, which is also known as the Green Card lottery, will not open by November 1. The order came as the government requested an injunction staying the previous order, under which the program would have opened. This is another legal setback for the Diversity Visa Program 2027 but Red Eagle Law, the immigration law firm that filed the lawsuit against Secretary of Marco Rubio in August, said they would move forward with other litigation to challenge the State Department's failure to carry out the DV program.

Timeline of what exactly happened

December 2025: The Trump administration paused the Diversity Visa programAugust 2026: The State Department announced another pause on issuing diversity visas, following a court order that had ended the earlier pause.August 2026: Immigration law firm Red Eagle Law sued the government over its failure to open DV-2027 registration.October 2026: A federal district judge ordered the State Department to reopen DV-2027 registration.October 2026: The Trump administration appealed the ruling and sought to suspend the order.October 2026: The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals granted the government's request to temporarily suspend the lower court's order. The stay is a temporary one on the ground that the law firm did not have the legal right to bring the challenge. People who would be affected should approach the court as the Green Card lottery was created to encourage immigration from countries with low US immigration rates, not to generate business for immigration law firms. The judges also pointed out that the firm had not brought the case on behalf of any prospective lottery applicants.

Who will be affected?

Those who were waiting for the registration to open on November 1.

India is not an eligible country for the Green Card lottery, as India's rate of US immigration is high. So Indians do not come under this.

What happens next?

The State Department is not required to open DV-2027 registration by November 1 because the appeals court has stayed that requirement.

The appeal against the district court's preliminary injunction is still pending.

The future of the 2027 registration process remains uncertain.

Does US want to stop Diversity Visa program?

Diversity Visa program admits 55,000 immigrants to the US annually from countries with historically low rates of immigration to the US. The State Department said it was pausing the program as it was undertaking a review of the screening and vetting protocols. "The Department of State is committed to ensuring that its visa process upholds the highest standards for US national security and public safety. This action is being taken in light of concerns raised by the shooting at Brown University and killing of an MIT professor suspected to have been committed by an individual admitted to the United States through the DV program. This pause will allow the Department to undertake a review of the screening and vetting protocols in the DV program. This review will address any vulnerabilities in the process to ensure the Department can adequately establish the identity of aliens who are selected through the DV entry lottery, establish the applicants’ visa eligibility, and ensure that they do not present a threat to national security or public safety," the State Department said. The department said they may conduct interviews but no Diversity Visa was being issued.

Contains scenes which some viewers may find upsetting. - Watch: Moment ICE agent hits Texas immigrant with vehicle

A US immigration agent has been charged with felony for allegedly hitting a man with a vehicle earlier this month in Texas, a prosecutor announced.

The prosecutor said US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer Mario Alberto Morales was indicted by a grand jury on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

Morales is accused of running over a Mexican national who was living in the US without legal documentation, leaving him with multiple leg fractures and a hip injury.

An ICE spokesperson dismissed the indictment as "nothing more than a political stunt" and described the allegations as "reckless and false".

The indictment comes amid the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration and a series of violent incidents involving federal agents that have resulted in injuries and deaths.

If convicted, Morales faces between two to 20 years in prison for the second-degree felony, according to Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare.

Teare said Morales pursued a vehicle driven by Miguel Parra-Hernandez, a 48-year-old Mexican national who has lived in Texas for more than 30 years without legal documentation, on the morning of 10 October.

Parra-Hernandez and another occupant fled the vehicle on foot before Morales "aggressively steered his vehicle" into the Mexican national, Teare said at a news conference in Houston on Friday.

He said Parra-Hernandez had no criminal record and was not subject to a deportation order.

"Not only did he hit Mr Hernandez, he ran over both of his legs, leaving him seriously injured and hospitalised to this day," Teare said.

Morales then called 911 to report that Parra-Hernandez had hit his car.

Teare said that ICE was allegedly pursuing a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, a Mexican national and undocumented immigrant, who has apparently been dead for nine years.

Immediately after the incident, an ICE spokesperson told the BBC's US media partner CBS News that Parra-Hernandez had run in front of the immigration agent's vehicle.

Following the indictment, ICE rejected the allegations brought by the grand jury - a panel of citizens empowered to determine whether there was sufficient evidence to bring criminal charges.

"This is nothing more than a political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians," an ICE spokesperson said in a statement to the BBC.

"Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE," the spokesperson said, adding that the men and women of ICE "are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct".

The statement added that federal officers acting in the course of their duties could only be investigated by other federal agencies. The spokesperson insisted that local governments did not have the authority to run such an investigation.

District Attorney Teare stressed that he had the utmost respect for law enforcement and believed that undocumented individuals who were violent felons should be deported.

He said he hoped the prosecution would not only deliver justice for Parra-Hernandez and his family but also send "a loud and clear message to every ICE officer who feels that they have a free pass to terrorise our streets".

title: Bigger budget, bigger role. Rights groups respond to Frontex reform - EU Perspectives
description:
Brussels wants Frontex to become the engine of Europe’s deportations, with almost twice the money to do it.
The European Commission wants €11.8bn for Frontex, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency.
In their view, more powers and money for Frontex could mean more rights violations at Europe’s borders.
Frontex gets a bigger role in returns and closer ties with non-EU countries.
In her view, the Commission “risks turning Frontex into a European version of ICE”, the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency.
text:
Brussels wants Frontex to become the engine of Europe’s deportations, with almost twice the money to do it. Rights groups are critical. They warn the plan could send migrants to countries they barely know and expose them to abuse far beyond the EU’s reach.

Money sits at the heart of the plan. The European Commission wants €11.8bn for Frontex, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency. The sum is part of the EU’s next long-term budget for 2028–2034. That is almost double the agency’s current allocation of about €6bn.

Magnus Brunner, Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration, presented the proposal on 27 October. He said member states themselves had asked for the increase. The reform has two aims. First, it should help Frontex protect the EU’s external borders. Second, it should turn the agency into the bloc’s operational arm for returns.

Human rights organisations did not wait for the details. Even before the reform came out, they raised the alarm. In their view, more powers and money for Frontex could mean more rights violations at Europe’s borders. Once the proposal was out, other groups joined in. Among them were Caritas Europa, a Catholic charity network, and the Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants (PICUM). They criticised a “political obsession with deportations that ignores the realities of migration and Europe’s own economies”.

New powers, old fears

The reform holds few surprises. Frontex gets a bigger role in returns and closer ties with non-EU countries. It also gets an explicit mandate to monitor public social media. In addition, it could help carry out returns from one non-EU country to another. Critics say this opens the door to so-called ‘return hubs’. These are centres outside the EU where member states can send people with no right to stay.

“These powers and resources risk exposing refugees and asylum seekers to a greater danger of persecution,” said Sissy Katsoni, a legal consultant for Front-LEX. She pointed to the agency’s failure to meet its fundamental rights obligations. Sarah Chander, director of the Equinox Initiative for Racial Justice, sees another risk. The reform, she warned, could deepen Frontex’s role in individual returns. At the same time, digital tools and data sharing could blur the line between migration control and police work.

Josephine Solanki of the Abolish Frontex network questioned the need for more money. “It is not true that there is a lack of resources to ensure safe and dignified reception for migrants. It is a matter of priorities,” she said. David Yambio, co-founder of Refugees in Libya, condemned interceptions at sea and the transfers to Libya that follow. In detention centres there, he said, people face torture, exploitation, and sexual violence. Mr Yambio wants guarantees for migrants who might end up in ‘return hubs’ in third countries. He also called for effective ways to protect their rights.

Together, the organisations want clear conditions. Any expansion of the agency’s mandate should depend on effective oversight and accountability. Stronger internal monitoring bodies are not enough, they argue, if violations carry no real consequences. Yet the proposal goes the other way. It would narrow the reach of the agency’s own rights watchdog and pass complaints on to national authorities.

Abuses beyond Europe’s borders

Caritas Europa then took a closer look at the proposal. Its analysis focused on Frontex’s wider cooperation with non-EU countries on returns. Secretary General Maria Nyman spoke to EU Perspectives. “This could open the door to Frontex involvement in return hubs, which may be established in third countries under the new EU return regulation. We reiterate our concerns regarding these hubs, which risk leading to widespread human rights violations, legal limbo, ‘chain refoulement’, and de facto detention outside of Europe,” she said.

‘Chain refoulement’ means that countries pass people on, one to the next, until they end up where they face persecution. Ms Nyman also warned about the hubs themselves. They are possible under the Return Regulation, in force since 16 October. Such hubs “could result in people being deported to countries with which they have little or no connection, potentially for extended periods of time”, she said.

Governments should be investing in policies that protect people’s rights (…) rather than pouring more resources into an increasingly expansive deportation apparatus. — Chiara Catelli, Advocacy Officer at PICUM

PICUM shares these concerns. “Deportation operations and immigration detention centres in the EU are already rife with abuse, and we fear that expanding Frontex’s role will exacerbate these abuses within the EU and extend them beyond its borders,” said Advocacy Officer Chiara Catelli. She also questioned the priorities behind the reform. “At a time of growing inequality and economic insecurity, governments should be investing in policies that protect people’s rights and enable them to move, settle, and work in dignity, rather than pouring more resources into an increasingly expansive deportation apparatus.”

Battle lines in Parliament

The reform still has a long way to go. Both the Council of the EU and the European Parliament must approve it. In Parliament, a common front of the European People’s Party (EPP) and the far right now backs tougher migration rules. The European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) group is already celebrating. In its view, the tighter rules follow “the political line charted by the Italian government”.

The Greens, however, see it very differently. “The Commission is pandering to populism and the far right on migration,” said MEP Tineke Strik (NLD). In her view, the Commission “risks turning Frontex into a European version of ICE”, the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. The Socialists and Democrats (S&D) group also rejects the plan. It opposes tasking Frontex with “implementing a ruthless deportation policy”, even beyond the EU’s borders.

text:
Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita wants a Marion County court to make Indianapolis Public Schools teach staff how to collect immigration information about students. This is the latest turn in the immigration lawsuit Rokita first filed in November 2025 against the district. At the time, IPS called the case "silly litigation and political posturing."

Rokita continues to argue IPS is violating the state's anti-sanctuary law because the district currently prevents staff from collecting students' immigration status.

In a new court filing dated Oct. 26, the attorney general asked the court to make IPS notify staff they are allowed to collect and maintain immigration information about students. Rokita also wants the district to train staff on the forms of information gathering and maintenance allowed. The judge has not yet ruled on Rokita's requests.

The state is also asking the court to impose civil penalties against the district of $10,000 for each knowing or intentional violation of the law.

This request comes two months after a judge ruled against a related request from the attorney general.

Rokita argues the district's policies could hamper federal efforts to locate unaccompanied migrant children. His filing says more than 300 of those children may have been placed in ZIP codes that include parts of the district.

"IPS's policies do not promote the safety of Hoosier schoolchildren. They undermine it," the filing says.

Earlier in this case, Rokita requested a preliminary injunction that, as the judge put it, would require the district to "follow the law." In August, the court denied that request saying it was too broad. The judge also said the attorney general did not show that he was likely to win the case on the merits and failed to show there was irreparable harm if the current policies continued.

The judge found the district's current policies do not restrict staff from cooperating with federal authorities on immigration matters. Instead, staff are directed to check with supervisors, who consult the district's lawyers before releasing information.

The judge wrote the current protocol is prudent, "Otherwise, law enforcement authorities could approach a school en masse, obtain consent or information from an unsuspecting and nervous custodian, librarian, substitute teacher, coach or anyone affiliated with a particular school without allowing that staff member to seek direction from an administrator or legal counsel on whether 'the enforcement actions do not violate federal or state law.'"

The court also found the district's practice of not collecting immigration status is consistent with 2021 guidance from the Indiana Department of Education.

IPS argued that ICE officers are not covered by an exception in federal student privacy law, known as FERPA, that allows some records to be shared with representatives of the U.S. attorney general. The judge agreed, but Rokita continues to argue the district is relying on "an incorrect interpretation of" of the law.

The lawsuit is ongoing.

text:
WORCESTER – Standing in the shadow of the federal courthouse on Main Street, dozens of residents spoke out in opposition to federal immigration detentions that activists say are happening constantly but quietly throughout the city.

The crowd came dressed in all black, with signs advocating for due process and human rights. Some carried pictures of people detained in high-profile arrests and others of those who have been arrested outside of a media spotlight.

Most signs – and chants, which were shouted as protesters marched to City Hall – called for an end to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity and the federal policies responsible for the uptick in detentions.

“When ICE gets someone, it’s quick and often people don’t know what happens. They become just another person who’s been disappeared,” said Frances Anthes, a LUCE volunteer, who helped organize the Worcester action.

LUCE, an organization that independently tracks detentions and provides mutual aid to impacted families, estimates that ICE has detained, on average, over 20 people per month since July in Worcester. In October, the group reports 31 known arrests in the city as of Wednesday, Oct. 28.

The federal Department of Homeland Security, in response to questions asking to verify the LUCE arrest numbers, defended the legality of the agency’s actions: “Every day, DHS enforces the laws of the nation across the country including in Massachusetts,” a spokesperson wrote to the Telegram & Gazette.

Anthes, who is chair of the Worcester Board of Health, is part of LUCE’s verified volunteer network that takes shifts at Worcester courthouses, where, she said, much of ICE’s activity is concentrated, to monitor when arrests happen. She also responds to on-the-ground reports of apprehensions that witnesses call in to the organization to help verify what has happened.

Outside of City Hall, not far from the federal courthouse, demonstrators paused their march to circle around a handful of speakers and passed LUCE hotline cards to passersby, encouraging Worcester residents to call if they see ICE.

The Rev. Judith Hanlon, senior pastor of Hadwen Park Congregational Church and founder of the LGBT Asylum Task Force, a group that houses and provides legal support to people seeking asylum, described the elevated feeling of fear asylum seekers are experiencing. She said she’s started advising them to “stay in the house, cower, keep hiding, do not get on a plane” to avoid any possible interaction with federal agents.

City Council Vice Chairman Khrystian King recited a poem by the late activist Ruth Rodriguez-Fay titled “Lady Liberty Dream Deferred,” and said this issue is “deeply personal” to him and his family, as the child of parents who emigrated to the United States from Bermuda. He condemned the federal policies and detention tactics ICE agents have employed against residents across the country.

“What we have here is an absolute failure, as it relates to making sure Worcester stays safe, as it relates to making sure that our kids and our families are able to navigate our city safely, and we know that on a daily basis here we have ICE in action, taking people with no criminal charges away from their families and impacting us as a city as a whole,” King said in an interview.

Motorists driving by the protest honked and a few people passing on the street jeered as the march continued to the Worcester County Courthouse, blocks away on Main Street. A moment of silence was held outside of the court before the protest dispersed.

Claire Schaeffer-Duffy, a LUCE volunteer and a founder of Saints Francis and Therese Catholic Worker House, recalled an instance two weeks ago where she watched as a friend, a Portuguese-speaking man she stood with at a Quincy courthouse to address a criminal charge, was detained by ICE agents while he was traveling from one courtroom to another.

“It was an astonishing intervention,” she said. “He stays at the Catholic Worker program, so he’s in an immigration process, which is being addressed. He has an attorney working on his asylum case. He has an ankle monitor. So, what else can this person do?”

text:
This spring, immigration agents detained a Nevada resident who held temporary protected status (TPS), a type of special deportation protection for immigrants from highly dangerous countries such as Venezuela or Ukraine.

The man in the case, Lucio Alexander Bernal Munoz, had lived in Las Vegas for decades, according to court records, migrating to the U.S. in the 1990s from El Salvador. After he was charged with drug possession in April, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement took him into custody, alleging he did not have a valid visa and was not properly admitted into the country.

At the time of the arrest, Bernal Munoz was waiting for his status to be renewed.

"That was the basis for his removal proceedings, and that's not true," Bernal Munoz's attorney, Melissa Corral, said in an interview.

In recent months, immigration officials have quietly detained or even tried to deport several TPS recipients in Nevada. In June, ICE officials in Reno detained a TPS holder from Haiti a month before the Department of Homeland (DHS) terminated the TPS program for nearly 350,000 Haitians nationwide. A couple months prior, a TPS recipient from Utah was detained at the Nevada Southern Detention Center after he was mistaken for his brother.

President Donald Trump has made slashing TPS a key part of his deportation agenda — eliminating TPS for more than a million people. However, for those still covered by the program, advocates and legal experts say the administration has misconstrued the grounds on which they can deport TPS holders, detaining them while they are awaiting renewals or facing administrative hurdles. Some said it falls into a broader pattern of Trump coming after immigrants who have temporary lawful status, such as Dreamers or certain green card holders.

"They're misinterpreting the law," Francis Garcia, a member of the National TPS Alliance, said in an interview. "What's happening is that the rights of people going through this process aren't being respected."

Ted Pappageorge, the secretary-treasurer of the Culinary Workers Union Local 226, said several union members who are TPS holders have been detained or "harassed" by ICE over the past year. The union counts thousands of El Salvadoran TPS holders among its members and has been an outspoken advocate of extending protections for them as the program's status remains in limbo.

Nevada has a particularly notable population of TPS holders from El Salvador, home to approximately 5,000 recipients. The Trump administration has yet to publicly announce if the program will be extended.

"TPS are workers that have suffered incredible trauma," Pappageorge said. "They've been given legal status to work and be productive and support their families here in the U.S."

What protections does TPS offer?

TPS, which has been in place since 1990, grants immigrants from designated countries lawful immigration status and access to work permits for renewable periods of up to 18 months. The program has widely been considered a lifeline for immigrants who face political persecution or other dangerous conditions, such as natural disasters, in their home countries.

But under the Trump administration, the program has essentially been quashed, with President Donald Trump eliminating the program for 13 of the 17 designated countries. Trump has previously said that the influx of TPS recipients in communities such as Springfield, Ohio, "just doesn't work" and that "we cannot destroy our country."

Michael Kagan, the director of the UNLV Immigration Clinic, said that when detaining people with "provisional statuses," such as TPS holders, ICE agents typically have a policy of "arrest first, ask questions later."

Kagan said that he's heard of a handful of cases in Nevada where TPS holders have been detained and that he is not seeing the "protection being respected." He said past administrations have not come after people who are renewing their TPS status and "penalize them for the slow processing."

"People end up in a window where they have sort of done everything correctly, but the government hasn't acted on their application, so ICE treats them like they can be deported," he said.

At the same time, the ability for courts to hear TPS related matters has been curtailed. In June, the Supreme Court ruled that courts had no jurisdiction to consider challenges that claimed DHS had broken the law in granting, renewing or terminating TPS, granting an exception for lawsuits brought on constitutional grounds.

Corral, the lawyer in Bernal Munoz's case, urged people with lawful immigrant status to resolve any pending legal issues, including something as small as a traffic violation.

"Anything little that you think somehow you might end up in local jail, take care of it," Corral said. "If you end up putting a foot in that jail, ICE will be alerted."

text:
The justices’ decision will determine whether tens of thousands of immigrants currently in federal detention can seek release on bond.

“The question of mandatory detention thus boils down to one question: Can we lock up noncitizens without giving them a day in court first?” said Jenifer Bizzotto, the Wisconsin attorney representing Jaciel Cirrus Rojas, the man at the center of the case. “The stakes could hardly be higher.”

Arrested as ‘collateral’

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents turned up at then-24-year-old Cirrus Rojas’ apartment in June 2025 in search of a prior tenant. They instead arrested Cirrus Rojas, who entered the U.S. in 2018 without a visa, as “collateral.” Wisconsin court records show no criminal convictions under his name.

He spent most of the next nine months in custody at the Dodge County Detention Center in Juneau, entangled in a new White House policy barring ICE detainees from posting bond — a departure from decades of precedent.

The 1996 Immigration Reform Act requires immigration authorities to detain — without bond — anyone found crossing the U.S. border without authorization. Prior administrations applied that rule narrowly, allowing many immigrants arrested in the country’s interior to seek a bond hearing in immigration court.

The Trump administration bucked that approach in July 2025, when ICE Director Todd Lyons issued a new legal interpretation requiring detention without bond regardless of where immigrants are arrested.

The Board of Immigration Appeals, a panel of judges who set the rules for the federal immigration court system, later signed off on the interpretation.

With bond off the table, tens of thousands of immigrants in ICE custody turned to a backup option: filing habeas corpus petitions in federal district courts to challenge their detention.

Unlike immigration courts, which are part of the U.S. Department of Justice, federal district courts belong to the judicial branch and, therefore, are technically independent of the White House. When a federal district court grants a habeas petition, it generally orders an immigration court judge to hold a bond hearing.

Wisconsin’s Western and Eastern District courts have received more than 100 habeas petitions over the past year.

A federal appeals court split

The 7th Circuit ruled 2-1 in Cirrus Rojas’ favor in July, joining appellate courts based in New York, Cincinnati, Denver, Atlanta and San Francisco in rejecting the policy.“If Congress had indeed demanded — but not funded — no-bond detention for all unlawful entrants, that may well have thrown the nation’s immigration system into chaos,” Judge Joshua Kolar, whom Joe Biden appointed to the court, wrote in the court’s majority opinion. “Immigration authorities might have found themselves quickly overwhelmed by a colossal unfunded mandate to arrest and detain millions.” Judge Diane Sykes, a George W. Bush appointee, dissented alone.

“At this point, only the Supreme Court can bring uniformity and settle this question once and for all,” she wrote. “I anticipate that it will do so soon.”

Cirrus Rojas left custody earlier this year after a federal district court judge in California vacated the mandatory detention rule. The San Francisco-based 9th Circuit Court of Appeals stayed that decision less than a month later.

The 7th Circuit allowed his case to move forward because federal authorities plan to re-detain him.

Supreme Court could have final say

“Nothing, absent our intervention, stops the government from making good on its promise,” Kolar wrote.The U.S. Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, is now asking the Supreme Court to step in.

The court agreed to take up another mandatory detention dispute earlier this month. That case involves a Brazilian national arrested during a traffic stop in Massachusetts last September.

DHS asked the justices to hold Cirrus Rojas’ case until they decide the Massachusetts case.

In Bizzotto’s view, both cases “offer the Supreme Court the opportunity to affirm that the Constitution means what it says.”

A ruling against the mandatory detention policy would open the door for thousands of ICE detainees — at least those within circuits that side with the Trump administration — to request bond hearings in immigration court. It would not require immigration court judges to grant their bond requests.

The Supreme Court also quietly declined this week to revive a Biden-era policy that allowed immigration court judges to pause deportation proceedings for immigrants seeking humanitarian visas or other forms of legal status.
