text:
Donald Trump’s administration is imminently expected to forcibly remove dozens of Afghans from the U.S. to Afghanistan, marking the first large-scale deportation flight of Afghans back into the hands of the Taliban, aid groups and human rights lawyers warn.

Roughly 150 Afghans are reportedly scheduled for the removal flight, which is being routed from Louisiana to Pakistan, where officials are expected to expel them to their home country.

Afghans on the flight include family members of U.S. allies who worked alongside military forces and aid groups, among others who could face discrimination and violence upon their return — including at least one LGBTQ+ person.

By sending the flight to Pakistan, the Trump administration has found a legally dubious workaround to send vulnerable immigrants to the country they fled, according to attorneys and refugee aid groups.

“By creating arrangements with countries such as Kuwait, Qatar, and now Pakistan, the Trump administration is effectuating removals to active war zones and severe security crises where individuals may be at grave risk,” according to former U.S. diplomat Uzra Zeya, president of Human Rights First.

The administration also is reportedly preparing another deportation flight forcing Iranian immigrants back to Iran, marking the first such removal flight since the onset of the U.S. war in February.

“The administration’s cruel mass deportation agenda has swept up family members of Afghan allies and Iranian political dissidents” who face “grave” consequences in their home countries, Zeya said.

In Afghanistan, returning dissidents are at risk of imprisonment, corporal punishment or execution, according to Shawn VanDiver, president of AfghanEvac, which helps resettle refugees including wartime allies.

“The Taliban is a regime that jails, tortures and kills the people it considers its enemies,” VanDiver said Friday.

“It has hunted down former soldiers, police officers, and the families of anyone who worked with the United States. It has erased women and girls from public life. Sending someone there is not a deportation. It is a sentence,” he said.

“Whatever path brought them here, the danger waiting for them is the same.”

The Trump administration has not publicly announced plans for the removal flight; unnamed officials speaking to media outlets, court filings, and statements from lawyers and advocacy organizations who fear for their imprisoned clients have outlined tentative plans to send Afghans out of the country.

Publicly available court filings in the case of at least one Afghan detainee indicate that a flight is expected to leave Louisiana within the first week of November.

In a statement to The Independent, a spokesperson for Homeland Security said that Immigration and Customs Enforcement “does not comment on prospective removal operations, including flight schedules, passenger manifests, destinations, or individual case details.”

“For operational security reasons and the safety of our officers, we would not confirm future removal operations,” the person said.

A State Department spokesperson told The Independent the administration does not have any plans to announce.

“We reaffirm our position that all countries must be able to manage their borders and immigration processes in a manner that ensures the safety, security, and prosperity of their citizens,” the person added.

Last year, the Trump administration pointed to an increase in tourism under Taliban-controlled Afghanistan to justify the cancellation of humanitarian protections for more than 11,000 Afghans in the U.S.

The administration announced plans to strip Temporary Protected Status from Afghanistan following the U.S. withdrawal in 2021, which led to the evacuation of tens of thousands of people in the wake of the devastating years-long war.

“We’ve reviewed the conditions in Afghanistan with our interagency partners, and they do not meet the requirements for a TPS designation,” then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said in a statement at the time. “Afghanistan has had an improved security situation, and its stabilizing economy no longer prevent [sic] them from returning to their home country.”

Homeland Security’s notice claims there have been “notable improvements” in Afghanistan’s national security and “requiring the return of Afghan nationals to Afghanistan does not pose a threat to their personal safety due to armed conflict or extraordinary and temporary conditions.”

The notice also claims that “the Taliban government is promoting tourism to shift its global image.”

“Tourism to Afghanistan has increased, as the rates of kidnappings have reduced,” the notice added. “Tourists are sharing their experiences on social media, highlighting the peaceful countryside, welcoming locals, and the cultural heritage, according to some reports.”

Pakistan, meanwhile, has launched its own mass deportation effort targeting Afghan refugees. More than 2.7 million Afghans have been expelled from the country since 2023.

The relationship between the two countries has continued to deteriorate following the withdrawal of U.S.-led foreign forces in 2021. Deadly border clashes and escalating attacks have resulted in closure crossings and growing fears of civilian casualties, while Islamabad has urged Kabul to dismantle militant groups including Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan accused of serving as proxies to launch attacks from inside the country.

“Pakistan is patently unsafe for Afghans. Its own government has made that clear by hounding them out of the country by the millions,” said Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president of Global Refuge.

“Deporting Afghans into that crackdown is a deliberate decision to put them in harm’s way,” she added.

text: Federal Judge Brendan Hurson in Greenbelt, Maryland, issued a temporary restraining order halting new policies adopted by the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump. According to human rights organizations, these policies aim to accelerate the deportation process for unaccompanied migrant children who have arrived in the country seeking asylum. The court's decision came in response to a lawsuit filed by legal and human rights organizations, including the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights and The Door. The plaintiffs argued that the amendments introduced by the U.S. administration are illegal and exceed the protections guaranteed by law to safeguard migrant children and ensure they receive a fair trial. The temporary restraining order prevents U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) from continuing to shorten the notice period children receive before their asylum interview dates. The decision also limits the authorities' ability to impose strict restrictions that prevent the rescheduling of these interviews, which are critical to the children's legal future. Judge Hurson ordered the U.S. administration to immediately return to the previous policies that governed this procedural process. This decision is set to remain in effect until mid-November, pending a deeper judicial review to consider the possibility of issuing a permanent injunction against these measures. The lawsuit, filed about two weeks ago, described the Republican administration's approach as a cruel scheme aimed at expediting the deportation of minors. Legal sources confirmed that the new policies make it nearly impossible for organizations to defend thousands of children in need of legal assistance. The legal actions targeted two specific policies adopted by USCIS in August and September. The first policy included the removal of a prior notice requirement that previously granted children and their guardians a 21-day window before the official asylum interview date. Under the suspended amendments, U.S. authorities began notifying unaccompanied children of their interview dates very shortly before they were scheduled to take place. Sources reported that some children were notified less than 24 hours in advance, depriving them of the opportunity for adequate legal preparation with their attorneys. The second policy covered by the suspension order relates to tightening the conditions for rescheduling interviews that children miss. USCIS required the existence of extraordinary, compelling circumstances to approve an interview postponement, a standard that legal experts described as much stricter and more complex than what was previously followed. In his ruling, Judge Hurson explained that the short notices implemented by the agency directly conflict with existing federal laws. He specifically pointed to the William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008, which mandates consideration of the special needs of this category of immigrants. The judicial ruling emphasized that U.S. law imposes a moral and legal obligation to consider the special needs of asylum-seeking children. The judge affirmed that this care must include all procedures preceding official interviews, not just during the hearings themselves, to ensure fairness. Through this legal move, human rights organizations seek to protect the rights of thousands of children fleeing difficult conditions in their home countries. Human rights defenders argue that accelerating deportation without legal safeguards puts these children's lives at risk and violates U.S. international obligations. This judicial confrontation is a new chapter in the series of legal disputes between the Trump administration and human rights organizations over immigration. The current administration is attempting to tighten border restrictions and reduce the number of asylum seekers, while organizations insist on the necessity of adhering to humanitarian and legal standards. It is expected that the coming weeks will see additional arguments before the federal court to determine the final fate of these policies. The government will have to provide strong legal justifications proving that its actions do not infringe upon the rights of migrant children guaranteed by the Constitution and laws protecting minors. If these policies remain suspended, it will give legal organizations more time to arrange the children's legal status and properly file asylum applications. Observers confirm that this ruling represents a temporary victory for immigrant rights advocates amidst the ongoing political tensions surrounding the border issue.

An ICE officer has been indicted after prosecutors say he struck a Houston man with an SUV during an immigration pursuit. Newly released video appears to show the officer turning his SUV toward the man as he runs away, knocking him to the ground and driving over his legs.

Mario Alberto Morales was indicted Friday on a second-degree aggravated assault charge with a deadly weapon in connection with the Oct. 10 collision that seriously injured 48-year-old Miguel Parra Hernandez in northwest Houston.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

During a Friday news conference, District Attorney Sean Teare played Morales' body-camera footage alongside surveillance video from the incident. The footage appeared to show Morales turning his SUV toward Parra Hernandez before striking him as he ran away. Parra Hernandez can be heard screaming in pain after the collision.

"Not only did he hit Mr. Parra-Hernandez, but he ran over both of his legs, leaving him seriously injured and hospitalized to this day," Teare said. "Then he called 911 and said Mr. Hernandez hit his car."

In the body-camera video, Morales gets out of the SUV and approaches Parra Hernandez, who is on the ground clutching his leg and yelling in pain. Morales asks where the other man is before Parra Hernandez tells him, "You ran over me." He later cries, "My foot."

WARNING: Graphic video. Discretion is advised as the footage depicts a vehicle striking a pedestrian and severe injuries.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Morales is then heard telling another officer, "He got hit with a car, bro," before adding, "I was coming in and I hit him with the car."

Teare said Parra Hernandez had lived in Harris County for about 30 years and had no criminal history or immigration proceedings.

In the 911 call released by prosecutors, Morales can be heard describing the pursuit to a dispatcher.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

"So we're following this guy, trying to pull him over. He jumped out of the vehicle. I tried to get around him, and he hit my car," Morales said.

The dispatcher later asked whether Parra Hernandez had obvious injuries or serious bleeding. Morales responded, "No," while Parra Hernandez's screams could be heard in the background.

But Parra Hernandez wasn't the man ICE said it was pursuing that morning.

In its initial statement to Chron, ICE identified Jose Mendoza-Cervantes as the intended target and said Parra Hernandez "ran in front of an ICE vehicle" before he was hit. ICE also described Mendoza-Cervantes as a man with previous arrests, convictions and deportations.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

There's just one massive problem with that account.

"Mr. Mendoza-Cervantes has apparently been dead for nine years," Teare said Friday.

FIEL Houston previously reported the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes was actually Jose Hector Jimenez, who died in 2017 near the Texas-Mexico border. The DA's office said its investigation also found no evidence that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were together in a vehicle, as ICE had claimed.

ICE has not responded to requests for comment about the discrepancy.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

"An ICE badge does not give you free reign to injure, kill or violate the constitutional rights of anyone," Teare said. "I hope it also sends a loud and clear message to every ICE officer who feels they have a free pass to terrorize our streets. The time to stop is now. And if you don't, you will be held accountable."

Sheriff Ed Gonzalez, whose office investigated the collision alongside the DA's office, said the case should be viewed separately from the broader debate over federal immigration enforcement.

Morales is now charged with a second-degree felony for aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, for which he could face two to 20 years in prison.

His attorney, per the Houston Chronicle, has called the indictment a "political prosecution" and defended his actions during the pursuit. title: New blood to rein in Trump | U.S. - EL PAÍS English
description:
But a closer look at the campaign messages of Democratic candidates across the country shows that they have found common ground, regardless of where they place themselves on the ideological spectrum.
Despite the favorable outlook for Democratic candidates, nothing is certain until the votes are counted.
And Trump, who has overcome some of the steepest odds in U.S. politics over the past decade, knows that better than anyone.
With Trump in the White House, Democrats will not be able to govern from Congress: most of their initiatives would die on the president’s desk.
It would serve little purpose for democratic socialists to push for another impeachment of Trump while pragmatists prefer to focus on more urgent problems.
text:
James Talarico in Texas, Jon Ossoff in Georgia, Abdul El‑Sayed and Donavan McKinney in Michigan, Darializa Ávila Chevalier in New York, Manny Rutinel in Colorado, JoAnna “Jo” Mendoza in Arizona. These are not only some of the most talked‑about names in the race for Congress; they also share one characteristic: they are all under 45. Not all of them may win on the night of November 3, but they each represent the long‑awaited generational renewal of the Democratic Party.

In the Senate races, their Republican opponents belong to an earlier generation. Their names are Ken Paxton (63), Mike Collins (59), Mike Rogers (63): familiar faces, worn by years in politics. Some, like Paxton, Texas attorney general since 2015, entered the campaign after surviving an impeachment over influence peddling and abuse of power.

Paxton is also an example of how the lines separating Democratic and Republican candidates are not only generational or ideological, but ethical as well. But the generational element is key. At the start of the current Congress, the average age was 57.9 in the House of Representatives and 63.9 in the Senate.

That is why candidates such as Talarico, 37, Ávila Chevalier, 32, and Rutinel, 31, signal that, after years of complaints about a gerontocratic leadership embodied by Nancy Pelosi, Joe Biden, Bernie Sanders and Chuck Schumer, a new generation has finally emerged. There are young Republicans in the House too, such as Gabe Evans, 40, Rutinel’s opponent in Colorado. But the MAGA succession does not respond to people’s needs; it responds to an ideology.

With just days to go before the midterms, it seems almost certain that Democrats will regain the House of Representatives. Yet this is not the moment to settle scores with the old guard. What matters most is that this new crop of politicians works with the different factions of the party in a new Congress capable of placing limits on the Trump era.

Easier said than done. For a start, Democrats will have to mend their internal divisions. In particular, the divide separating the progressives, led by Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and, further to the left, democratic socialists such as Zohran Mamdani, from the pragmatic center represented by Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries.

Progressives and democratic socialists rightly argue that the pragmatists became complacent with their territorial strongholds, adopting an accommodating stance toward corporate power, turning their backs on the working class and failing to offer an economic vision capable of attracting and mobilizing younger voters. They advocate healthcare for all, free education, less brutal immigration policies and higher taxes on corporations and the super-rich. It is an agenda that stands in stark contrast to that of Trump, the MAGA movement and the plutocratic and Big Tech interests that now swarm around the White House.

But a closer look at the campaign messages of Democratic candidates across the country shows that they have found common ground, regardless of where they place themselves on the ideological spectrum. Their central message — that the cost of living has become unaffordable — resonates across the electorate.

Zohran Mamdani struck a chord when he made the issue the centerpiece of his 2025 campaign, and the party has since embraced it, pairing it with the defense of healthcare and rights such as abortion and civil liberties, calls for less dehumanizing and abusive immigration policies, and denunciations of the rampant corruption within the Trump administration.

The Bernie effect

It is ironic that Bernie Sanders, an octogenarian independent, has been the architect of the Democratic comeback. The Vermont senator was farsighted enough to look beyond his own ambitions: he set aside his presidential aspirations and helped clear the way for a new generation.

Just as Mamdani provided a political framework for addressing the affordability crisis in housing and public services in New York, the other candidates owe an intellectual and ethical debt to Sanders and the progressives for spending more than a decade tirelessly denouncing the grip of big corporate money on the political system and the corruption that comes with it, while demanding that the wealthiest Americans pay their fair share in taxes.

That is not to deny the role played by Schumer and Jeffries in building a broad political center.

Whether they acknowledge it or not, the Bernie factor has been a positive influence on this generation of Democrats, helping define the boundaries between what is politically defensible and what is morally reprehensible. Among the latter is the concentration of wealth and corporate power as a driver of extreme inequality in the United States, a reality best captured by the numbers: today, the wealthiest 1% of Americans hold roughly one-third of household net wealth, nearly the same share as the bottom 90% combined.

What to do with the gains?

Polls have consistently shown Democrats holding a lead of between eight and 12 percentage points over Republicans in the race for the House of Representatives, despite the fact that a sizable share of voters view both parties unfavorably. Senate contests, by contrast, remain much tighter, and the outcome is still far from certain.

The latest national Latino voter survey by Equis, published on October 13, found Democrats enjoying their largest advantage of the cycle: 26 points. In competitive districts, Democratic support has already surpassed 2022 levels, while Trump’s approval rating among Latinos has fallen to 30%. Latinos place greater trust in Democrats on the economy, the cost of living, healthcare and immigration. Even on border security, long considered a Republican stronghold, the two parties are now running neck and neck.

Among the Democrats seeking seats in Congress this year are Latinos with very different political profiles: Ávila Chevalier, the democratic socialist who defeated the chairman of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus in the primary; Rutinel, an economist and lawyer; Mendoza, a former Marine drill instructor backed by the Blue Dogs, the party’s centrist faction; and the singer Bobby Pulido, who rejects partisan labels and describes himself as a conservative, a man of faith, a supporter of gun ownership and an advocate of a secure border.

They all, however, share the same concern about their voters’ economic hardships and access to health services and insurance. They also oppose the impact that ICE raids have had on Latino communities.

Despite the favorable outlook for Democratic candidates, nothing is certain until the votes are counted. And Trump, who has overcome some of the steepest odds in U.S. politics over the past decade, knows that better than anyone.

The president heads into the election with the worst numbers of his political career. He is being dogged by stubborn inflation and a war with Iran that has driven up fuel and energy prices, while corruption scandals continue to swirl around his administration. With an approval rating barely above 30%, he is, quite simply, an unpopular president.

Yet, as his campaign sprint of recent weeks has shown, Trump is willing to go to the ends of the earth and spend a large share of the Republican war chest. On the campaign trail, he labels Democrats communists, terrorists, extremists and jihadists. He invokes familiar ghosts from U.S. history because it is a tactic that has worked for him before. By now, however, the trick may be wearing thin.

Not even the more than $350 million that Elon Musk has poured into this election cycle to support Republicans may be enough to reverse the trend in Democrats’ favor. Even so, Trump is still capable of springing surprises, as he did on January 6, 2021. Polling has been spectacularly wrong before. Still, it is hard not to believe that Democrats will make net gains compared with the past two elections.

A critical question is what to do with that political capital and how to manage it so that it does not dissipate, as so often happens after legislative victories. With Trump in the White House, Democrats will not be able to govern from Congress: most of their initiatives would die on the president’s desk. But they can set the agenda and force him to bear the political cost of every veto.

Their first 100 days should focus on the issues voters care about most. First, legislation to protect health insurance programs such as Obamacare and Medicaid, allow public negotiation of prescription drug prices, and subsidize childcare and elder care. Second, tackling the cost-of-living crisis, beginning with housing, through a major affordable-housing construction program and incentives to bring down rents. Third, pressing for an end to the war with Iran and to Russia’s war in Ukraine, both to stabilize and reduce global energy prices and, above all, in the interest of peace itself.

Finally, they should move to rein in the indiscriminate targeting of immigrants. ICE’s funding is secured through 2029, but Congress still retains the power to investigate through hearings, subpoenas and public scrutiny of every abuse. All of this should be done with a clear assignment of responsibility: who drove up costs, and who sought to bring them down.

One more thing: a Democratic victory would be the product of a virtuous convergence among the party’s different factions, and it would require maintaining negotiations between them. It would serve little purpose for democratic socialists to push for another impeachment of Trump while pragmatists prefer to focus on more urgent problems.

Nor should Democrats forget that, if the party retakes Congress, even if only the House of Representatives, it will owe much to the momentum generated by a new generation. Space must be made for that generation to replace the old guard.

If Democrats can convince middle- and working-class Americans that they are on their side, through actions rather than campaign promises alone, they will have cleared half the path back to the White House. The other half will depend on the quality of their candidate.

text:
For immediate release

October 30, 2026 | 3:00 p.m. EDT

Contact: Omer Kanat, +1 (202) 790-1795

The Uyghur Human Rights Project (UHRP) urgently calls upon the Thai government to halt any plans to deport the two Uyghur men currently held in immigration detention who reportedly face imminent return to China, where the men face grave risk of torture, enforced disappearance, and other severe human rights violations. UHRP also urges governments worldwide to press the Thai government to prevent further deportations and calls on third countries to offer resettlement to all five Uyghurs who remain in detention in Thailand.

The reports come less than two years after Thailand forcibly returned 40 Uyghur men to China in February 2025, despite widespread international condemnation and warnings that they faced severe human rights violations. The fate and whereabouts of those 40 men remain unknown, with no independently verified proof of life. Thailand previously deported another 109 Uyghurs to China in 2015.

“Thailand must not repeat its devastating mistakes of the past by sending these men back into the hands of the Chinese government,” said UHRP Executive Director Omer Kanat. “We have already seen what happens when Uyghurs are forcibly returned to China. The Thai government must uphold its international human rights obligations.”

The five men are among approximately 300 Uyghurs who fled persecution in East Turkistan and were detained by Thai authorities in 2014. They have since endured more than a decade of arbitrary detention in inhumane and degrading conditions, with inadequate access to medical care. Five Uyghurs, including young children, have died in Thai custody.

Any further deportations would once again violate the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning individuals to countries where they face a serious risk of torture, persecution, or other grave human rights violations. Thailand has an obligation under international law to uphold this fundamental principle, further reinforced by its status as a State Party to both the Convention against Torture (CAT) and the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance (ICPPED).

UHRP calls on the Thai government to immediately halt any deportations, release the five remaining Uyghur detainees, and facilitate their safe resettlement in third countries. UHRP further urges other governments to use all available diplomatic channels to prevent further deportations and offer concrete pathways to resettlement.

text:
Video shows an ICE agent pointing a gun at a bystander during an apparent immigration arrest in North Hollywood on Friday morning.

Witnesses say immigration agents stopped a man while he was on a sidewalk on Ostego Street and that when a passerby had words with the agents, the situation escalated and a gun was seen pointed at that man.

Cellphone video shared with NBC Los Angeles shows a man on the ground shouting for help, surrounded by ICE agents — their clothing marked as such.

"This morning, I was out on my balcony, and I heard a bang," witness Damari Butler said. "And when I looked over, I saw a guy walking down the street, and then I saw two ICE agents come and tackle him into the bushes."

Butler took the video from his fifth-floor balcony around 8:20 a.m.

"They grabbed him," Butler said. "They didn't ask him for ID. They didn't ask him for his name. They didn't say anything to him."

Rocio Gutierrez was among other neighbors who came out when they said they heard the commotion on their usually quiet street.

"They started tackling him," Gutierrez said. "The guy tried to get away, and that's where it began. They just started arresting him, holding him down the floor. The guy went into panic mode. He was yelling for help. He looked scared."

Both witnesses describe another man who was walking his dogs at the time agents arrived.

"The guy with the dog, he actually, when he stepped in, another ICE agent actually came out with a gun and put it directly to his face while he was in the bushes," Butler said.

Gutierrez said that man yelled at the agents, asking what they were doing.

The video taken by Butler also shows moments after what happened in the bushes. The man with the dogs is seen going into the street. He picks up an unknown item from the ground, and that's when one of the agents runs toward him and takes out what looks like a pepper spray canister toward the man, who runs away.

A couple minutes later, the man who had been the focus of the agents was put in one of their cars.

It's unclear where he was taken, as well as what preceded or followed the moments captured by Butler on his cellphone.

"It's a very concerning thing, though, and especially to see people coming with masks on," Butler said, later adding, "That could have been my son. My son walks out in the mornings, and it's just worrisome. It's horrible what's happening right now.

NBCLA reached out to the Department of Homeland Security about what happened and did not receive an immediate response.

The neighbors say they do not know the man who was taken by the agents.

In a statement, LA Mayor Karen Bass called Friday's incident "unacceptable" and said it would "not be tolerated" in the city.

“I’m engaging the Attorney General’s Office to investigate and prosecute any wrongdoing by these federal agents," the statement read, in part. "Additionally, I referred this matter to the Office of U.S. Representative Robert Garcia, the ranking Democrat leading oversight on federal immigration enforcement abuses."

California Gov. Gavin Newsom's office also responded, referring to the incident as "absolutely disgusting and telling constituents to report potential misconduct by federal agents on the Office of the Attorney General of California's website.

"This kind of violence has no place in our communities," an X post from the governor's office read in part. "Trump’s secret police are completely out of control. There must be oversight, investigations, and accountability for this pattern of behavior.

"Stephen Miller should be fired. Tom Homan should be fired."

Last year, California became the first state to ban most law enforcement officers, including federal immigration agents, from covering their faces while conducting official business. A federal judge blocked the law from going into effect, only requiring that they clearly identify themselves, their agency and badge number.

text:
A federal judge has ordered the Department of Justice (DOJ) to turn over its list of approximately 20,000 suspected noncitizen voters in California to immigration advocacy groups by 5 p.m. Friday.

Chief Judge James “Jeb” Boasberg ordered the DOJ to provide the list to attorneys representing the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights of Los Angeles (CHIRLA) and a California voter during a hearing Friday.

The order comes as a federal appeals court Friday rejected the DOJ's demand that California election officials hold back the midterm ballots from 20,000 people over claims they were likely noncitizens.

Read More on News

The legal challenges are part of a broader confrontation between the Trump administration and California officials over federal authority to investigate voter registration records and potential noncitizen voting.

Newsweek has reached out to the DOJ and CHIRLA for comment.

Judge Questions DOJ Over Plans for More Voter Lists

During Friday's hearing, Chad Dunn, legal director of the UCLA Voting Rights Project, who represents the plaintiffs, argued that the government's voter investigations were creating uncertainty among California residents.

"If you're a voter in California you have to wonder if you're on this list; will you ever be on this list?" Dunn said.

He told the court that CHIRLA had received calls from concerned individuals who were worried about their inclusion on the government's list.

Some callers, he said, were asking how they could determine whether their names appeared on it, while others expressed concerns about voting.

"It absolutely has a suppressive effect," Dunn told the court.

The administration said that U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services had compared voter registration information with federal immigration records to identify potential matches. The government, in its complaint, said it used multiple identifiers to establish what it described as high-confidence matches, with additional searches intended to determine whether individuals had subsequently become naturalized citizens or obtained citizenship through their parents.

Boasberg ordered the government to provide the list by Friday evening, giving the plaintiffs an opportunity to examine whether their members or clients had been identified. However, the judge placed restrictions on how the information could be used. Under the order, the plaintiffs cannot distribute the list beyond their legal team. They are permitted, however, to make public statements and draw conclusions about whether individuals they represent appear on the government's list.

Boasberg also questioned the DOJ's refusal to commit to not sending additional lists of suspected noncitizen voters to election officials. At one point, Boasberg pressed government attorneys to provide an assurance that no further lists would be distributed.

"You could all sit down and have a nice weekend if you say you won't send lists," Boasberg told DOJ attorney Ty Trejo.

Trejo declined to make that commitment, maintaining that the federal government had authority to enforce voting laws if public officials failed to act. He said he believed no additional lists would be created but that the government reserved the right to update existing lists.

A DOJ spokesperson previously told Newsweek that approximately 20,000 individuals had been manually verified to date, adding that the number could increase.

Previous Judge Rejected DOJ Bid to Set Aside Ballots

Boasberg's order follows a separate ruling Wednesday by U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who rejected the DOJ's request to require California election officials to segregate approximately 20,000 ballots allegedly cast by noncitizens.

The federal government had sought a temporary restraining order against California and Los Angeles County election officials while its lawsuit proceeded.

Carter rejected the request, warning that the government's proposed intervention could disrupt an election already underway.

"If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," Carter wrote.

He also warned that separating ballots based on unproven allegations could cause lasting harm to voters and election officials.

The judge questioned whether the federal government had demonstrated sufficient legal grounds to compel California to change its ballot-counting procedures. Carter also raised concerns about the reliability of the government's evidence, including potential inaccuracies in databases used to identify individuals believed to be noncitizens.

The ruling allowed California election officials to continue counting ballots under existing state procedures while the underlying litigation continues.

The administration had appealed the decision, but on Friday an appeals court again rejected the bid. The 9th Circuit ruled 2-1, citing the Constitution's Elections Clause and the National Voter Registration Act.

More Legal Challenges Ahead

The latest dispute is part of a growing number of legal challenges involving the Trump administration's efforts to obtain voter registration information and investigate suspected noncitizen voting.

A September 18 lawsuit challenged the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) home visits to suspected noncitizens as part of the so-called Unlawful Voter Initiative.

The plaintiffs, which include the California Nurses Association, National Nurses United, Santa Clara County, the City and County of San Francisco and Voto Latino Foundation, allege that the DHS compiled lists of suspected noncitizens they distributed to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) field offices. Agents were allegedly then directed to conduct in-person investigations at people's homes.

According to the lawsuit, the database matching process risked incorrectly identifying naturalized U.S. citizens and other eligible voters, potentially exposing them to questioning about their citizenship and voting history.

The plaintiffs argue that the investigations could intimidate eligible voters and violate federal voting protections, including Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act, which prohibits voter intimidation, threats and coercion.

On October 21, a federal judge in the Northern District of California granted the plaintiffs a preliminary injunction restricting DHS from conducting certain election-related operations against individuals it suspects, or should suspect, are U.S. citizens during the active election season. The administration has challenged the injunction, and the litigation remains ongoing.

Meanwhile, the DOJ has escalated its dispute with California by directing federal prosecutors to pursue criminal grand jury subpoenas targeting state and local election officials.

DOJ leadership directed federal prosecutors in California to seek subpoenas concerning officials' handling of voter registration records and the administration's allegations of noncitizen voting. The move came shortly after Carter rejected the administration's request for California election officials to set aside approximately 20,000 ballots.

Subpoenas were subsequently issued to employees of the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder's Office, according to ABC News, which reviewed copies of the documents. Some officials were ordered to appear before a federal grand jury on November 4, the day after the midterm elections.

Prosecutors are seeking internal documents and communications concerning federal requests to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, as well as records detailing how election officials screen for potentially unlawful voting by noncitizens.

At least four California election workers had received federal grand jury subpoenas, according to local reporting, including an Orange County election office that received a subpoena seeking unredacted voter records concerning 60 individuals.

The move prompted criticism from Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan, who said the DOJ had adopted a "confrontational, adversarial approach" toward election officials.

"Threats and intimidation have no place in elections," Logan said in a statement.

The subpoenas followed Carter's warning to federal prosecutors that threats against election officials needed to stop. In his October 28 ruling, the judge wrote: "Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch."

The DOJ has defended its actions, arguing that suspected noncitizen voting is a criminal matter that warrants investigation.

text:
PHOENIX, Ariz. – During the week of enforcement operations from Oct. 24 through Oct. 30, 2026, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Arizona brought immigration-related criminal charges against 336 individuals. Specifically, the United States filed 171 cases in which aliens illegally re-entered the United States, and the United States also charged 143 aliens for illegally entering the United States. In its ongoing effort to deter unlawful immigration, the United States filed 18 cases against 22 individuals responsible for smuggling illegal aliens into and within the District of Arizona.

These cases were referred or supported by federal law enforcement partners, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations (ICE-ERO), ICE- Homeland Security Investigations (ICE-HSI), U.S. Border Patrol, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the FBI, the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS), and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF).

Recent matters of interest include:

United States v. Marquise Deone Isomi, et al. Marquise Deone Isomi and Rayla Storm Hunt Gagliardi were charged by criminal complaint on Oct. 24, with Transportation of an Illegal Alien.

On Oct. 22, a local police officer in Florence, AZ performed a traffic stop on a GMC Sierra pickup truck with a camper shell that was speeding on Highway 79.

The driver, later identified as Isomi, and a passenger, later identified as Gagliardi, were seated in front of the vehicle with two juveniles located in the rear passenger area. The juveniles, who were clothed in camouflage, were not wearing seatbelts and were surrounded by large amounts of clutter. A second officer that arrived at the stop observed the truck rocking back and worth, indicating weight shifting in vehicle’s bed. The officer shined a flashlight into a gap between the truck's body and the camper shell and observed multiple people inside wearing camouflaged clothing and shoe covers. The officers suspected that they had encountered a human smuggling event and contacted Border Patrol.

Border Patrol Agent (BPAs) arrived at the scene and discovered that 11 people were in the truck’s bed, one of whom was a juvenile. BPAs determined that the 11 individuals in the truck’s bed, and the two juveniles inside the cabin, were citizens of either Mexico or Guatemala and illegally present in the United States. Of the three juveniles, two were unaccompanied minors. BPAs further learned that Isomi and Gagliardi used WhatsApp to coordinate with human smuggling coordinators and had trafficked aliens in a similar manner on multiple prior occasions. [Case Number: 26-MJ-3448]

A criminal complaint is a formal accusation of criminal conduct. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

title: In its Final Days, this Congress Can Take Bold Steps for Peace and Dignity
description:

The Trump administration has willfully ignored or distorted Congress’ spending directives with little consequence.

text:
Following the mid-term elections, the 119th Congress is set to return for a final session. Members of Congress should take bold steps to end the war in Iran, stop funding foreign wars, and begin to restore a budget process that centers the needs of working families.

The past two years have seen a further weakening of Congress’ influence, especially regarding federal spending and the use of force at home and abroad. The Trump administration has willfully ignored or distorted Congress’ spending directives with little consequence. This Congress is on track to have passed fewer bills into law than any other session in a half century.

Americans want more from their legislators. According to recent polling, a strong majority of Americans support stronger congressional oversight and checks on executive power. This is especially the case with consequential, costly decisions to launch foreign wars.

As the Congress takes up three pending bills, FCNL urges members of Congress to take bold steps to promote peace and dignity.

Defense Authorization: It should not be business as usual as the United States continues to spend over a $1 billion a day on an unauthorized war in Iran. We urge Congress to use the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) to press for end to the war or at least an explicit prohibition on funds being used to sustain the war without authorization. At the same time, Congress should oppose dangerous provisions in the NDAA that would establish or expand new nuclear and autonomous weapons systems, or that would deepen U.S. military integration with Israel or other foreign countries engaged in human rights abuses. Congress should prevent the diversion of military resources into domestic enforcement, such as immigration and local civilian policing. FCNL has provided Congressional negotiators with recommendations for ensuring defense policies that promote peace and dignity.

Appropriations: As Congress debates and finalizes its FY27 appropriations package, we urge that it rebalance federal spending away from a skyrocketing military budget to programs that foster peace, well-being, and safety at home and abroad. We join faith groups across the country in rejecting the proposed increase in military spending to $1.15 trillion, while urging increased, dedicated funding for peacebuilding and humanitarian assistance in the Middle East, Africa, and beyond. At home, we call for: increased funding for programs to prevent community violence; increased resources for detention oversight measures; report language on strengthening guidance, training, and reporting related to immigration enforcement at sensitive locations; and investments to fulfill the U.S. federal government’s public safety obligations to tribal nations. Finally, we urge Congress to enhance legislative safeguards to ensure that funds are spent as intended. FCNL has outlined specific recommendations for Congressional negotiators working on appropriations bills.

Farm Bill: Congress should advance a bipartisan Farm Bill that strengthens environmental conservation, supports sustainable agriculture, and protects the natural resources upon which rural communities depend. Legislation should maintain robust funding for voluntary conservation programs, including the Environmental Quality Incentives Program (EQIP), Conservation Stewardship Program (CSP), and Regional Conservation Partnership Program (RCPP), which help farmers improve soil health, conserve water, and protect wildlife habitats. Congress should also preserve and expand the Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) to help farmers and rural small businesses invest in renewable energy and energy efficiency, reducing operating costs and strengthening energy security.

In whatever legislative vehicle possible, it is critical that Congress acts before the end of the year to delay a major shift in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits that could cause millions of more Americans to lose access to food assistance. Since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21) passed in July 2025, more than 5 million people have lost these benefits, including 2 million children. Under the current provisions, for the first time in the program’s history, states will soon have to pay a portion of SNAP benefits, based on the state’s error rate. This could cost states hundreds of millions of dollars they do not have and lead to more people losing benefits. A few select states, those with the highest error rates, get an additional two years before they must pay part of SNAP benefit costs.

Along with a coalition of faith-based partners and others, FCNL is urging Congress to act before the end of the year to delay the SNAP benefit cost shift onto all states and give states additional time to responsibly get their error rates down without dropping eligible people from the program. The timing is urgent because state legislatures will soon be deciding their budgets. Amid an affordability crisis, now is not the time to cut people’s food assistance.

text:
Federal

Deportations Climb to Nearly 980,000 Under the Second Trump Administration

The Trump administration carried out an estimated 980,000 deportations during the first 18 months of President Donald Trump’s second term, according to a new Migration Policy Institute analysis by former Department of Homeland Security (DHS) official Marc Rosenblum. The analysis projects approximately 660,000 deportations for fiscal year 2026, a 26 percent increase from the annual average under the Biden administration. Those numbers, however, still fall short of the administration’s goal of 1 million deportations per year, which it said additional funding from Congress would allow it to achieve. More than two-thirds of the 980,000 deportations involved people initially encountered at the border, although deportations following arrests within the United States have steadily increased. The total also includes about 170,000 voluntary departures, with advocates saying some people abandoned their immigration cases to avoid remaining in detention. The findings come as DHS has largely stopped releasing detailed enforcement data, making the administration’s deportation claims difficult to independently verify.

The analysis found that only 20 percent of those deported had a criminal conviction. Among those deported who had lived in the United States for at least two years, 71 percent had never been convicted of a crime, despite the administration’s stated focus on people with serious criminal histories. Recent cases illustrate the broader reach of its enforcement efforts. Luis Arreguin, a father of four who had lived near Fresno since he was five, was detained on his way to work and deported to Mexico within 16 days. ICE said Arreguin had a criminal history and had previously been deported, although he reported no recent interactions with law enforcement, and a public records search found no recent criminal history. Moussa Diawara, a Texas father with no criminal record, was deported to Ghana and days later sent to Mali after local officials forced him onto a flight, despite a U.S. immigration judge’s previous ruling that he would likely face persecution there. Of the 63 people aboard Diawara’s deportation flight to Ghana, 62 percent had no criminal record, 19 percent had traffic violations, and 19 percent had been charged with or convicted of other offenses.

U.S. Plans to Deport Afghans to Pakistan, Raising Fears of Return to Taliban Rule

The Trump administration is preparing to deport Afghans to Pakistan, including relatives of people who worked with U.S. military forces before the fall of Kabul, according to reports from attorneys, advocacy organizations and a federal official familiar with the plans. Afghans in immigration detention have received notice from immigration officers that they could be placed on a flight expected to depart in the coming weeks. The flight has not been publicly announced. AfghanEvac, an organization supporting Afghan allies, said family members of former U.S. military partners were among those notified. Human Rights First warned on October 29 that the planned operation could involve hundreds of Afghans and result in their forced return to Afghanistan through Pakistan.

The proposed transfers raise concerns that Pakistan could send deportees onward to Afghanistan, where people associated with U.S. forces and aid organizations face risks of retaliation under Taliban rule. Pakistan is already forcibly returning large numbers of displaced Afghans, and Human Rights First explained that routing removals through another country would not eliminate the danger of persecution or torture. The organization cited arbitrary detention, executions and retaliatory violence in Afghanistan, alongside severe restrictions on women’s and girls’ access to education, employment and public life. It called for the flights to be stopped and for congressional oversight, warning that the operation could become the first large-scale U.S. deportation flight returning Afghans to Taliban-controlled Afghanistan.

Legal

Justices Decline to Restore Biden-Era Rule Allowing Deportation Case Suspensions

The Supreme Court declined on October 27 to restore a Biden-era regulation allowing immigration judges to temporarily suspend certain deportation proceedings, leaving in place a judgment obtained through an agreement between Texas and the Department of Justice (DOJ). The brief, unsigned order offered no explanation and noted no dissents. The 2024 regulation authorized “administrative closure,” a tool allowing judges to pause cases while individuals pursue immigration relief through U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), including certain crime victims seeking visas and people eligible for permanent residence through a U.S. citizen spouse. Baltimore, New Haven, Connecticut, Columbus, Ohio, and the legal services organization Centro Legal de la Raza had asked the justices to restore the rule while they appealed a lower court’s refusal to let them intervene to defend it. The Supreme Court’s order leaves the restrictions in effect but does not resolve the underlying legal dispute.

The case began June 22, when Texas challenged the regulation, arguing that immigration judges lacked authority to suspend proceedings rather than decide whether a person should be removed. Within hours, DOJ agreed with Texas and asked a federal district judge to invalidate the rule and prohibit a similar regulation in the future. The cities and Centro Legal argue that the agreement allowed the administration to eliminate a regulation without following the usual administrative process for changing agency rules. They also warn that limiting administrative closure could lead to the deportation of residents with pending applications for lawful status and discourage crime victims from cooperating with local law enforcement. The district judge denied their request to intervene for lack of standing, and the Fifth Circuit declined to pause the judgment while their appeal proceeds.

Fifth Circuit Upholds Trump Administration’s Mandatory Detention Policy as Constitutional

On October 23, the full U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruled that the Trump administration’s policy of detaining people who entered the country unlawfully without access to bond hearings does not violate due process, even when they have lived in the United States for years. The 10-7 decision reversed a three-judge panel’s ruling that the policy was unconstitutional as applied to three men who had each lived in the country for more than a decade. Writing for the majority, Judge Cory Wilson, a Trump appointee, said that because the men had never been lawfully admitted, the Constitution did not entitle them to additional proceedings beyond those Congress provided before detention pending removal. The ruling applies in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi.

The decision closes an avenue for challenging detention that had remained available after the Fifth Circuit upheld the policy’s statutory basis in February. Despite that earlier ruling, federal district judges in Texas had ordered bond hearings or release for more than 2,000 detainees on constitutional grounds. The administration’s policy treats people who entered without lawful admission as “applicants for admission” subject to mandatory detention, regardless of how long they have lived in the country, departing from decades of practice generally allowing those arrested in the interior to request bond hearings. Nine of the 11 federal appeals courts to address the policy have rejected the administration’s interpretation of immigration law. Earlier in October, the Supreme Court agreed to review whether the policy complies with the Immigration and Nationality Act, a statutory question distinct from the constitutional challenge the Fifth Circuit rejected.

State and Local

Rapid Expansion of 287(g) Agreements Strains Communities

More than 1,850 state and local law enforcement agencies had joined Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) 287(g) Task Force Model as of October 1, according to an October 28 analysis. The model, revived by the Trump administration in 2025, allows deputized officers to carry out immigration enforcement during routine policing, including traffic stops, rather than limiting their role to people already in local custody. FWD.us estimates that more than 29,000 officers in 30 states are now deputized, more than twice ICE’s own deportation officer workforce. Arrests involving 287(g) officers increased from just over 1,000 in August 2025 to more than 6,600 in July 2026, following the introduction of federal financial incentives. Participating agencies are eligible for an estimated $2 billion in payments through fiscal year 2026, including reimbursements for personnel and equipment. DHS maintains that the partnerships are a critical tool for addressing crime and unlawful immigration.

The expansion is bringing immigration enforcement into everyday encounters while straining relationships between police and the communities they serve. In Ingram, Texas, police recorded 194 immigration-related incidents by August, a number equivalent to roughly 10 percent of the town’s population, although officials could not say whether every transfer to ICE resulted in deportation. Residents and business owners described family separations, lost workers and delays in flood recovery, while police denied targeting Latinos. In Florida, wildlife officers’ investigation of alleged fishing violations led to immigration detention, illustrating how the program has expanded beyond traditional police and sheriff’s departments. Yet participation remains uneven: more than 30 South Florida municipalities with their own police departments have not joined, despite state pressure, and only about one-third of those in Miami-Dade and Broward counties have signed agreements. Advocates warn that linking routine policing to immigration enforcement discourages residents from reporting crimes or seeking help, undermining the cooperation local agencies need to protect public safety.

Tennessee Law Blocks Driver’s License Renewals for DACA Recipients and Work Permit Holders

Tennessee has stopped accepting employment authorization documents as sufficient proof of eligibility for temporary driver’s licenses, leaving Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients and other immigrants with federal work permits unable to obtain or renew licenses. The Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security attributes the change to a 2025 law requiring applicants to demonstrate a specific period of federally authorized stay. Although the law took effect January 1, attorneys and advocates say denials emerged in recent months, with reports increasing in early October. The department says DACA does not confer lawful immigration status and a work permit alone does not establish the period of authorized stay required by state law. Employment authorization cards remained on the state’s list of acceptable documents as recently as August but had been removed by September.

The change could affect approximately 6,000 DACA recipients in Tennessee, along with other work-authorized immigrants, including some people with pending asylum applications. Attorneys say none of the alternative documents now accepted for temporary licenses are available to DACA recipients and several other affected groups. The National Immigration Law Center disputes the state’s interpretation, arguing that Tennessee law leaves the determination of authorized presence to the federal government. Advocates warn that losing the ability to drive legally threatens residents’ access to work, school and medical care, while driving without a license could expose them to arrest and possible immigration enforcement. Governor Bill Lee said on October 28 that he had only recently learned of the change and was reviewing whether the interaction between state and federal law had created “unintended consequences” and whether changes were needed.

BILLS INTRODUCED AND CONSIDERED

H.R. 10943

To amend the William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008 to direct the Secretary of Health and Human Services to provide counsel for unaccompanied alien children in immigration proceedings, and for other purposes

text:
CHICAGO (AP) - Three people detained at an Indiana immigration facility known as the “Speedway Slammer” say detainees languish in solitary confinement for weeks, are denied essential medical treatment and are subjected to abuse and racial slurs by facility officials.

The detainees alleged in a lawsuit filed Thursday that conditions at the Miami Detention Center in Bunker Hill, Indiana, are inhumane, and officials’ neglect has created a “dangerous medical crisis,” according to a copy obtained by The Associated Press.

The American Civil Liberties Union filed the lawsuit in federal court in the Northern District of Indiana.

The AP has previously reported on medical neglect, dangerous conditions and human rights abuses at immigration detention facilities across the country. At least 37 people have died in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody this fiscal year, the most in the agency’s history, according to the Migration Policy Institute.

Two people have died at the Indiana facility this year — Tuan Van Bui, a 55-year-old Vietnamese man, and Lorth Sim, a 59-year-old Cambodian man. Sim’s son sued ICE in August saying it withheld information about his father’s death.

The Miami Detention Center, around 60 miles (100 kilometers) north of Indianapolis, was a maximum security prison before the Trump administration converted it into an immigration detention facility last year. As a prison, it had a record of inhumane conditions, violence and inmate deaths.

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately return a request for comment on the allegations in the lawsuit.

None of the three detainees in the lawsuit have ever been convicted of a crime in the U.S., according to the complaint. While the Trump administration has said its immigration crackdown is focused on immigrants with criminal records, recent data shows most of those arrested have no criminal convictions.

The plaintiffs say officials deny detainees medical treatment for severe conditions, leaving some in agony and crisis.

Cynthia Acevedo, a Guatemalan national arrested by ICE in July, suffered from multiple seizures a week after officers at the facility switched her to a medication less effective at treating her epilepsy, and officials often failed to give it to her regularly, according to her attorneys. She also alleges she was sexually assaulted soon after arriving at the facility, and that officials waited days to take her report and never provided her with a rape kit, HIV test or medication.

A man who could barely walk due to inflamed leg wounds also received no care despite multiple requests for help, according to the complaint.

Officials at the facility use “abusive forms of punishment” on detainees and “excessive force bordering on torture,” attorneys wrote in the complaint. State staff direct racial slurs at detainees, and have told them to go back to their country and referred to them as a “plague,” they added.

Sergei Vasenin, a Ukrainian-born man who has been detained in the facility for more than a year, was once thrown in solitary confinement for around nine weeks, according to the complaint. He “spent up to 23 to 24 hours per day in a tiny, frigid cell,” his lawyers wrote. Vasenin talked out loud to himself “to stay sane” and contemplated suicide multiple times, they added.

Recently, one man attempted suicide after other detainees “begged” officers to help him for days, the complaint said. Officers instead locked him in a cell and failed to remove a cable that he then used to hang himself.

Detainees are held in cells “smaller than an average parking space” with one small window slit, according to a description and image included in the complaint. Solitary confinement cells are so cold that some people stuff toilet paper in the vents to try to staunch the frigid air. Detainees are allowed to leave to shower “every few days,” the complaint said.

Kemoye Muslar, the third plaintiff in the lawsuit, alleged his cell flooded with sewage water for three days, which he spent trying not to “slip and fall into human waste,” his attorneys wrote. They said that staff wear masks to keep out the smell of blood and feces on the floor and clogged toilets.

WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) – President Donald Trump’s administration plans to deport some Afghan immigrants to Afghanistan, a US official and a coalition of veterans and advocacy groups said on Friday.

• Many facing removal fled Afghanistan after the 2021 Taliban takeover and US withdrawal, said Shawn VanDiver, head of #AfghanEvac.

• Some facing deportation are “brothers and sons of men who served alongside US forces, families the Taliban already has every reason to target,” VanDiver added.

• Over 150 Afghan immigrants are expected to be deported, the New York Times reported, in one of the largest single expulsions of Afghans.

• The administration detained dozens of Afghan immigrants in Louisiana and plans to deport them, the newspaper said, adding the first flight is expected as soon as Monday.

• A US official said deportations would be via Pakistan. Washington cannot directly arrange deportations to Afghanistan as it lacks diplomatic ties with the Taliban.

• Trump says his immigration crackdown and deportation drive aim to improve domestic security.

• Rights advocates say the crackdown violates due process and free speech and has created an unsafe environment for minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

• The Homeland Security Department said it would not confirm future removal operations, citing operational security.

• VanDiver urged Congress to pass legislation granting Afghans in the US temporary protected status to protect them from deportation.

• Pakistan has expelled over 2 million Afghan nationals to Afghanistan since 2023.

text:
A Cuban pastor's son detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is awaiting a hearing in his deportation case in the coming weeks after an immigration judge scheduled a new court date, according to the United Kingdom-based Christian Solidarity Worldwide.

Daniel Arcadis Solano Jaume recently appeared before an immigration judge, who set another hearing for two weeks later, CSW told The Christian Post.

The development comes as the Christian advocacy organization disputes allegations made by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security concerning Solano Jaume's immigration history and criminal charges.

Solano Jaume, 19, was detained by ICE on June 25 in Florida after he was stopped by police for a traffic violation. He was later transferred to the Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego, California.

CSW has warned that deportation to Cuba could put him at risk of imprisonment and further persecution because of his family's history of religious persecution in the communist country.

In a statement to CP, a DHS spokesperson said ICE arrested Solano Jaume on June 25, 2026, describing him as a "criminal illegal alien from Cuba" who had been charged with three counts of felony drug possession.

The spokesperson also alleged that Solano Jaume entered the United States illegally through Nogales, Arizona, on Aug. 30, 2023, and was released into the country by the Biden administration.

"All of his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process," the spokesperson said, adding that Solano Jaume would remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

The DHS spokesperson also emphasized that a pending application for immigration benefits does not confer legal status in the United States.

"Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, if you break the law, you will face the consequences," the spokesperson added. "Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S."

CSW disputed both the criminal allegations and the department's characterization of Solano Jaume's entry into the country. The organization acknowledged that Solano Jaume was initially charged with three felony drug offenses but said a judge subsequently dismissed the charges.

“As such, they should not be used as legal grounds or any kind of justification for deportation. His father reiterates that Daniel has a clean record and the only thing pending is the traffic violation,” a CSW spokesperson told CP.

The spokesperson also rejected the allegation that Solano Jaume entered the United States illegally, explaining that a legal appointment process was available at the time for Cubans and Nicaraguans seeking entry from Mexico.

Under the process, applicants could apply online while in Mexico to schedule an appointment at a U.S. border crossing, where their eligibility to enter the country would be reviewed.

“The family followed this process, went to Mexico, kept their appointment in Nogales, Arizona and were admitted into the US by Border Patrol, as stated in our press release. Daniel was underage and entered with his parents and sister,” the CSW spokesperson stated. “They then began the process, while Daniel was still underage, of registering for residency one year later under the Cuban Adjustment Act, which, at the time, was also the typical legal route for Cubans.”

“We were in regular communication with the family from their departure from Cuba, visited with them in Mexico after they arrived there, and were in daily contact with them in the run-up to and after their entry into the US,” the spokesperson added.

Solano Jaume's father, the Rev. Arcadis Solano Silvera, was a Baptist pastor in Santiago de Cuba and a member of the Baptist Convention of Eastern Cuba. According to CSW, Cuban authorities targeted him for years, threatening to close or destroy his church and subjecting him to harassment and questioning by State Security.

In March 2023, members of Cuba's Revolutionary Armed Forces reportedly visited the family's home seeking to register Solano Jaume for military service. He was 15 at the time, while Cuban law sets 17 as the minimum age for compulsory military service.

Solano Silvera is a hospice chaplain who has also served as an adjunct professor with B. H. Carroll Theological Seminary and East Texas Baptist University.

"We are grateful for every prayer, expression of solidarity, and practical act of support," the father said in a statement.

"Our hope is that Daniel's situation will be evaluated fairly, that his dignity and health will be protected, and that he will be able to return to his family and continue building his future. Above all, we continue trusting God as our attorneys pursue every appropriate legal avenue."

text:
US lawmakers are urgently demanding that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) disclose how many pregnant immigrants have experienced miscarriages, stillbirths and pregnancy-related hospitalizations while in the its custody, after the agency admitted it lost count last year.

US representatives sent the request following a recent Guardian investigation revealing that the Trump administration is detaining a record number of pregnant women and teens, and at the same has lost track of how many suffered miscarriages.

In a letter sent this month to ICE’s acting director, David Venturella, Democratic representatives Brittany Pettersen, Joyce Beatty and Robin Kelly also asked the immigration enforcement agency to explain what – if any – steps have been taken to recover any missing data about these cases.

Government documents obtained by the Guardian found that ICE had placed more pregnant immigrants in detention last fall and winter than at any time over the previous year. The agency recorded 18 miscarriages during the first nine months of the Trump administration, the documents found, but the agency has no data on miscarriages after 3 October 2025.

Detained pregnant women said that they were struggling to access routine and emergency medical care. Medical experts told the Guardian that lapses in care both during pregnancy and during and after miscarriage could escalate treatable conditions into life-threatening emergencies.

In their letter, the representatives also cite a 2021 directive instructing ICE to wholly avoid detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants “unless release is prohibited by law or exceptional circumstances exist” – and ask the agency to clarify on what grounds it is detaining pregnant immigrants. The directive also requires ICE to closely monitor and document the health of all pregnant people in its custody, and continuously evaluate whether it is medically advisable to keep them detained.

“ICE’s inability to follow agency directives, provide adequate medical care and maintain accurate records of pregnancy-related medical outcomes is unacceptable,” the lawmakers wrote in their letter, which was cosigned by 64 other representatives.

In an interview, Pettersen said it was “deeply concerning” that ICE had failed to account for a full year of pregnancy outcomes. “I’m just devastated for the people who have gone through this, who’ve lost pregnancies unnecessarily, who have been left without the medical care that they need after miscarrying,” she said. “It’s hard to imagine how we are ever going to right these wrongs.”

In internal agency documents, ICE said it had no data on miscarriages because the agency changed medical billing providers in October. The agency’s medical claims processing has been delayed for months. Immigration attorneys and former government officials told said it was odd, but plausible, that ICE was keeping track of miscarriages solely via its medical billing provider.

In response to follow-up questions about its tracking practices after 3 October 2025, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, first said that the agency was tracking miscarriages in monthly reports. But later, the spokesperson confirmed what was in the ICE internal documents – the agency does not have data on miscarriages between October 2025 through June 2026.

The DHS did not confirm to the Guardian whether it had received the letter from Congress members. “Claims that any pregnant detainees are receiving subprime care are FALSE,” an agency spokesperson said.

In their letter, lawmakers asked ICE’s acting director to detail when “ICE leadership first became aware of concerns regarding miscarriage reporting and deficiencies in agency tracking systems”. They gave the agency until 6 November to respond.

Prior to the Guardian’s reporting, the agency had never acknowledged that it had lost count of miscarriages – not even when US senators asked the agency for the data.

The Guardian filed a Freedom of Information Act request and then filed suit in collaboration with the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press to obtain data on the number of pregnant people in ICE detention, and the health outcomes for this population.

The Harris County Sheriff's Office responded to the crash.
